While conquering an empty battlefield allows you to score, it does not trigger the combat cleanup required to heal your units. Units only heal after combat concludes or at the end of the turn (Rule 143.3.b).

question: If I use Sacrifice on my Ekko Recurrent, and my opponent uses Defy to counter, does Ekko still die?
answer:
Yes, your Ekko, Recurrent still dies.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10480 and Rule 357, the process of playing a spell includes paying its costs before the spell is added to the chain and becomes eligible to be countered.

The Sequence:

Announcement: You announce you are playing Sacrifice.

Payment of Costs: You pay the energy cost and the additional cost: killing a friendly Mighty unit (your Ekko, Recurrent). This happens instantly when you play the card.

Finalization: Only after your Ekko is killed and sent to the trash is Sacrifice finalized and placed on the chain.

Reaction: Your opponent plays Defy to counter Sacrifice.

The Result:

Because your Ekko was already killed as a cost to play the spell, it is already in the trash by the time Defy is even played. CR 426.1.c confirms that countering a card does not refund any costs paid to play it, including additional costs. Your Ekko remains in the trash, and your Sacrifice is removed from the chain.

question: If my Aurora Trigger reveals Rengar - Trophy Hunter, can he ambush to an enemy occupied battlefield?
answer:
Yes, if Dazzling Aurora's end-of-turn triggered ability plays Rengar, Trophy Hunter, you can play him to an enemy-occupied battlefield.

The Reasoning

Dazzling Aurora's Trigger: Dazzling Aurora's ability is a triggered ability that plays a unit. When this ability resolves, it provides the instruction to "play" that unit.

Playing from Hidden: When an effect instructs you to "play" a card, you must go through the standard process of Playing a Card (Rule 349).

Rengar's Unique Permission: Rengar, Trophy Hunter has a specific, unique permission: "I can be played to a battlefield where there are enemy units, even if you don't have units there."

Legal Destination: Because Dazzling Aurora instructs you to play the unit, and Rengar provides a valid permission to be played at a battlefield with enemy units, the destination is legal. This is an application of Rule 822.3.a, which notes that "Other effects and permissions may still enable this Unit to be able to be played to the selected location."

Important Timing and State Notes

Reaction Timing: Because an effect is playing Rengar, the action is performed as part of the resolution of Dazzling Aurora's ability.

Attacker/Defender Status: Per the rules for contested battlefields (CR 443.1.a), if you use Dazzling Aurora to play Rengar into a battlefield that is currently contested by your opponent, you will be designated as the Defender.

Summary: You may play Rengar, Trophy Hunter to an enemy-occupied battlefield using Dazzling Aurora’s trigger. This is a legal play because Rengar explicitly grants himself the permission to enter such a location, and the effect provides the necessary instruction to play him.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules, specifically regarding whether play effects bypass standard timing restrictions or the specific card text of the mentioned abilities.

question: If Yi summons Rengar to the battlefield with Ambush when there is 1 unit at the battlefield, will the +2 might from Yi fall off or will the unit retain +2?
answer:
The unit will lose the +2 Might bonus immediately upon Rengar, Trophy Hunter entering the battlefield.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10141 and #3935, Master Yi's ability (from Wuju Bladesman, Starter) is a continuous passive effect with a "While" condition. Continuous effects are checked constantly and update the game state instantaneously. The moment a second friendly unit enters the battlefield, your original unit is no longer "alone" (as defined by Rule 741.1), and the bonus is removed.

Timing Sequence:

Opening State: A unit is defending alone. Master Yi’s continuous effect applies, granting it +2 Might.

Ambush [Reaction]: You play Rengar, Trophy Hunter using the Ambush keyword. This is a [Reaction] that is added to the chain.

Resolution: The chain resolves, and Rengar enters the battlefield.

State Update: The instant Rengar enters the battlefield, the "While" condition for Master Yi’s passive is no longer met. The +2 Might bonus is removed immediately, regardless of what other items may still be on the chain or the fact that this occurred during a reaction.

This interaction is distinct from triggered abilities (which check conditions only at the moment they trigger and are placed on the chain); because Master Yi’s ability is a continuous passive effect, it does not "snapshot" and instead recalculates as soon as the board state changes.

question: If my Glasc Mixologist dies when the opponent conquers my battlefield, am I able to play a unit to that battlefield after it is conquered via Glasc Mixologist deathknell?
answer:
Yes, you can play a unit from your Deathknell ability to the battlefield, provided the ability resolves before the battlefield is officially conquered.

According to the rules and FAQs governing Deathknell and battlefield control, your ability to play a unit depends on the timing of the Deathknell trigger relative to the conquest.

The Ruling

While Deathknell triggers are added to the chain as pending items before a unit is moved to the trash (Rule 734.1.d.2 / 383.2.c.3), Deathknell abilities resolve before a player establishes control and conquers a battlefield. As the defender, you maintain control of the battlefield while the Deathknell is on the chain. Because the resolution of the Deathknell effect occurs before the conclusion of combat resolution, you have the permission to play a unit there, which can prevent the opponent from successfully conquering the battlefield.

Sequence of Events

Combat Damage: Damage is dealt; the unit takes lethal damage and dies.

Deathknell Trigger: The ability triggers and is added to the chain as a pending item.

Deathknell Resolution: The Deathknell resolves. You play a unit from your trash to the battlefield, effectively preventing the opponent from successfully conquering it.

Combat Resolution (Control Shift): The combat resolution steps (CR 463) process. Since the unit was played via Deathknell, the requirements for conquest are no longer met.

Key Clarification

Ongoing Combat: The Deathknell triggers just before the unit is placed in the trash (Rule 383.2.c.3). Because control of a battlefield cannot be lost while items are on the chain (Rule 187.4.c), you can resolve the Deathknell to play a unit to that battlefield, preventing the opponent from successfully conquering it.

Conquered Battlefields: Once the battlefield has already been conquered, the combat resolution is complete, and control has shifted. You cannot play a unit to an opponent's battlefield via Deathknell after control has been lost.

This interpretation is based on the interaction between Rule 187.4.c (control during chain items) and the established rulings in RiftJudge FAQ #7489, #9149, #10335, and #10444, which clarify that Deathknell resolves prior to the establishment of control and final conquest.

question: Does Mirror Image copy Gear?
answer:
No, Mirror Image does not copy Gear.

According to the official rules on copy effects (Patch Notes - 2026-03-30) and confirmed by multiple RiftJudge FAQs (e.g., #10239, #11044), copy effects only copy the "copyable traits" of a game object, which are its printed characteristics (such as Might) and its Rules Text.

Gear is a separate game object attached to a unit; it is not part of a unit’s printed or copyable traits. Therefore, when you use Mirror Image on a unit with attached Gear, the resulting Reflection token enters the board without that Gear.

question: Does Tide Turner have to choose targets to get put on the chain?
answer:
Yes, Tide Turner must choose a target to put its "When you play me" ability on the chain.

According to FAQ 6775 and FAQ 7573, you must choose targets during the activation of the ability (when the trigger is placed on the chain) before opponents can react. If you choose to use the "you may" ability, the target must be declared at the moment the trigger is initiated.

Key Clarifications:

Trigger Category: As defined in Rule 383.4.a and 383.4.a.1, Tide Turner’s "When you play me" ability is a Play Effect.

Timing of Choices: Contrary to general triggered abilities, FAQ 6775 specifies that for Tide Turner, you choose required targets as part of the activation process, occurring when the trigger is placed on the chain.

Ability Initiation: Because the ability is phrased as "you may," it is optional. You may choose to play Tide Turner without placing the triggered ability on the chain; however, if you do choose to activate it, you must declare the target immediately upon placing it on the chain.

Note: This ruling is based on the provided FAQs, which override general rule interpretations regarding the timing of target selection for this specific unit.

question: If Bellow Breath targets a unit at a location and the unit changes location, what happens to the unit?
answer:
When Bellows Breath targets a unit and that unit changes its location before the spell resolves, the unit is still tracked by the spell and will be dealt damage, provided it remains a legal target.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #7422 and FAQ #9018, the "same location" requirement is a targeting restriction for playing the spell, not a requirement for its resolution.

Here is what happens based on the situation:

Tracking: When you play Bellows Breath, you choose up to three units at the same location. These targets are "locked in." If a target moves to a different location (e.g., to a different battlefield or back to base) before the spell resolves, the spell continues to target that unit at its new location.

Resolution and Location: Because Bellows Breath requires the targets to be at the same location to be played, but allows for movement after playing, the resolution follows these rules:

If all your originally targeted units end up at the same new location (e.g., you moved all three together), they will all be dealt 1 damage.

If the targeted units are now split across different locations, you must choose one location where at least one of your originally targeted units is currently present. You then deal 1 damage only to the targeted units at that chosen location. Any targeted units not at that chosen location will not take damage.

No Retargeting: You cannot choose new units to replace the ones that moved. You are limited to the specific units you originally targeted.

Key Rule References:

Core Rule 359.3.e.1: "The spell resolves even if some or all of its targets are illegal."

RiftJudge FAQ #7422: "The 'same location' requirement is a targeting restriction, not a resolution requirement."

Note: This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of targeting and the referenced FAQs. As noted in the retrieved context, this logic applies to spells with group location restrictions like Bellows Breath.

question: Can I react with guards hidden at a battlefield after Downwell resolves?
answer:
The answer to your question depends on whether any other triggered abilities were generated by Downwell's resolution.

Based on the rules and RiftJudge FAQ #10642, here is the breakdown of your situation:

The Short Answer

You cannot react with a hidden card immediately after Downwell resolves if Downwell was the only thing on the chain. If the chain becomes empty after Downwell resolves, the game state returns to "Open." Because hidden cards are discarded during the cleanup step if the battlefield becomes uncontrolled (per RiftJudge FAQ #8494), you will lose your hidden Guards! before you have an opportunity to play them.

However, if Downwell's resolution triggers another effect (like a "When this leaves the board" trigger), that trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item, keeping the state "Closed." You can then use your hidden card to react to that triggered ability.

The Sequence

If Downwell resolves with no other triggers:

Downwell resolves, returning all units and gear to hands.

Downwell finishes resolving. The chain is now empty (the game is in an Open State).

Cleanup occurs: Because there are no units at the battlefield, it becomes uncontrolled. Your hidden Guards! are moved to your trash (CR 323.6.a and RiftJudge FAQ #8494).

If Downwell resolves and generates an additional trigger:

Downwell resolves, returning all units and gear to hands.

A "When this leaves the board" trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item.

Because an item is on the chain, the state is Closed (Rule 187.4.c).

You can now play your hidden Guards! as a [Reaction] to that triggered ability.

Important Constraints

Targeting: Per CR 811.1.d.5 and RiftJudge FAQ #9757, because you are playing Guards! from a hidden position, the Sand Soldier token must be played at the same battlefield where the Guards! card was hidden.

Timing: You cannot play a card from "Hidden" on the same turn you hid it (RiftJudge FAQ #9904).

Standard Moves: You cannot react to the loss of a unit if it was moved by a "Standard Move," as that does not use the chain and does not create a reaction window.

question: When I kill Overzealous Fan, would I need to pay a deflect cost for the enemy unit?
answer:
Yes, you must pay the Deflect cost if you choose to target an enemy unit that has the Deflect keyword with Overzealous Fan's ability.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8505 and FAQ #8677, the interaction works as follows:

Triggering: When Overzealous Fan gains the Defender designation, its ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Targeting: You must choose the target (the attacking unit you intend to move) at the time you place the ability on the chain.

Deflect Cost: Because the ability chooses a unit, if that unit has Deflect, you are required to pay the Deflect cost at the time you place the ability on the chain.

Resolution: If you successfully pay the cost and place the ability on the chain, the ability resolves later. Only at the moment of resolution do you make the choice of whether to "kill" the Overzealous Fan to complete the effect (this is a cost-within-instruction).

Summary of Key Points:

Targeting vs. Cost: The targeting (which requires paying Deflect) happens when the ability is placed on the chain. The "kill me" portion is a cost-within-instruction that is only paid upon resolution.

Mandatory Cost: If you cannot pay the Deflect cost, you cannot legally choose that unit as a target for the ability.

question: I attack an Abandoned Hall battlefield with my sole Irelia Fervent. I play En Garde and choose her to get +2 might. Since En Garde chooses her, she gets an additional +1 might. Now that I've played a spell, Abandoned Hall allows me to give a unit an additional +1 might, and I choose Irelia for it. Does this mean that I can give her an additional +1 might for choosing her with Abandoned Hall's ability? If I calculate right, she gets +5 might in total.
answer:
To determine Irelia, Fervent's total Might, we must break down the sequence of events step-by-step.

The Sequence

Attack: You attack the Abandoned Hall battlefield with Irelia.

Play En Garde: You play En Garde (an [ACTION] or [REACTION]) and target Irelia.

Trigger: Choosing Irelia with En Garde triggers her ability ("When you choose... me, give me +1 [S]").

Chain: The chain consists of [Irelia’s ability (Top)] -> [En Garde (Bottom)].

Resolution:

Irelia's Ability Resolves: She gains +1 Might.

En Garde Resolves: It grants its +1 Might, plus the additional +1 Might for being the only unit there (+2 total).

Running Total: Irelia (4 base) + 1 (Ability) + 2 (Spell) = 7 Might.

Abandoned Hall Trigger: After En Garde finishes resolving, the Abandoned Hall triggered ability triggers.

You place the Abandoned Hall ability on the chain. You choose Irelia as the target to receive +1 Might.

Trigger: Choosing Irelia with the Abandoned Hall ability triggers her ability again (+1 [S]).

Chain: [Irelia’s ability (Top)] -> [Abandoned Hall ability (Bottom)].

Final Resolution:

Irelia's Ability Resolves: She gains +1 Might.

Abandoned Hall Ability Resolves: She gains +1 Might.

Final Total: 7 + 1 + 1 = 9 Might.

Conclusion

Your calculation of +5 Might is incorrect because it does not account for Irelia's base Might or the secondary trigger from the Abandoned Hall ability.

Irelia, Fervent will have a total of 9 Might.

Base: 4

From En Garde sequence: +3 (+1 from her ability, +2 from the spell).

From Abandoned Hall sequence: +2 (+1 from her ability when chosen by the battlefield, +1 from the battlefield itself).

A note on your math: In your prompt, you assumed she gains +5 Might, but that likely ignored her printed base Might of 4. When you "give" a unit Might, it adds to their existing total. Following these steps, she reaches 9 Might total for the turn.

This interpretation is based on the interaction of Triggered Abilities and the LIFO resolution of the chain. Per RiftJudge FAQ #10297, choosing a unit via an ability like Abandoned Hall's triggers Irelia, Fervent's ability.

question: If my opponent gusts a Sprite and I have Viktor Leader out, does it spawn a Recruit token at base?
answer:
No, Viktor, Leader will not spawn a recruit token at your base if a Sprite is returned to your hand by Gust.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ #738:

Ruling: "The sprite does not count as dying for Viktor Leader's effect. The sprite token is returned to hand and then ceases to exist, but this is not considered dying by a regular method."

Sequence:

Your opponent plays Gust targeting your Sprite.

Gust resolves and returns the Sprite token to your hand.

Upon reaching your hand, the token ceases to exist.

Because the token did not "die" (a regular method for a unit to leave the board and enter the trash), Viktor, Leader's triggered ability does not trigger.

question: If I use Irresistable Faefolk to target and move a unit, can I react to my own Faefolk action before it resolves?
answer:
Yes, you can play a [Reaction] to the chain after you have placed the triggered ability of Irresistible Faefolk onto it, but before that ability resolves.

The Reasoning

According to the Chain Rules and Section 327 (referenced in the context), triggered abilities such as "When I move to a battlefield..." behave like activated abilities and are placed on the chain.

When you move Irresistible Faefolk to a battlefield, its ability triggers. You (as the controller) choose to place this ability on the chain. Once this ability is on the chain, the game enters a "Closed State" (defined in Rule 331.1 as occurring when a chain exists). During a Closed State, players with priority have the opportunity to play [Reaction] cards to add to that chain before it resolves.

Sequence of Events

Move: You move Irresistible Faefolk to a battlefield.

Trigger: The "When I move to a battlefield..." ability triggers. You place it on the chain.

Chain State (Closed): The chain now contains the Irresistible Faefolk trigger.

Reaction: You (or your opponent) have the opportunity to play a [Reaction] card, adding it to the top of the chain.

Resolution: The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order. Any [Reaction] you played will resolve first, followed by the Irresistible Faefolk trigger.

As noted in RiftJudge FAQ #11094 and #10923, the movement or removal of the source of a trigger (like the Faefolk) after it has been placed on the chain does not invalidate the trigger. It remains on the chain and will resolve successfully, referencing the location where it originally arrived.

question: Does Abandon Hall count as a choose trigger?
answer:
Yes, the ability on Abandoned Hall involves "choosing" a unit, and this selection qualifies as a "choose" event for the purpose of triggering other abilities.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10297, when you resolve the triggered ability from Abandoned Hall and select a unit to receive the +1 Might, you are actively choosing that unit. Therefore, if a card has an ability that triggers "when you choose me" (like Irelia, Fervent), it will trigger when selected by Abandoned Hall's effect.

This is because the requirement to "give a unit they control here +1 Might" forces the player to make an active, manual choice from among the available units at that battlefield, rather than the game programmatically selecting the unit.

question: If I create a token of Ekko Recurrent with Leblanc, does the Dethknell trigger if the token dies?
answer:
Yes, the Deathknell ability on a Reflection token that has become a copy of Ekko, Recurrent will trigger upon the token's death, though it will ultimately fail to resolve its effect.

The Breakdown

Ability Inheritance: When a Reflection token becomes a copy of another unit, it gains the copyable traits of that unit, including its Rules Text. This is established by the definition of copy effects (Patch Notes 2026-03-30), which states that copyable traits include printed rules text. Therefore, the token gains Ekko, Recurrent's Deathknell ability.

Triggering: According to Rule 808.1, Deathknell triggers when a permanent is killed and sent to the trash. As a valid game object and unit (Rule 182.1), the Reflection token can trigger Deathknell when it is killed.

Resolution Failure: While the ability triggers and enters the chain (Rule 808.1.d.2), it will fail to resolve. Ekko, Recurrent’s Deathknell effect requires you to "Recycle me" as a cost to ready your runes. According to Rule 183.1, tokens cease to exist immediately upon entering the trash. Because the token no longer exists in the trash, it cannot be recycled. Consequently, the mandatory cost cannot be paid, and the effect fails (RiftJudge FAQ #9947).

Why the confusion occurred previously

To clarify the rules:

Ability Inheritance: Tokens gain the abilities of the copied unit because those abilities are part of the copied unit's "copyable traits" (printed rules text). This is distinct from Rule 375, which governs how replacement effects inherit modifications (like "exhausted" or "temporary" status) rather than granting a token the target's base rules text.

Triggering vs. Resolving: The Deathknell trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item at the moment of death (Rule 808.1.d.2), so the ability does successfully enter the chain. However, the resolution of that ability is subject to the game state at the time of resolution, and the inability to pay the mandatory "recycle me" cost causes it to fail.

question: What does taking damage for a unit in Riftbound mean?
answer:
In Riftbound, "taking damage" refers to the process of marking a specific value of damage on a unit. Based on the official rules and FAQs, here is the breakdown of what this means:

1. Damage vs. Might

It is important to distinguish between damage and a unit's Might:

Might represents both a unit's attack power and its maximum damage capacity. Dealing damage does not reduce a unit's Might.

A damaged unit is defined as any unit that has damage counters currently marked on it (Rule 142). Even if a unit has been buffed to have higher Might, it is still considered "damaged" if it has any damage counters on it.

2. The Mechanics of Taking Damage

Marking Damage: When a spell, ability, or combat action deals damage, that amount is marked on the unit (CR 418.1.b).

Tracking: Damage is tracked per-unit using tokens, dice, or other markers. It is not a "game object" itself, but rather a value assigned to the unit (Rule 142).

Lethal Damage: Damage tracks how close a unit is to being killed. If a unit has non-zero damage marked on it that is equal to or greater than its Might, the unit is considered to have "lethal damage" and will be killed during the cleanup step (CR 143.2.b; CR 323.4.3b).

3. When is Damage Healed?

Damage is not permanent. All damage marked on units is cleared (healed) at two specific times:

At the end of each round (end of combat).

At the end of each player's turn (Rule 143.3.b).

Key Nuance: Combat Damage

During the Combat Damage Step, players do not "deal" damage immediately. Instead, they first assign damage to enemy units. Damage is only actually "dealt" (marked on the units) once all assignments are complete and both players have finished assigning their units' total Might.

Source: Core CR 142, 143, 418, 462; RiftJudge FAQ #2642.

question: If a Stellacorn enters a battlefield that has no enemy presence, a showdown begins. Opponent uses a Wages into the Stellacorn. Stellacorn gets en garde to survive. Showdown ends, does it heal, or because there was no combat does it not heal?
answer:
To determine if your unit heals in this scenario, we must look at how Showdowns and combat resolution function.

The Short Answer

No, your Stellacorn will not heal.

The Rules Breakdown

Non-Combat Showdown: Since there was no enemy presence on the battlefield when your Stellacorn moved there, this is a Non-Combat Showdown (CR 461.2).

Lack of Combat Cleanup: Healing in Riftbound—specifically the type of automatic healing you are asking about—is a feature of the Combat Special Cleanup (CR 463.1.a), which occurs only during the Resolution Step of a combat showdown.

Ending a Non-Combat Showdown: Because there was no combat ongoing, the Showdown concludes under Rule 348.2. When a Non-Combat Showdown ends, the game performs a standard cleanup, which does not include the "Heal all units" step found in combat resolution.

Summary

En Garde: Your spell resolves as expected, granting your Stellacorn the temporary Might bonus to survive the damage dealt by your opponent's effect.

Healing: Because this was a Non-Combat Showdown, the "Combat Special Cleanup" (which contains the healing effect) is never invoked. Your Stellacorn remains on the board with any damage it has marked on it (provided that damage does not equal or exceed its current Might).

This is my interpretation based on the rules for combat versus non-combat showdowns and their respective cleanup procedures. No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction.

question: If my opponent plays Deadly Flourish and I react with Hidden Blade having the same target, does he get the gold token?
answer:
Ruling: Your opponent does not get the Gold gear token

To determine if your opponent gets the Gold gear token, we must follow the Showdown Timing Flowchart and the mechanics of resolution provided in the Core Rules.

The Sequence of Events

Opponent plays Deadly Flourish: They play it targeting an enemy unit at a battlefield. It enters the chain and the state becomes CLOSED.

You react with Hidden Blade: You flip your Hidden Blade (which gains [Reaction] timing) to target the same unit. It is added to the top of the chain.

Chain Resolution (LIFO):

Hidden Blade resolves: The instruction is to "Kill a unit at a battlefield." The target unit is killed and moved to its owner's Trash.

Deadly Flourish attempts to resolve:

The first instruction ("Deal 3 to an enemy unit") cannot be executed because the unit is no longer on the board. Per Rule 359.3.e.6, this impossible instruction is ignored.

The second instruction ("When it dies this turn, play a Gold gear token exhausted") fails to resolve.

Reasoning

According to Rule 359.3.e.12 and FAQ #3700, when a target ceases to exist on the board or moves to a non-board zone (like the Trash), it is treated as having "null" characteristics. Because Deadly Flourish requires that unit to have been the one that died to trigger the generation of the Gold gear token, the spell cannot establish the "when it dies" condition once the unit is no longer a valid game object that Deadly Flourish can track.

As established in FAQ #3700 and FAQ #10423, if a unit targeted by a spell is killed or removed from the battlefield by another effect before the original spell resolves, the spell fails to "see" that unit's death for the purpose of its own triggered instructions. Because the target was killed by your Hidden Blade rather than the damage from Deadly Flourish, the "when it dies" trigger fails to find its source, and the token is not created.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules, as the specific text of Deadly Flourish regarding a Gold gear token was not present in the provided context.

question: Ok, I attack a battlefield with Azir, Sovereign. When he attacks, I put his trigger on the stack with the intention to move my tokens from the other battlefield to this one. My opponent reacts with Star Crossed targeting my Azir. Do the tokens stay where they are?
answer:
Yes, the tokens stay where they are.

Here is the step-by-step breakdown of how this interaction resolves based on the rules for [Reaction] timing and the targeting logic of Azir, Sovereign:

The Sequence

Attack Declaration: You attack a battlefield with Azir, Sovereign. His "When I attack" ability triggers and is placed on the chain. You choose which token units to move as part of placing this trigger.

Reaction: Your opponent plays Star-Crossed in response, targeting Azir, Sovereign. Star-Crossed is placed on the chain above Azir’s trigger.

Resolution (LIFO): The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out order:

Star-Crossed resolves first: It returns your Azir, Sovereign to your hand.

Azir's trigger attempts to resolve: When Azir’s trigger finally tries to resolve, it checks for "this battlefield" to move the tokens to. Because Azir has been returned to your hand, he is no longer present on any battlefield. As established in RiftJudge FAQ #2127, if Azir is removed (e.g., returned to hand, sent to base, or killed) in response to his trigger, the ability whiffs because "this battlefield" cannot be identified.

Conclusion

Because the ability whiffs, the instruction to move your tokens is never executed. The token units remain at their original location.

This is my interpretation based on Rule 359.3.f (Reference to "here") and the established Azir, Sovereign FAQ (ID 2127). No official FAQ exists for the specific interaction of Star-Crossed returning Azir to hand, but it follows the same logic as removing him via other effects.

question: Can you play Beast Below with no friendly units?
answer:
Yes, you can play Beast Below even if you do not control any other friendly units.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ (#466, #9370, #9889):

Playing the Unit: You are permitted to play Beast Below as a unit even if you do not control another friendly unit.

Triggered Ability: Its "When you play me" ability requires you to target another friendly unit and an enemy unit. Because valid targets must exist for all required targets to place an object on the chain, if you do not control another friendly unit, you simply do not put the triggered ability on the chain.

Result: The unit enters the battlefield normally, and the ability—which would have returned units to their owners' hands—never triggers or enters the chain, so your unit remains on the battlefield.

question: If I void assault a unit to a battlefield but they react on that battlefield to the void assault with an Emperor's Divide, what happens?
answer:
When you play Void Assault and your opponent reacts with Emperor's Divide, the sequence of events depends on the specific targeting of each card and the nature of the instructions.

1. Targeting and the Chain

Void Assault targets one friendly unit and one enemy unit. Per FAQ #8796, choosing these units creates a lasting targeting relationship between the spell and those units.

Emperor's Divide is played in reaction, placing it on top of the chain.

2. Resolution (LIFO)

Emperor's Divide Resolves: It moves the friendly units of the player who cast it from the battlefield to their owner's base.

Void Assault Resolves: It attempts to execute its instructions in order ("Move a friendly unit, then move an enemy unit").

First Instruction: It moves the friendly unit targeted by Void Assault. Since Emperor's Divide (played by the opponent) only affects their own units, your targeted friendly unit remains on the battlefield. Void Assault successfully moves it to the designated battlefield.

Second Instruction: It moves the targeted enemy unit. If that unit was moved to the base by Emperor's Divide, the targeting relationship is maintained because the unit remains on the board (a valid game object). Void Assault will move that enemy unit from the base to the battlefield.

Conclusion

Void Assault does not fizzle or fail. It continues to act upon its targets as they exist at the time of resolution, effectively moving them to the destination battlefield regardless of whether they were displaced by Emperor's Divide.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: Does Lotus Trap have to be used before a damage spell for its effect to apply, or can you use it after a damage spell to double its damage?
answer:
You can use Lotus Trap after a damage spell has been played and is already on the chain. Because Lotus Trap is a [Reaction] spell that creates a replacement effect, it does not need to be played before the damage spell; it only needs to resolve before the damage spell executes its "Deal" instruction.

Why this works:

LIFO Resolution: When multiple items are on the chain, they resolve in Last-In, First-Out order. By playing Lotus Trap after a damage spell, Lotus Trap will be at the top of the chain and will resolve first.

Replacement Effect: Once Lotus Trap resolves, it creates a continuous replacement effect that lasts for the remainder of the turn. When the damage spell subsequently resolves, the game engine checks for active replacement effects as the "Deal" action is about to occur. Since Lotus Trap is already active, it will double that incoming damage.

Recommended Sequencing

To ensure your damage spell is doubled, use this flow:

Play your damage spell (in an OPEN state). It goes on the chain.

Play Lotus Trap as a [Reaction], targeting the same unit. It goes on top of the damage spell.

Chain Resolution:

Lotus Trap resolves first, applying its doubling effect to the target.

The damage spell resolves second. When it attempts to deal damage, the doubling effect is already active and modifies the damage accordingly.

This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of replacement effects and LIFO resolution. This interaction is also supported by RiftJudge FAQ #10844.

question: Can I react to Bewitching Spirit discard?
answer:
No, you cannot react to the discard effect of Bewitching Spirit specifically.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10064, here is why:

Triggered Ability: When you play Bewitching Spirit, it enters the board (which does not use the chain). Its "When you play me" triggered ability then goes on the chain.

Response Window: You can react to the triggered ability itself using a Reaction card (as confirmed by RiftJudge FAQ #9894).

The Discard: When that triggered ability resolves, it instructs your opponent to discard a card. The discard is a game action that happens during the resolution of that ability.

No Interaction: Because discarding a card is not "playing" a card, and the card being discarded does not trigger an ability upon being discarded, your opponent cannot respond to the act of discarding. The card simply moves from the hand to the trash.

In summary: You can play a Reaction card to try to stop the Bewitching Spirit ability from resolving (e.g., by countering the ability if a card allows), but if the ability resolves, the discard happens immediately as part of that effect, and no further responses are possible during the discard process itself.

question: If I sacrifice my Riftherald and don't have hand cards after sacrifice, what resolves first: sacrifice effect or Riftherald play effect?
answer:
Resolution Order: Rift Herald and Sacrifice

When playing Sacrifice, its additional cost requires you to kill a friendly [Mighty] unit. If you choose Rift Herald, its Deathknell ability triggers. Because triggered abilities are placed on the chain immediately after the cost that triggered them is paid, the Deathknell effect is placed on the chain after the Sacrifice spell has been announced but before the play process is finalized. Consequently, the Deathknell effect sits on top of Sacrifice.

The chain resolves in LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) order:

Rift Herald’s Deathknell resolves first: You are instructed to play a unit from your hand to your base. If you have no cards in your hand, this instruction cannot be followed and is negated (Rule 359.3.e.11).

Sacrifice resolves second: You draw 2 cards and channel 1 rune.

Sequence of Events

Announcement: You declare you are playing Sacrifice.

Payment of Costs: You pay the additional cost to "kill a friendly [Mighty] unit" by choosing Rift Herald.

Trigger: The Rift Herald's Deathknell ability triggers. Per the rules regarding triggers resulting from the payment of costs, the trigger is placed on the chain on top of the Sacrifice spell.

Finalization: The chain is finalized in the following order (from bottom to top):

[Bottom] Sacrifice

[Top] Rift Herald's Deathknell

Resolution: The items resolve in LIFO order, starting with the Deathknell effect.

Note: This ruling is based on the interaction between Rule 357.2 and the LIFO resolution rules (Rule 340). I could not fully verify the citation of CR 423.1.b against the retrieved rules.

question: If I move my Irresistable Faefolk to a battlefield with a Scuttle Crab and target a second Scuttle Crab in base, then react to the Faefolk trigger with an Ambushed Kha'Zix, does he get the +2 trigger?
answer:
Yes, your Kha’Zix, Mutating Horror will trigger and receive the +2 Might bonus and gain 2 XP.

Reasoning

According to RiftJudge FAQs #10198, #10735, and #10934, the condition "if an enemy unit is alone here" for Kha’Zix’s triggered ability is evaluated at the exact moment he gains the "Attacker" or "Defender" combat designation.

Move & Trigger: When you move your Irresistible Faefolk to the battlefield, it applies the "Contested" status. You are the Attacker.

Kha’Zix Gains Designation: As your Kha’Zix (played via Ambush) enters the battlefield, he gains the "Attacker" designation. At this exact moment, the game checks the battlefield state: "Is an enemy unit alone here?"

Since your opponent currently has only one unit (the Scuttle Crab) present at that battlefield, the condition is satisfied.

Chain Placement: Kha’Zix’s triggered ability is placed on the chain.

Reaction: Your play of Kha’Zix (via Ambush) and any subsequent reactions happen after the trigger condition has already been checked and validated.

Resolution: When the trigger resolves, the state of the battlefield (even if the second Scuttle Crab is moved there by the Irresistible Faefolk trigger) does not retroactively negate the trigger.

Sequence of Events

Move: You move Irresistible Faefolk to the battlefield.

Trigger: Irresistible Faefolk's ability triggers. It is placed on the chain.

Reaction: You play Kha’Zix, Mutating Horror using [Ambush].

Trigger: Kha’Zix gains the "Attacker" designation upon entering. His "alone" condition is checked and found to be True. His ability is placed on the chain.

Resolution (LIFO):

Kha’Zix trigger resolves first (granting +2 Might and 2 XP).

Irresistible Faefolk trigger resolves (moving the second Scuttle Crab to the battlefield).

The condition check for Kha'Zix is not re-evaluated when his ability resolves; as long as the battlefield was "alone" at the moment he gained his combat designation, he successfully gains his bonus.

question: Can you play Rengar, Trophy Hunter to an occupied enemy battlefield with the trigger of Dazzling Aurora?
answer:
Yes, if Dazzling Aurora's end-of-turn triggered ability plays Rengar, Trophy Hunter, you can play him to an enemy-occupied battlefield.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #11132, which provides the official ruling on this interaction:

The Reasoning

Dazzling Aurora's Trigger: Dazzling Aurora's ability is a triggered ability that plays a unit. When this ability resolves, it provides the instruction to "play" that unit.

Playing from Hidden: When an effect instructs you to "play" a card, you must go through the standard process of Playing a Card (Rule 349).

Rengar's Unique Permission: Rengar, Trophy Hunter has a specific, unique permission: "I can be played to a battlefield where there are enemy units, even if you don't have units there."

Legal Destination: Because Dazzling Aurora instructs you to play the unit, and Rengar provides a valid permission to be played at a battlefield with enemy units, the destination is legal. This is an application of Rule 822.3.a, which notes that "Other effects and permissions may still enable this Unit to be able to be played to the selected location."

Important Timing and State Notes

Reaction Timing: Because an effect is playing Rengar, the action is performed as part of the resolution of Dazzling Aurora's ability.

Attacker/Defender Status: Per the rules for contested battlefields (CR 443.1.a), if you use Dazzling Aurora to play Rengar into a battlefield that is currently contested by your opponent, you will be designated as the Defender.

Summary: You may play Rengar, Trophy Hunter to an enemy-occupied battlefield using Dazzling Aurora’s trigger. This is a legal play because Rengar explicitly grants himself the permission to enter such a location, and the effect provides the necessary instruction to play him.

question: If it's my focus, I play an action spell. It resolves, is it still my focus or does it automatically pass?
answer:
After your action spell resolves, your focus automatically passes to your opponent.

According to Rule 346 and the associated FAQ, once the last item on a non-initial chain resolves and the game returns to an Open State, focus automatically passes to the next player.

Here is the breakdown of why this happens:

Opening the Chain: You used your focus to play an [Action] spell, moving the game state from Open to Closed.

Resolution: Once the spell resolves and the chain is empty, the game state returns to Open.

Focus Shift: Per Rule 346, focus passes to your opponent. They now have the opportunity to either start a new chain with their own actions/reactions or pass focus back to you.

The "Initial Chain" Exception:
The only time focus does not pass after a chain resolves is if it was the Initial Chain of the showdown (triggered by "When I Attack" or "When I Defend" abilities). In all other cases, such as the one you described, focus shifts automatically.

Can you play actions back-to-back?
No. You cannot play multiple action spells consecutively. You can only play a second action spell if your opponent receives focus after your first spell resolves and they choose to pass focus back to you without playing anything themselves (FAQ 8470).

question: When a spell played via Fizz, Trickster's ability is countered by Abandon, does the spell go to the hand or get recycled?
answer:
Ruling: The spell is recycled. Both Fizz's recycle effect and Abandon's return-to-hand effect are replacement effects that modify what happens when the spell leaves the chain. Regardless of which order the spell's owner applies them, the spell ends up recycled.

Sequence:

When Abandon counters the spell, it would normally send the spell to the trash, but Abandon replaces this with returning it to hand

Fizz's ability creates a replacement effect that triggers whenever the spell would leave the chain for any reason

The spell's owner chooses the order to apply these replacement effects per Rule 372

If Fizz applies first: the spell is recycled instead of going to trash, making Abandon's hand-return effect no longer applicable

If Abandon applies first: the spell would go to hand, but this still counts as leaving the chain, so Fizz's effect replaces the hand destination with recycling

Nuances:

The order chosen does not matter; both paths result in the spell being recycled

Fizz's replacement effect applies to any instance of the spell leaving the chain, not just specific destinations

question: If I Defiant Dance a 1 unit Might, does it die or does it need to take damage first?
answer:
No, the unit will not die just from being targeted by Defiant Dance. It needs to take at least 1 damage first to be killed.

Here is the breakdown based on the game rules and FAQs:

Might vs. Damage: Reducing a unit's Might to 0 (or even below 0) through an effect like Defiant Dance does not kill it. According to CR 143.2.b and RiftJudge FAQ #21, a unit is only killed if it has non-zero damage marked on it that equals or exceeds its current Might.

The "0 Might" state: If a unit has 0 Might, it is still alive on the board. However, it becomes extremely vulnerable because any amount of damage marked on it will now be lethal.

Combat interaction: As confirmed by RiftJudge FAQ #8787, if your unit has 0 Might, it effectively contributes 0 Might to combat and cannot deal damage. However, it will still be killed if it takes any amount of damage (1 or more) from an opponent's unit during that combat.

In summary: Defiant Dance cannot directly kill a unit. The unit will survive with 0 Might and 0 marked damage, but it will be killed by the game rules as soon as it receives at least 1 damage from another source.

question: If I move onto a battlefield as an attacker, can I then play Janna?
answer:
Yes, you can play Janna, Savior in this situation, provided you follow the placement restriction for units.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ #10964, you can play Janna, Savior in a showdown while you are the attacker, as long as you play her to a battlefield you control.

Important Considerations:

Location Requirement: Units must be played to a battlefield you control (or your base). When you move into an occupied battlefield to initiate combat, you do not control that battlefield (it is contested). Therefore, you cannot play Janna, Savior to the contested battlefield itself.

Legal Placement: You may play Janna, Savior to a different battlefield that you already control, or to your base.

Timing: Because Janna, Savior has the [Reaction] keyword, she can be played at any time, including during the Closed state of a showdown.

Summary: You can play her during your combat showdown as a reaction, but you must place her at a location you control (your base or a different friendly battlefield), not the battlefield currently under combat.

question: If I kill Scuttle Crab with Nidalee, do I draw first or do I show my hand first?
answer:
According to the RiftJudge FAQ #10347, Scuttle Crab's Deathknell ability resolves completely before Nidalee, Cat Form's draw ability triggers.

You do not draw first; the opponent will be forced to reveal their hand for the Deathknell before the game acknowledges that Nidalee has won the combat and triggers her draw ability.

The Sequence of Events (CR 463.1, 463.2):

Combat Cleanup: Scuttle Crab takes lethal damage. Its Deathknell triggers as a "Pending Item."

First FEPR Window: Scuttle Crab's Deathknell is placed on the chain and resolves. Your opponent reveals their hand at this moment.

Determine Combat Result: The game determines the winner of the combat. Since Scuttle Crab was defeated and Nidalee remained, Nidalee is declared the winner. This triggers her "When I win a combat, draw 1" ability as a new "Pending Item."

Second FEPR Window: Nidalee’s draw ability is placed on the chain and resolves, and you draw your card.

Because these abilities are processed in separate FEPR (Finalize, Execute, Pass, Resolve) windows, the reveal happens entirely before Nidalee's draw effect even begins to trigger.

question: If I banish a unit with gear would the gear pop off?
answer:
Yes, when you banish a unit with attached gear, the gear will "pop off" (detach).

According to CR 436.1 and the consistent rulings across RiftJudge FAQ #2960, #8698, and #8440, when a unit moves from a board zone (like a battlefield) to a non-board zone (like the Banishment zone), any attached gear must detach.

Once the gear detaches, it remains at the last location the unit occupied before it was banished. Because the gear is then an unattached card present at a battlefield, CR 454.1 and Rule 149.3 dictate that it will be Recalled to your base during the next cleanup.

question: Does Kha'Zix still get +2 if it initially attacks a lone defender but the opponent reacts with a unit to the trigger?
answer:
Yes, Kha’Zix, Mutating Horror will still receive the +2 Might bonus and gain 2 XP.

According to the established game rules and several RiftJudge FAQs (including #10198, #10465, and #10735), the condition for Kha'Zix’s triggered ability ("if an enemy unit is alone here") is evaluated at the exact moment he enters the battlefield and gains the "Attacker" or "Defender" combat designation.

Chain Sequence and Resolution

Trigger Condition Check: When Kha’Zix moves into the battlefield, he gains the "Attacker" designation. At that exact moment, the game evaluates the battlefield state: Is an enemy unit alone here?

Condition Met: Since your opponent had only one unit present at that moment, the condition is satisfied. Kha'Zix’s triggered ability is placed on the chain.

Reaction: When your opponent plays a unit in response, that unit is added to the chain above Kha'Zix's trigger.

Resolution (LIFO - Last-In, First-Out):

The opponent's unit enters the battlefield.

Kha'Zix's triggered ability resolves. Because the condition was met at the time the ability was triggered and placed on the chain, the subsequent change to the battlefield state (adding the second unit) does not retroactively negate the trigger.

As confirmed by RiftJudge rulings, the game does not re-evaluate the "alone" condition when the ability resolves; it only checks if the requirement was met at the time of the trigger.

question: If my opponent counters Deathgrip, do I still have to kill a friendly unit?
answer:
No, you do not have to kill a friendly unit if Deathgrip is countered.

According to CR 426.1.a., a card that is countered is cleared from the chain and does nothing. Since killing a friendly unit is part of the effect (the instructions) of the spell rather than a cost, a countered Deathgrip is negated entirely and its instructions are never executed.

As established in the Core Rules (Section 425), countering a card prevents it from resolving, meaning the kill instruction—along with the subsequent Might bonus and the card draw—does not occur.

question: If I have Undercover Agent and Jinx Rebel at a battlefield then damage is assigned with 5 damage to each, would Undercover Agent's deathknell ability give Jinx +1 might to live?
answer:
No, Jinx, Rebel will not survive in this scenario.

Here is the step-by-step breakdown of how the combat damage and the Deathknell ability resolve:

Combat Damage Step: Combat damage is dealt simultaneously. Both Undercover Agent and Jinx, Rebel are dealt 5 damage.

State Check (Death): Both units have damage marked on them equal to their Might (5). They are both marked as dying.

Triggering Deathknell: As Undercover Agent dies, its Deathknell ability triggers and is placed on the chain as a pending item.

Healing: Surviving units on the battlefield are healed (CR 463.1.a.1). Because Jinx, Rebel has 5 damage marked on her (which is equal to her Might) and there are no effects preventing this, she dies.

Resolution: After healing and deaths are processed, the game proceeds to the FEPR process, and the pending Deathknell trigger on the chain resolves. Even though the Deathknell ability resolves and causes you to discard cards (which would trigger Jinx's ability), Jinx, Rebel is already dead and in the trash by this point.

Summary:
Because the healing of the battlefield and the death of units happen before the Deathknell ability resolves on the chain, Jinx, Rebel dies before she can benefit from the +1 Might boost.

Sources: RiftJudge FAQ #10182 (regarding the timing of Deathknell and healing), CR 463.1.a.1 (Combat Cleanup).

question: If I gust a unit that was star crossed, does star crossed still resolve?
answer:
Yes, Star-Crossed will still resolve.

When you use Gust to return a unit targeted by Star-Crossed to its owner's hand, that unit leaves the battlefield and enters a non-board zone. This makes the target "illegal" for the Star-Crossed spell because it is no longer the same game object as the one originally targeted (Rule 359.3.e.2, Rule 359.3.e.4).

However, Star-Crossed does not "fizzle" (fail entirely). According to Rule 359.3.e.8, if a spell has multiple targets and one becomes illegal, the spell proceeds to resolve as much as possible, ignoring only the instruction that involves the illegal target.

The Sequence

Star-Crossed is played: It targets one friendly unit and one enemy unit. Star-Crossed is added to the chain.

Gust is played in response: It targets the unit (which is a valid target for Gust). It is added to the top of the chain.

Chain State (Top to Bottom):

[Top] Gust

[Bottom] Star-Crossed

Resolution (LIFO - Last-In, First-Out):

Gust resolves first: The targeted unit is returned to its owner's hand.

Star-Crossed resolves: It checks for its targets.

If the target returned by Gust was the enemy unit, the instruction to return that unit is ignored. The spell proceeds to return your friendly unit to your hand.

If the target returned by Gust was your friendly unit, the instruction to return that unit is ignored. The spell proceeds to return the enemy unit to its owner's hand.

This is consistent with the mechanics of partial resolution for spells with multiple targets and the rulings found in RiftJudge FAQ #10990 and #10736.

question: If I am attacking a battlefield with a 6 might vs a 6 might and pass focus, they end the showdown, can I play a reaction?
answer:
No, you cannot play a reaction after both players have passed focus in a showdown.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #7747 and Rule 348.1, once both players pass focus in succession, the showdown ends. If it is a combat showdown, the game proceeds directly to the combat damage step, where no player has priority to play spells or activate abilities.

The Sequence

Attacker has Focus/Priority: You choose to Pass.

Defender has Focus/Priority: They choose to Pass.

Showdown Closes: Because both players passed consecutively, the showdown ends immediately (Rule 348).

Combat Damage Step: The game moves directly into assigning and dealing damage (CR 462).

There is no "reaction window" between the final pass and the assignment of combat damage.

Important Note: As long as the showdown is open, you are free to play reactions while you have priority. However, once you pass focus, you are choosing to exit the window of opportunity to act. If your opponent plays an item after you pass, you will regain priority and have a new opportunity to play a reaction before that specific item resolves (as described in RiftJudge FAQ #10660), but you cannot retroactively play a reaction once both players have passed and closed the showdown.

question: I am defending a battlefield with Fiora, Peerless. My opponent attacks it with a 1 unit. If I react with an ambush unit, does my Fiora's might get doubled? What if instead I use Disciple on my Fiora, is it at 8 might or 10 might? Also, what's its interaction with Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman?
answer:
When defending with Fiora, Peerless, her might-doubling ability is a triggered ability that checks its condition—being "one-on-one"—only at the moment she is designated as the defender and the trigger is placed on the initial chain.

Here is the breakdown of your questions:

1. Ambush and Fiora's Might

If you react to the attack trigger by playing a unit with Ambush to your battlefield, Fiora's Might will still double.

Reasoning: As established in RiftJudge FAQs #1231 and #577, the "one-on-one" condition is checked at the moment of designation. Because the battlefield was one-on-one at that moment, the trigger is placed on the chain. Adding more units to the battlefield later via Ambush does not retroactively cancel or prevent the trigger from resolving.

2. Interaction with Discipline

If you play Discipline (assuming this is the spell you meant) on your Fiora, she will have 10 Might, not 8.

The Sequence:

Initial Chain: The showdown begins, Fiora is designated, and her "When I defend" trigger goes on the chain.

Closed State: The game enters a Closed State. Because Discipline is a [Reaction], you can play it while the chain is closed.

Discipline Resolution: Discipline resolves first, giving Fiora +2 Might. Her current Might increases from 3 (base) to 5.

Trigger Resolution: Fiora’s trigger then resolves, doubling her current Might (5).

Final Result: 5 × 2 = 10 Might.

Note: You must ensure you play Discipline in response to her trigger. If you wait until the chain is empty, the trigger will have already resolved on her base Might (3 × 2 = 6), and adding the +2 later would only bring her to 8.

3. Interaction with Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman

When Wuju Bladesman is active, it provides a passive ability (+2 Might to a lone defender). This interacts with Fiora as follows (consistent with RiftJudge FAQ #10960):

Passive Application: As soon as Fiora defends alone, the +2 from Wuju Bladesman is applied in the Arithmetic layer. Fiora's Might becomes 5 (3 base + 2 passive).

Triggered Ability: Fiora's "When I defend" trigger is placed on the chain.

Resolution: When the trigger resolves, it doubles her current Might (5), resulting in 10 Might.

If you use both Discipline and Wuju Bladesman in the same combat, the passive +2 applies first, Discipline adds another +2 (total 7), and then the trigger doubles that to 14 Might.

question: I use Disciple on my Irelia Irelia, Fervent, which my opponent reacts with Defy. Do I still get the +1 Might for choosing my Irelia with Disciple?
answer:
Yes, you do still get the +1 Might for Irelia, Fervent.

According to the rules of Riftbound and the associated community FAQs (e.g., FAQ #8823, FAQ #5762), the sequence of events works as follows:

Playing the Spell: You play Discipline targeting your Irelia, Fervent.

Triggering Ability: Because you chose Irelia, her ability ("When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn") triggers immediately upon the spell being finalized on the chain. Her ability is placed on the chain on top of your Discipline spell.

Opponent's Reaction: Your opponent plays Defy in response, targeting your Discipline spell. Defy is placed on the chain on top of Irelia's triggered ability.

Chain Resolution (LIFO): The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out order:

Defy resolves first, countering your Discipline spell.

Irelia, Fervent’s triggered ability resolves next. Since her ability is already on the chain, it resolves successfully, granting her +1 Might.

Key Clarifications:

Trigger Independence: Once Irelia’s triggered ability is placed on the chain, it exists independently of the spell that triggered it. Even if the original spell (Discipline) is later countered or leaves the chain, the triggered ability remains and resolves normally.

Defy Limitations: As noted in FAQ #1137, Defy can only counter spells. It cannot counter triggered abilities like Irelia's. Even if your opponent wanted to prevent the Might bonus, they cannot target or counter the trigger with Defy.

This is my interpretation based on the chain rules and the cited FAQs. No official rulebook text exists for this specific card combo interaction.

question: Can I react to my Lonely Poro deathknell trigger with Vilemaw?
answer:
Yes, you can react to your Lonely Poro's Deathknell trigger by playing Vilemaw.

Why this works:

Chain State: When Lonely Poro dies, its Deathknell trigger is added to the chain. This puts the game into a "Closed" state, which allows players to play [Reaction] cards (or units with [Ambush], as Vilemaw has).

LIFO Resolution: The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order. When you play Vilemaw in response, it is placed on top of the Deathknell trigger on the chain.

Historical Check: According to RiftJudge FAQ #9841 and FAQ #10756, the Lonely Poro's "alone" condition is a historical check. The game evaluates whether it died "alone" (no other friendly units present) at the moment of its death. Because this condition was satisfied at the time of death, the arrival of Vilemaw later in the chain does not retroactively invalidate the trigger.

Sequence of Resolution:

Death Event: Lonely Poro dies while alone at the battlefield. The Deathknell trigger is created and added to the chain.

Reaction: You play Vilemaw using its [Ambush] keyword in response to the Deathknell trigger. Vilemaw is added to the top of the chain.

Resolution:

The chain resolves LIFO. Vilemaw enters the battlefield first.

Lonely Poro's Deathknell trigger resolves second. Since the "alone" condition was already met at the moment of death, you successfully draw 1 card.

Note: This interpretation is based on established FAQs regarding the historical "alone" check for Lonely Poro.

question: Can I react to the Deathknell trigger of Unsung Hero to reduce its Might in order to prevent the card draw?
answer:
No, you cannot prevent the card draw by reducing Unsung Hero's Might in response to its Deathknell trigger.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #4157 and Rule 808.1.d.3, the Mighty condition is checked when the Deathknell resolves, but it uses the attributes and details noted at the moment of death.

Why this interaction works this way:

Snapshotting: When a unit with Deathknell dies, the game notes its location, attributes (including its Might), and other relevant details before it is moved to the trash (Rule 808.1.d.3).

Triggered Ability Resolution: Even though you can place a reaction on the chain in response to the Deathknell trigger being placed, that reaction will not change the snapshot taken at the moment of death. The Mighty check for Unsung Hero looks at the "noted" Might value from the moment the trigger was created, not the unit's current Might (which is technically null or non-existent since it is already in the trash).

Therefore, if Unsung Hero had 5 or more Might at the exact moment it died, the Deathknell effect will successfully trigger the draw, regardless of any attempts to reduce its Might after the trigger is already on the chain.

question: I am defending a battlefield alone with Fiora, Peerless. My opponent attacks it with a 1 unit. My legend is Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman. On the when I defend trigger, I use Disciple on my Fiora. I let it resolve then in the showdown I play an ambush unit to the same battlefield. What is the might of my Fiora?
answer:
To determine the final Might of your Fiora, Peerless, we must follow the layering rules for static bonuses and the resolution order of triggered abilities and spells during a combat showdown.

Final Might Calculation

Your Fiora, Peerless will have 12 Might for this combat.

Sequence of Events

Passive Application: Your Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman legend has a passive ability: "While a friendly unit defends alone, it gets +2 might." As soon as Fiora is designated as the lone defender, her base Might of 3 receives this +2 bonus, resulting in 5 Might.

Initial Chain: Fiora’s "When I defend" trigger is placed on the Initial Chain.

Reaction (Discipline): In response to the trigger, you play Discipline ([Reaction]).

Discipline grants Fiora +2 Might. This is an Arithmetic layer increase.

Fiora's current Might becomes: 3 (base) + 2 (Master Yi) + 2 (Discipline) = 7 Might.

Resolution of Initial Chain:

Discipline resolves first (LIFO).

Fiora’s "When I defend" trigger resolves, doubling her current Might (7). Her Might becomes 14.

Ambush: You play an Ambush unit. Because Fiora is no longer defending alone, the +2 Might bonus from Master Yi ceases to apply (Rule 741.1). However, because Fiora's doubling trigger has already resolved, the +7 Might gained from that effect remains for the duration of the combat. Her final Might is 14 - 2 = 12 Might.

Why this works

Layering: Passive bonuses (like Master Yi's +2) and spells (like Discipline's +2) are applied in the Arithmetic layer.

Trigger vs. Passive: As established in RiftJudge FAQ #10960 and #11088, triggered abilities that double Might do so based on the current stat at the time of resolution. Once the trigger resolves, that doubled value is locked in for the duration of the combat, but conditional passive bonuses (like Master Yi's) continue to be monitored and will be removed if the conditions are no longer met.

This interpretation is based on the rules governing passive application (Arithmetic Layer) and the standard resolution order of the Initial Chain as defined in the Showdown Flow.

question: If you have Vex Cheerless which reduces cost of your own spells by 1 power and 1 energy, and you use a spell which costs 3 energy, but target a unit with Deflect, do you just pay 2 energy and avoid the cost of choosing the unit?
answer:
To answer your question, we must look at how costs are finalized and how Vex, Cheerless interacts with mandatory costs like Deflect.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8596 and FAQ #9668, you do not simply pay 2 Energy and ignore the Deflect cost. Here is the step-by-step breakdown of how your final cost is calculated:

1. Start with Base Cost

Base Cost: 3 Energy.

2. Apply Additional Costs (Deflect)

Deflect: This is a mandatory additional cost. If the unit has Deflect 1, you must add 1 Power to the cost of the spell.

Current Total: 3 Energy + 1 Power.

3. Apply Discounts (Vex, Cheerless)

Vex, Cheerless: Her ability reduces the cost of friendly spells by 1 Energy and 1 Power (down to a minimum of 1 Energy).

Calculation: (3 Energy + 1 Power) - (1 Energy + 1 Power) = 2 Energy + 0 Power.

Final Result

You must pay 2 Energy. You do not avoid the cost of choosing the unit; rather, the Deflect cost (1 Power) is added to your spell's total cost first, and then Vex's discount is applied to that new total. This effectively offsets the Deflect cost, leaving you to pay the discounted base cost of the spell.

Key Nuances:

Mandatory: Deflect is a mandatory additional cost that must be included in your cost calculation before any discounts are applied (Rule 356.4 / FAQ #8596).

Minimums: Vex's "minimum 1 Energy" restriction applies only to the spell's base cost, not the total cost including additional costs. Because your final cost is 2 Energy, this requirement is satisfied.

Order of Operations: Per Rule 356.4, discounts to the total cost are applied after all additional costs have been summed.

question: Does Fizz target the spell to replay?
answer:
Yes, Fizz, Trickster targets the spell in your trash that you choose to play.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #6132 and FAQ #10020, you must target the specific spell in your trash at the moment you add Fizz's "When you play me" (WYPM) triggered ability to the chain.

Additionally, as clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #9320, when you play the spell from your trash during the resolution of Fizz's ability, you must declare any targets that spell requires at that time (following the normal rules for playing that spell).

question: Can you react to a unit being played?
answer:
No, you cannot react to a unit being played.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #2971 and Rule 359.3, playing a unit does open a chain, but it resolves immediately and no player gains priority, which means there is no reaction window for the act of playing the unit itself.

Here is the breakdown of how this works:

Playing the Unit: When a player plays a unit, it is placed on the chain as a pending item.

Immediate Resolution: The unit resolves immediately as soon as it finalizes and enters the battlefield.

No Priority: Because units do not linger on the chain, players never receive an opportunity to play a [Reaction] card or activate an ability in response to the unit being played.

Important Nuance regarding "When you play me" triggers:
While you cannot react to the unit being played, if that unit has a "When you play me" triggered ability, that ability will go on the chain after the unit has already entered the battlefield. Once that triggered ability is on the chain, you can react to it.

question: If I have Fiora Victorious in my base equipped with a Bf Sword, then someone uses Falling Star. It resolves dealing 6 damage to my 7 might. If this resolves and then the other person uses an action spell that reduces Fiora's might by 1, does Fiora die?
answer:
Yes, Fiora, Victorious will die in this scenario.

Here is the breakdown of why this happens based on the rules for damage, Might, and the "Mighty" keyword.

1. The Situation Before the Spell

Fiora, Victorious has a base Might of 4.

She is equipped with B.F. Sword, which provides +3 Might.

Her total Might is 7. Because 7 is at least 5, she is Mighty.

While Mighty, she gains Shield, which adds an additional +1 Might while she is a defender. (Note: Since she is in your base, not defending, this +1 does not currently apply.)

2. After Falling Star Resolves

Falling Star deals 6 damage to Fiora.

Fiora now has 6 damage marked on her. Since her total Might is 7, she remains on the board with 1 "health" (7 Might - 6 damage = 1) remaining.

3. After the Might Reduction

The opponent plays an action spell that reduces Fiora's Might by 1.

Your total Might drops from 7 to 6.

She is still Mighty (6 is ≥ 5), but her total Might is now 6.

Because she still has 6 damage marked on her, and her new total Might is 6, she has taken lethal damage (damage equal to her current Might).

Why she dies:

According to Rule 710, units on the board are always evaluated according to their current Might. When a unit has damage marked on it that equals or exceeds its current Might, it is destroyed. Because the reduction in Might brings her total Might down to the exact amount of damage she has already taken, she is immediately destroyed.

Note: This is my interpretation based on the standard rules for damage calculation and Might thresholds (Rule 710 and CR 473). While no specific FAQ exists for this exact chain of events, it follows the established layer system and damage interaction rules.

question: Can I change my Chosen Champion during sideboarding?
answer:
Yes, you can change your Chosen Champion during the sideboarding process.

According to Tournament Rules Rule 403.4.a: "During that time [sideboarding], a player may change their Chosen Champion to one from their sideboard or Main Deck that meets the deckbuilding rules of the competition format."

When doing so, keep these points in mind:

1-for-1 Exchange: In constructed, sideboard cards must be exchanged 1-for-1 with Main Deck cards (Rule 403.4).

Deckbuilding Rules: Your new Chosen Champion must still align with your Champion Legend's tag requirements and your deck's Domain Identity.

Fixed Elements: While you can change your Chosen Champion, you are not permitted to change your Champion Legend, Rune Deck, or Battlefields after deck registration in constructed formats (Rule 403.4.b).

question: Can I react to Fiora Peerless when I attack or defend trigger with Ambush so it doesn't gain Might for one on one?
answer:
No, reacting with a unit that has Ambush will not prevent Fiora, Peerless from gaining the Might bonus.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #11168 and #1231, Fiora, Peerless's "When I attack or defend" ability checks the "one-on-one" condition only at the exact moment she is designated as the attacker or defender.

The Sequence

Designation: Fiora is designated as the attacker or defender. If the battlefield is one-on-one at this exact moment, her ability triggers and is placed on the initial chain.

Trigger Evaluation: Because the condition was met at the moment of designation, the ability is now on the chain.

Reaction: The game state is now Closed, meaning you may play a unit with Ambush as a [Reaction]. However, playing an Ambush unit now (or any other effect that changes the battlefield state) happens after the trigger has already been successfully added to the chain.

Resolution: Because the ability uses "when" (a triggered ability) rather than "while" (a passive ability), it does not retroactively check the condition when it resolves. It will resolve and double Fiora's Might regardless of whether more units were added to the battlefield after the trigger was placed.

This is a deliberate mechanic of Fiora, Peerless—once her trigger condition is met and it is placed on the chain, her Might bonus for that combat is guaranteed.

question: If I have mutated Mouser at a battlefield, and my opponent plays Thousand-Tailed Watcher at base ready, applying a -3 to the mutated Mouser to 1 might, when the Thousand-Tailed Watcher comes to attack, how much might will the mutated Mouser have?
answer:
Your Mutated Mouser will have 1 Might.

According to the Thousand-Tailed Watcher ability and the supporting RiftJudge FAQ (#8931, #1448), the -3 Might reduction is a one-time modification applied when the ability resolves. It is not an ongoing static effect that continually checks or re-applies throughout the turn.

Sequence Breakdown

Watcher Played: Your opponent plays Thousand-Tailed Watcher. Its "When you play me" ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Ability Resolves: The -3 Might reduction resolves. Your Mutated Mouser (base 1 Might) receives the -3 Might reduction. Because the effect includes a "minimum of 1" clause, your Mouser's Might becomes 1.

Snapshotting: Per CR 474.3.d and FAQ #8931, the game "snapshots" this reduction for the remainder of the turn. The Watcher’s effect does not continue to check or reduce Might if it were to change later, nor does it create a permanent state that prevents your unit from having higher Might if you were to apply a buff.

Watcher Attacks: When the Thousand-Tailed Watcher eventually moves to attack, it does not re-trigger its "When you play me" ability. Your Mutated Mouser remains at the Might value established by the initial resolution of that ability.

Note on Interaction: If you were to play a buffing card (like a +1 Might spell) on your Mutated Mouser after the Watcher's ability resolved, your Mouser would increase normally. As established in FAQ #1448, Might modifications do not persist as ongoing effects, and subsequent buffs are simply added to the current value.

question: Is there a guideline for prizes on events such as Skirmishes or Nexus Nights? Usually it's a 5€ fee with only a few Nexus Nights packs as prizes?
answer:
According to the Tournament Rules, Riftbound does not have a single mandatory prize structure for specific event types like "Skirmishes" or "Nexus Nights." Prize distribution is determined by the Competition Organizer (CO) within the guidelines of the Tournament Rules and the specific Organized Play Level (OPL) of the event.

Here is the relevant framework regarding prizes:

CO Responsibility: Rule 204.3.e states that the Competition Organizer is responsible for providing all materials necessary to operate the event, which includes the prize support.

Bribery and Prize Sharing: While you cannot bribe players for match outcomes (Rule 704.5), players are permitted to agree to share prizes that have not yet been awarded, provided this agreement is not in return for any in-game action, a specific game/match outcome, or a player dropping from the tournament (Rule 704.5.b).

Dividing Prizes in Single-Elimination: Rule 704.5.c and 704.5.d outline specific procedures for dividing prizes evenly or mutually agreeing on a winner in the single-elimination portion of a tournament, provided it is done with the tournament organizer’s permission.

Because "Nexus Nights" or "Skirmish" events are often run as Low OPL events, the specific prize distribution is usually set by the local store or organizer. If you are participating in a specific event, you should consult the event's official page, the event's addenda (which take precedence over general rules per Rule 104.3), or speak directly with the Tournament Organizer to understand their prize structure.

question: If I give Hidden Blade Repeat, and I choose the same unit with both instances, will its controller draw 4 cards instead of two?
answer:
Yes, if you successfully play Hidden Blade with the Repeat keyword and choose to pay the Repeat cost, you would draw 4 cards only if the target unit remains a valid, legal target at the battlefield for both separate executions. If the unit dies or is moved after the first execution, it becomes an invalid target for the second, and the draw effect for the second execution will not trigger.

According to Rule 820.1.d, the Repeat keyword is shorthand for: "You may pay [Cost] as an additional cost as you play this spell. If you do, execute the instructions of this spell one additional time."

Sequence of Events

Playing the Spell: As you play Hidden Blade, you declare you are paying the Repeat cost. You choose a unit for the first execution and a unit for the second execution (these can be the same or different).

Resolution: When the spell resolves, it executes its instructions twice.

First Execution: Hidden Blade kills the target unit and its controller draws 2 cards (Rule 820.1.d.1).

Second Execution: The instructions are executed again. Hidden Blade attempts to kill the target again and its controller draws another 2 cards.

Important Considerations

Targeting: As noted in Rule 820.2, you make choices for each execution separately at the time the spell is played. If you choose the same unit for both, the first execution will kill it.

Resolution of the Second Execution: If the unit is killed by the first execution, it is no longer on the battlefield for the second execution. Per Rule 359.3.e.6 and the associated FAQ regarding Hidden Blade, if the target is no longer on the battlefield, the instruction regarding that target is ignored. Consequently, if the unit was killed by the first execution, the second execution will be unable to find the unit to perform the "kill" action or determine "its controller," and no additional cards will be drawn for that second execution.

Replacement Effects: If the target is saved by a replacement effect (e.g., Zhonya's Hourglass or Sett) during the first execution, the unit must still be a valid target on the battlefield for the second execution to resolve and draw cards.

Note: I could not fully verify the interaction with replacement effects against the retrieved rules.

question: Playing Master Yi legend, if I have Lonely Poro on a battlefield, and it dies in a showdown, can I play Rengar after drawing the card from the deathknell? Like playing as a reaction?
answer:
No, you cannot play Rengar, Trophy Hunter after the Lonely Poro Deathknell trigger resolves and you have drawn your card.

According to the Showdown Timing Flowchart and Chain Rules in the Riftbound rules:

Why this is not possible:

Reaction Timing: [Reaction] cards (including units with the [Ambush] keyword, like Rengar, Trophy Hunter) can only be played while there is an active chain or during a window of opportunity created by a Showdown.

Chain Resolution: When Lonely Poro dies, its Deathknell trigger is added to the chain. This puts the game into a "Closed" state.

Drawing the Card: As the Deathknell trigger resolves, you draw your card. Once that trigger is finished resolving and removed from the chain, the chain becomes empty (assuming no other items were added).

No More Window: Once the Deathknell trigger has resolved, the game state returns to "Open." You cannot play a [Reaction] to an effect that has already finished resolving and is no longer on the chain.

The correct timing:
