The card text "Swap the Might of two units at the same battlefield" requires you to pick two specific units — that's a targeting choice made during Step 2 of playing a card (Rule 355.5–355.8). You must have two legal targets available at the same battlefield before you can even play it.

If an opponent reacts by moving one of the targeted units off that battlefield, you can't swap the target to a different unit — the original targets are locked in. On resolution, if a target is no longer at the same battlefield (or otherwise illegal), Switcheroo simply fails to affect that unit, but the swap still applies to the other target if it remains legal.

question: If your unit has 6 might and 5 damage on it. Then you use Jax to move the gear to a new unit. Does the unit die? Or does it need to be damaged again?
answer:
Yes — it dies if the gear was providing Might. When Jax moves the gear away, the unit's Might drops. If that reduced Might is now equal to or less than the 5 damage already marked, the unit will be killed during the next Cleanup (CR 323.4, 143.2.b).

Example: A unit with base Might 4 has a gear giving +2 Might, making it 6. With 5 damage marked, it's alive. Jax removes the gear → Might drops to 4. Since 5 damage ≥ 4 Might, the unit dies at the next Cleanup.

It doesn't need to be damaged again — the damage was already there. The death check is: non-zero damage ≥ current Might. Lowering the Might below the existing damage is enough.

Only exception: If the gear you moved wasn't providing Might (e.g., it gave a keyword or ability instead), the unit stays at 6 Might with 5 damage and lives.

question: If I push a Draven - Audacious onto an empty battlefield and conquer, do I get 1 or 2 points?
answer: 1 point. Moving Draven to an empty battlefield means there's no combat — no opposing units to fight. Since there's no combat, his "first time I win a combat" ability doesn't trigger. You only get the 1 point from Conquering the battlefield (per FAQ #9136).

question: My opponent plays Challenge, I reveal a hidden Bone Skewer bringing Pyke into the battlefield where I have a Sneaky Deckhand. My opponent has a Sand Soldier in their other base. The opponent has declared that Challenge will target my Deckhand and their Recruit. Does this cause the showdown to occur killing Pyke and my Deckhand before the Challenge damage fizzles because the Deckhand is dead?
answer:
No — the Showdown does not interrupt Challenge. The damage from Challenge happens first, and Sneaky Deckhand survives it.

Here's the sequence:

Challenge targets are locked in when it's played — your Sneaky Deckhand (2 Might) and the opponent's Recruit (1 Might).

Bone Skewer resolves first (it's on top of the chain). Pyke enters the battlefield where Sneaky Deckhand is, making it Contested. Per Rule 321, cleanup triggered here becomes an Outstanding Task — it doesn't interrupt the chain. A Showdown is staged but cannot initiate while Challenge is still on the chain (Rule 344).

Challenge resolves. Both targets are still valid and on the board. The Recruit deals 1 damage to Sneaky Deckhand. Sneaky Deckhand deals 2 damage back. Sneaky Deckhand (2 Might) survives with 1 damage. The Recruit (1 Might) dies.

After the chain empties, the cleanup runs. The staged Showdown/Combat now initiates between Pyke (Stunned) and Sneaky Deckhand (1 damage).

So Challenge's damage does not fizzle — Sneaky Deckhand is still alive when Challenge resolves. The Showdown only begins after all chain business is done, meaning the two units will fight it out in the upcoming Combat Showdown.

question: If I cast Hostile Takeover against an attacking unit with Assault, does it retain the Might bonus after I gain control?
answer:
Ruling: No. The unit loses the Assault Might bonus after Hostile Takeover resolves because it loses the Attacker designation during the subsequent Cleanup.

Sequence:

The attacking unit has Assault and gains +X Might while it has the Attacker designation

Hostile Takeover resolves, changing the unit's controller to the defending player

A Cleanup occurs after Hostile Takeover resolves

During Cleanup, the unit is present at the battlefield with the Attacker designation, but its controller is the Defender

Per Rule 323.2.b, the unit loses the Attacker designation and gains the Defender designation because it has the opposite designation of its controller

Once the unit becomes a Defender, Assault no longer applies and the Might bonus is lost

question: Do I play Guards! It says: "Play a 2 might SS unit token. You may pay Order power to ready it." Thinking that they wouldn't defy the spell, I add a SS token and I pay the power cost and ready the SS. The opponent exhausts his runes and plays Defy. So I'm like okay, I get the power back and rewind a step, and they're like no, it's all paid at the same time and insisted that I couldn't take it back. The question is, do I lose that power or not?
answer:
No, you do not lose that Order power. Here's why.

The "pay [C] to ready it" on Guards! is an instruction that happens during the spell's resolution — it's written in the ability text box, not as "as an additional cost to play me." This is the same class of cost as Bullet Time's power cost or Thrill of the Hunt's banish (see FAQ #11228, #5229). If the spell is countered while still on the chain, that instruction never executes, and the [C] is never spent.

What you do lose: the 3 Energy you paid to play Guards! itself — that's the cost to put the spell on the chain, and per CR 426.1.c, countering doesn't refund costs paid to play a card. But the [C] for readying was never a cost of playing the spell, so it never entered the payment flow.

Timing note for the table: Defy must be played while Guards! is still on the chain (before it resolves). If you already resolved Guards! — played the token, paid [C], and readied it — it's too late for Defy; the spell already happened. If they want to Defy, they need to do it while Guards! is a pending Chain Item, which is before any of its text-box instructions occur.

question: If an opponent uses Gust to remove a unit in response to Gutter Palace's win condition trigger, does Gutter Palace still win the game?
answer:
Ruling: Yes, Gutter Palace still wins the game. The win condition is checked when the trigger is placed on the chain, not when it resolves. Once the trigger has been placed on the chain, removing a unit in response does not prevent the win.

Sequence:

At the start of your Beginning Phase, the game checks if you have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields

If true, the trigger is placed on the chain and finalizes

Opponents may play reaction cards like Gust in the resulting closed state

When the trigger resolves, it wins the game without rechecking the condition

Nuances:

The conditional "if you have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields" appears directly after the trigger condition, making it part of the trigger requirement rather than part of the effect

Conditions are only checked at the moment the trigger would be placed on the chain, not upon resolution

question: Can you cast Void Assault targeting a unit that has been stunned by Vex, Apathetic and is restricted from moving?
answer:
Ruling: Yes, you can cast Void Assault targeting a unit that cannot move due to Vex, Apathetic's "can't move it this turn" restriction. The unit is still a legal target as it meets the targeting requirement of being a friendly unit. At resolution, the first move instruction is negated due to the movement restriction, but under DAMAYC (Do As Much As You Can), the second instruction to move an enemy unit still resolves normally since it is an independent instruction that does not reference the first move.

Sequence:

Cast Void Assault, targeting the restricted friendly unit and an enemy unit (such as Vex)

At resolution, the first move instruction is negated because the unit can't be moved

The second move instruction executes independently, moving the enemy unit

Nuances:

The two move instructions in Void Assault are not linked instructions under Rule 359.3.e.14, as the second does not reference any Game Object or Game Action from the first

Vex's "can't move" restriction is absolute and prevents movement by any means

The unit must still be a valid target when casting (a friendly unit exists), but the instruction does not need to be executable at resolution

question: If a spell is countered, does it count as played for Battering Ram discount effect?
answer:
Yes - a countered spell does count as played toward Battering Ram's cost reduction.

The answer used to be no, but starting with Vendetta the core rules were updated to clarify all "Play" definitions and changed this interaction.

The CR 420.4.b. explicitly addresses this interaction:

Non-triggered abilities that check cards being played do so by means of referencing whether said cards have been Finalized.
Example: A player plays a spell, which is countered by Defy. Any Legion abilities of game objects controlled by that same player will be active.
Example: A player plays a spell, which is countered by Defy. If that player plays Battering Ram and has played no other cards that turn, it will cost [4] Energy.

question: Does the 4 damage from Ruined Rex get added onto the Showdown Might calculation? (i.e. does my unit fail to conquer if the damage from Ruined Rex + the Might total of the defense is higher than my Might?)
answer:
No — Ruined Rex's Deathknell damage is never added to the Showdown Might calculation, and it cannot cause your unit to fail to Conquer in that way.

Damage and Might are separate values (FAQ #2478, #3817). The Deathknell deals 4 damage to an enemy unit — it does not increase the enemy's Might. The Might totals that determine who wins the Showdown are summed during the Combat Damage Step (CR 462.2.a–b), which happens well before the Deathknell trigger even resolves.

The full sequence:

Combat Damage Step — Might totals are summed, damage is assigned and dealt. Ruined Rex dies here.

Combat Cleanup — all surviving units are healed (any combat damage they took is removed).

Deathknell resolves — dealing 4 damage.

Combat result is determined.

So the Deathknell's 4 damage lands after the Might comparison is already done and after the healing step. It can kill a weakened unit and potentially affect which units remain at the battlefield for the result check — but it never factors into the Might totals that determine who "wins" the Showdown.

question: Can I charm a unit that is played this turn but stunned by Vex Apathetic?
answer:
Yes, you can Charm a unit that's been stunned by Vex, Apathetic.

The key is who the "they" refers to in Vex's text: "They can't move it this turn." That restriction applies to the unit's controller (your opponent) — not to you. Charm is your spell moving an enemy unit, so the restriction doesn't stop you.

However, watch the timing window. Charm is an [Action] spell, not a [Reaction] — so you can't play it while Vex's trigger is on the chain in a Closed State. You'll need to wait until after Vex's trigger resolves and the game is back in an Open State during your Main Phase. Once there, go ahead — the stunned unit is a perfectly legal target for Charm, and you're free to move it wherever you like.

question: Can I play Shadows Call without having a unit on the board and still draw 2 or must I have a unit on the board?
answer:
No, you cannot play Shadow's Call if you have no friendly units on the board.

The card instructs you to "Choose a friendly unit without [Temporary]." That choice is a target (Rule 355.10), and you must have at least one legal target to put the spell on the Chain. The draw-2 only happens as part of the spell's effect — you can't bypass the targeting requirement just to get the cards.

question: With Soraka, if you use Blade of the Ruined King to kill something with less might than her to equip it, does that unit get healed from Soraka?
answer:
Yes — the unit gets healed, exhausted, and recalled to base by Soraka, and you still successfully equip Blade of the Ruined King.

Soraka's ability is a replacement effect (Rule 369). When you attempt to kill a friendly unit with less Might than her as the equip cost, Soraka's ability replaces that death with "heal it, exhaust it, and recall it" instead. The unit doesn't die — it gets healed, exhausted, and sent back to your base.

Crucially, per Rule 357.2.a, costs that are replaced by replacement effects are still considered paid. So even though the unit was saved, you've still fulfilled the equip cost, and Blade of the Ruined King attaches to its target normally. This is directly confirmed by FAQ #374 and #9045.

question: If I trigger Dazzling Aurora and draw Rengar Trophy Hunter and my opponent has a battlefield occupied, can I play him to their battlefield and choose who I deal damage to?
answer:
Yes, you can play Rengar, Trophy Hunter to an enemy-occupied battlefield off Dazzling Aurora's trigger — the FAQ directly confirms this (RiftJudge FAQ #11156). Rengar's unique permission ("I can Ambush to a battlefield where there are enemy units, even if you don't have units there") overrides the normal restriction that would otherwise prevent you from playing a unit to a battlefield you don't control.

However, Rengar doesn't have an ability that deals damage when played or Ambushed. His card only grants permission to enter battlefields with enemy units — there's no "deal damage to a target" on his text. So there's no damage to choose or assign when he enters play via Aurora. Once he's there, he'd be the Defender at that contested battlefield, and any damage would occur during the subsequent combat step like normal.

question: If Void Assault starts 2 Showdowns, which one happens first?
answer:
The turn player chooses which showdown to resolve first.

Here's the breakdown: Void Assault resolves as a single spell — first moving the friendly unit, then the enemy unit. Both battlefields become contested during the spell's resolution, but no showdown begins until the spell fully completes (FAQ #10632).

After Void Assault finishes, the next Cleanup stages a Showdown at each battlefield that was made contested (CR 323.7). Since more than one Showdown is staged and the game is returning to a Neutral Open State, the turn player chooses which battlefield's showdown to start first (CR 323.10, FAQ #10342). The first showdown resolves completely — including all combat, conquering, and triggers — before the second one begins (FAQ #7567, #4822).

question: I move to uncontested Forbidding Waste with my irresistible Faefolk. I charm enemy Sonya into it. Who gets the -2?
answer:
The -2 penalty applies to Sona. She's the defender and she's defending alone.

Here's the sequence:

You move Irresistible Faefolk to the uncontested Forbidding Waste. Because you applied Contested first, you are the attacker (per FAQ #11223, CR 461.2.b.1).

Faefolk's trigger resolves and moves the enemy Sona to that same battlefield. She becomes the defender.

Forbidding Waste checks: "While a unit here is defending alone, it has -2 [S]. (It's alone if there are no other friendly units here.)"

Sona is the only unit her controller has at that battlefield — Irresistible Faefolk is an enemy unit, not a friendly one. So Sona is defending alone, and the -2 [S] penalty applies to her.

Irresistible Faefolk is the attacker, so it never checks "defending alone" — it's unaffected. If you later moved a second friendly unit alongside Sona, the penalty would immediately cease (FAQ #10921).

question: If I give an equipment temporary, does it die?
answer:
It depends on how the equipment gained Temporary.

If Temporary was printed on the equipment (e.g., Spinning Axe): No, it does not die while attached. When equipment is attached, its printed rules text becomes Inactive (Rules 135.4, 718.2), so printed Temporary cannot trigger.

If Temporary was granted by an external effect (e.g., Turn to Dust): Yes, it dies. Granted rules text remains active even while the equipment is attached. That active Temporary will trigger at the start of its controller's next Beginning Phase and kill it.

Same goes if the equipment already has printed Temporary and gets a second copy granted — the granted one stays active and will kill it.

question: Can I float power/energy whenever I want? If I would like to deramp from 10 to 6 runes can I?
answer:
Yes — you can float power/energy whenever you have priority or are in the middle of paying a cost. Both basic rune abilities have Reaction speed, so you can exhaust a rune for energy or recycle it for power in any priority window (your Main Phase, in response to a spell/ability, during a Showdown, etc.) and during cost payment steps. The resource sits in your rune pool until the end of your draw phase or end of turn (Rule 166).

Recycling is an activated ability on each rune — not something you need a separate card to do. So whenever you have priority, you can simply activate "Recycle this: Add [C]" on any of your runes. That power floats in your pool (and will be lost if unused), and the recycled rune goes to the bottom of your rune deck.

On "deramping" — yes, mechanically you can recycle runes just to put them back in your deck and reduce your active rune count from 10 to 6. Each recycle is a legal activation; you don't need a target or a reason beyond adding the power to your pool. The rune goes to the bottom of your rune deck, so you'd need to draw through it again to get it back.

However, there are two practical limits:

You can only do this during priority windows or while paying costs — not mid-resolution without a cost to pay.

At competitive rules enforcement, intentionally cycling runes with no game purpose other than to reshape your board could draw Slow Play scrutiny if it wastes time (Tournament Rule 703.2). But as a legal game action, it's allowed.

question: In Vendetta we will get a new Legend, Kennen. Chaos (purple) and Order (yellow) are its domains. This means we can combine Baited Hook with Nocturne. If I activate Baited Hook and in the 5 cards I look at, I get a Nocturne and a unit with Legion, would I be able to play Nocturne with his own ability and then the Legion unit through the Baited Hook and get its Legion effect?
answer:
Yes, this works. Nocturne gets played via his own ability during the Baited Hook look, then Baited Hook plays the Legion unit. Because Nocturne finalizes before the Legion unit (pending items finalize oldest-first), the Legion condition — "another card has been Finalized this turn" (Rule 812.1.c) — is satisfied, and the Legion unit enters with its Legion ability active.

The full sequence during Baited Hook's resolution:

Kill the friendly unit (creates any Deathknell triggers as pending).

Look at top 5 — you see Nocturne. His ability lets you banish him and play him for [A] (any rune). Nocturne goes on the chain as pending.

Baited Hook continues — Nocturne is no longer "among them," so you pick the Legion unit from the remaining cards and play it (ignoring cost). It goes on the chain as pending too.

Recycle the rest.

Baited Hook finishes resolving. Pending items finalize in order: any Deathknell triggers → Nocturne → Legion unit. Since Nocturne was already finalized, the Legion unit's condition is met.

One heads-up: make sure the Legion unit's Might is ≤ the killed unit's Might + 1 — Legion doesn't help with that requirement, so you'll need the stats to line up.

question: Is the "do one of the following" portion of Hwei's ability a reflexive trigger?
answer:
No, the "do the following based on the discarded card's type" portion of Hwei's ability is not a reflexive trigger.

CR 388.1 identifies reflexive triggers by the exact phrases "Do this:" or "Do one of the following:". Hwei's text uses neither — it reads "do the following based on the discarded card's type." That's a linked instruction (Rule 359.3.e.14), not a separate trigger. The "Then" ties it all together as one sequential effect within the same triggered ability.

So when Hwei's "When I move" trigger resolves, the entire sequence — draw 1, discard 1, then check the discarded card's type for the conditional effect — all happens as one chain item with no reaction window between the discard and the conditional outcome. Opponents get their Reaction window before the whole ability resolves (when it's placed on the chain), not between its sub-steps.

question: Is Hwei a reflexive trigger and when do you know when a card is a reflexive trigger?
answer:
No, Hwei, Brooding Painter does not have a reflexive trigger. His ability is a standard triggered ability ("When I move...") followed by conditional instructions that resolve as part of that same triggered ability.

How to identify reflexive triggers: Per CR 388.1, reflexive triggers are recognized by the specific phrases "Do this:" or "Do one of the following:". Hwei's text says "do the following based on the discarded card's type" — that's a conditional branching instruction within the triggered ability's effect, not a reflexive trigger.

Reflexive triggers create new, separate Chain items when their condition is met (CR 389.1). Hwei's branching effect (Spell → draw, Gear → ready runes, Unit → +3 Shield) all happen as part of the single triggered ability resolving on the Chain — no new chain items are created.

TL;DR for spotting them: If a card says "Do this:" or "Do one of the following:", it's a reflexive trigger and creates separate chain items. Otherwise, it's likely a regular triggered ability or inline instructions.

question: If my opponent moves into an uncontested battlefield and I play Rengar as a reaction, am I the defending player?
answer:
Yes, you are the defending player.

Your opponent is the Attacker — their unit moved first to the open battlefield, causing it to become Contested (CR 447–448, and per 459.2.b.1 the player whose unit applied Contested is the Attacker). When you play Rengar, Trophy Hunter into that already-Contested battlefield via his special Ambush ability (which lets him enter battlefields with enemy units even if you have none there), you become the Defender (459.2.b.2).

Note this only works with Rengar, Trophy Hunter specifically. Rengar, Pouncing requires you to be the attacker ("I can be played to a battlefield you're attacking"), so he can't be played this way.

The full sequence: opponent moves → battlefield becomes Contested → non-combat showdown opens → you play Rengar, Trophy Hunter as a [Reaction] (since Ambush grants Reaction timing) → you're designated Defender → if both players still have units when the chain clears, the showdown transitions into combat with you as Defender.

question: Define an "activated ability" - how does this differ from a triggered ability?
answer:
Activated Ability: A repeatable effect with the format [Cost]: [Effect] — cost, then a colon, then the effect (Rules 376–377). You choose when and whether to use it during your own Main Phase in an Open State (Rules 378, 381). It goes on the Chain like a spell without a card, creating a Closed State.

Triggered Ability: An effect that happens automatically when a condition is met — recognized by "When…", "At…", or "The [Nth] time…" (Rules 382–383). You don't choose when they activate (except "you may" triggers); the game puts them on the Chain as soon as their condition is fulfilled.

Key differences

ActivatedTriggered

InitiativeYou choose to activateCondition triggers automatically

TimingYour turn, Main Phase, Open State only (default)Any turn, any state (Open or Closed), any phase

Format[Cost]: [Effect]When/At/[Nth] time…, [Effect]

"You may"Always optional (you decide to activate)Optional only if the text says "you may" — otherwise mandatory

Bottom line: Activated abilities are manual — you pay a cost for a benefit when you want it. Triggered abilities are automatic — the game fires them when the right event happens, whether you wanted it or not.

question: Is an equip cost an example of an activated ability?
answer:
Yes. Equip is explicitly an Activated Ability keyword.

Per Rule 818.1: "Equip is an Activated Ability keyword." It follows the full activated ability process — you declare the activation, pay the cost (which may include energy, power, or non-resource costs), choose a target unit, and the ability goes on the Chain. Since it uses the Chain, opponents can respond with [Reaction] cards or abilities before the Gear attaches (FAQ #10589, Rule 818.1.c.1).

question: If I play a Longsword, which has quick-draw keyword, does the quick-draw equip count as using an activated ability?
answer:
No, the Quick-Draw attach does not count as using an activated ability. Quick-Draw is a Triggered Ability keyword (Rule 819.1), while Equip is an Activated Ability keyword (Rule 818.1) — they are mechanically distinct.

When you play Long Sword, you pay only the play cost (2 Energy + 1 Power). Quick-Draw then triggers automatically as a play effect: "When you play this, attach it to a Unit you control" (Rule 819.1.d). This triggered ability places itself on the chain and resolves for free — no Equip cost, no activation of the Equip keyword, and no targeting step on your part beyond the trigger's own choice.

The Equip ability ([C]: Attach this to a unit you control) only comes into play later if the gear becomes unattached and you want to re-attach it. That would be activating an activated ability and would require paying the [C] cost.

question: Is "When you play me" text considered an activated ability since you have to pay the cost of the card to play it?
answer:
No. "When you play me" is a Triggered Ability (specifically a "Play Effect"), not an Activated Ability.

The key distinction: paying the card's cost to play it is the cost of playing the card itself (following the normal six-step play process from Rule 349). An Activated Ability has its own cost followed by a colon ([Cost]: [Effect]), per Rule 377.1. Those are two separate things, even though both can involve spending resources.

When you play a unit with "When you play me…", the unit enters the battlefield immediately, and then that text goes onto the Chain as a triggered ability (Rule 383.4.a). Opponents can react to the trigger, but not to the unit entering play itself (FAQ #5735).

question: When I equip B.F. Sword to my Unsung Hero, he becomes and I exhaust Fiora. My opponent reacts and plays Stupify to the Unsung Hero. Do I still channel one rune exhausted?
answer:
Yes, you still channel 1 rune exhausted.

Fiora's triggered ability fired the moment Unsung Hero became Mighty (2 + 3 from B.F. Sword = 5). That trigger is now on the Chain. When it resolves, the effect is simply "you may exhaust me to channel 1 rune exhausted" — there is no re-check of whether the unit is still Mighty at resolution. Stupefy reducing Unsung Hero's Might to 4 doesn't stop the channel.

This is consistent with how Riftbound treats trigger conditions vs. effects: the condition is evaluated when the trigger would go on the Chain (Rule 382). The effect executes what's written — and Fiora's effect doesn't say "if that unit is still Mighty." (Compare Unsung Hero's Deathknell, which does re-check — "If I was Mighty, draw 2" — and would fail here per FAQ #4157.)

question: Does Fiora lose her Double Might if someone ambushes after we start?
answer:
No, Fiora does not lose her doubled Might.

Fiora's ability checks the "one-on-one" condition only at the exact moment she is designated as the attacker or defender. If the battlefield is one-on-one at that moment, her triggered ability goes on the chain immediately. Playing an Ambush unit as a Reaction happens after the trigger is already on the chain—so the Ambush resolves first, then Fiora's trigger resolves and doubles her Might regardless of the new unit.

Because her ability uses "when" (a triggered ability) rather than "while" (a passive ability), it doesn't re-check the battlefield state on resolution. The bonus is locked in once the trigger is placed. (FAQ #11178, #1231)

question: Can I trigger Defender effect after Reaction?
answer:
It depends on what you mean by "after."

If you're asking about the normal Combat Showdown flow — no. "When I defend" triggers are placed on the chain before any player can play a Reaction. The order is fixed (CR 461.2.d): Attack triggers → non-defender triggers → Defend triggers are placed last. Only after all triggers and their targets are locked in does the state become Closed and reactions become legal. You cannot play a Reaction first and then have a defender trigger appear in response to it during this initial chain (FAQ #10000, #11216).

However, if a Reaction causes a new unit to arrive at the battlefield mid-combat (e.g., Flash moving a unit in), that unit will gain the Defender designation during the cleanup after that action resolves (CR 461.2.b.4.a). Since it's gaining Defender for the first time this combat, its "When I defend" ability will trigger — creating a new chain and a new reaction window (FAQ #4303, #1829). So yes, in that specific case, a defender trigger can happen after a Reaction resolves.

question: If Fiora Peerless attacks a battlefield, and the enemy ambushes, does she still get double might or does it fail on the chain?
answer:
Yes, Fiora still gets double Might.

The condition — being "one-on-one" — is checked only at the exact moment she is designated as the attacker. Since it was met then, her triggered ability ("When I attack...") is already on the chain. Ambushing in a unit happens as a Reaction while the chain is closed, after the trigger is placed. That doesn't retroactively cancel or negate the trigger — it resolves and doubles her Might regardless.

This is the difference between "when" (triggered, snapshots the condition) versus "while" (passive, continuously checks). Fiora uses "when," so the bonus is locked in. (FAQ #11178, #1231)

question: What does Azir Ascendant's ability have to target on finalization?
answer:
On finalization, Azir, Ascendant's ability needs to target one unit you control.

Here's the breakdown:

The target: "Choose a unit you control" — per Rule 355.5 and 355.7, "choose" = targeting. You pick one friendly unit as the target when finalizing the ability on the chain.

Move destinations: Rule 355.4 says to choose a valid Location as a Move Destination for each move, but Azir's ability doesn't let you independently pick them. The destinations are defined by game state: "its location" (where the chosen unit is) and "my original location" (where Azir is). Per Rule 359.3.f.2, location references like "here" are checked on execution (resolution), not finalization — so those aren't separate targeting choices during finalization.

Summary: You choose one unit you control as the target on finalization. That's it. The swap locations are determined at resolution based on where that unit and Azir currently are — if someone reacts by moving either one, the swap destinations adjust accordingly.

question: If I enter the battlefield with 5 might and my opponent has 5 units with 3 might, and I use Imperial Decree, do I kill all units or how does it resolve?
answer:
No, you do not kill all units — you kill at most 2 of the 5 defending units, and your own unit dies too.

Here's why. During the Combat Damage Step (CR 462.2.c), you must assign lethal damage to one defender before moving to the next. Your single 5-Might unit assigns damage like this:

Defender #1 (3 Might) → assign 3 (lethal ✓)

Defender #2 (3 Might) → assign your remaining 2 (not lethal, but that's all you have left)

Defenders #3, #4, #5 → 0 damage assigned (you ran out of Might)

Meanwhile, the defenders have 15 total Might to assign back to your single unit — easily assign 5 (lethal). All damage is dealt simultaneously.

Then Imperial Decree triggers: each point of damage dealt to a unit kills it. Your unit (took 5) dies. Defender #1 (took 3) dies. Defender #2 (took 2) dies. But Defenders #3, #4, #5 never took any damage at all — they survive untouched.

Combat result: Opponent still has units remaining, you have none → opponent wins combat, establishes control, and conquers the battlefield (CR 463.3.a, 463.5).

The key trap: Imperial Decree doesn't let you bypass the lethal damage assignment rule. You still need enough total Might to reach each defender in sequence — Decree only kills them after damage actually lands on them.

question: Can I play the same unit I sacrifice to Heedless Resurrection?
answer:
No. You cannot kill a unit with Heedless Resurrection's cost and then resurrect that same unit.

When you play Heedless Resurrection, you first choose a target unit from your trash (Step 2: Make Choices). The unit you intend to kill is still on the board at that point — it's not in your trash yet, so it can't be chosen as a target. Choices are locked in during Step 2, and only in Step 4 do you pay the cost by killing a friendly unit. By then, your target is already set, so you cannot retroactively pick the newly-killed unit (FAQ #9523; Rules 355.5, 355.9.a, 355.15).

question: Can Fizz play Drag Under from the trash since its cost becomes 3 mana and 1 Power? When Fizz checks for its costs, does he see Drag Under as a 3 cost spell or does he see it for its original cost of 5?
answer:
No. Fizz, Trickster cannot play Drag Under from the trash.

Fizz's ability checks the spell's printed Energy cost (the number on the card), not any discounts that would apply while playing it. Drag Under costs 5 Energy printed — well above Fizz's limit of 3. Even though it would cost only 3 when played "from anywhere other than your hand," Fizz's check happens before any cost modifications, so it sees 5 and can't target it.

Rule 131.4 confirms: effects that determine a card's cost for any purpose always use its printed cost, even if that cost is altered or ignored later. FAQ #7430 directly rules on this exact scenario: Fizz Trickster does NOT work with Drag Under.

question: If I'm running Master Yi Legend Wuju Master, could I use spells that have Pay: Calm OR Order?
answer:
No, you cannot use spells that require Order power with Master Yi, Wuju Master.

Master Yi, Wuju Master has domain Calm/Body, so your deck's domain identity is Calm/Body (CR 103.2.b, 175.1). Your Main Deck and Rune Deck can only contain cards whose domains are fully within Calm and Body.

Here's what that means:

Calm spells (like Yi, Meditative or Master Yi, Unstoppable) — yes, you can include and play them

Body spells — yes

Calm/Body spells (Alpha Strike, Highlander) — yes

Order spells — no. Order is not in your domain identity, so you can't put them in your deck, and you can't produce Order power since your Rune Deck only has Calm and Body runes

question: When an ability says once per turn, does that mean once per player turn, or does turn 10 mean both players' turns?
answer:
"Once per turn" in Riftbound refers to once per player's turn, not once per turn cycle. So turn 10 means you can use the ability on your own turn and your opponent can use the same ability on their turn — each player gets one use per their respective turn.

This is confirmed in FAQ #7963: "Once per turn" means once per player's turn, not once per turn cycle, and there is no "half turn" system in Riftbound. So if both players control a copy of the same card with "once per turn," each can activate it on their own turn independently.

question: For Vi Legends, if I take with a 2 might unit and a 3 might unit into a 2 might unit, have I dealt 3 excess damage?
answer:
Yes, you've assigned 3 excess damage.

Here's the breakdown:

Total attacking Might: 2 + 3 = 5

Single defending unit: 2 Might

Lethal damage for a 2 Might unit = 2 damage

Per CR 462.2.c.4, since there are no further defending units after that one, you can assign the remaining damage to it: 5 total assigned

Excess damage = total assigned − lethal = 5 − 2 = 3

FAQ #11256 confirms: "Excess damage is the amount of damage assigned to a unit that goes beyond the amount required to kill it (lethal damage)."

So when you conquer that battlefield, Piltover Enforcer will see that you assigned 3 excess damage — meeting its "3 or more" threshold — and you may exhaust it to ready a unit.

question: Does Lux still draw a card if you counter her spell?
answer:
No. Lux's legend ability only triggers when a spell is played (resolves), and a countered spell is not considered played (CR 426.1.b, 420.4.b). Countering prevents resolution entirely, so Lux does not draw.

This is different from a spell whose targets become illegal — that spell still resolves (doing nothing), and Lux does trigger. But if it's countered (e.g., by Wind Wall), no draw.

question: If my opponent is attacking at a battlefield and I stun their 4 might unit against my 3 might unit, what happens?
answer:
The attacker's 4 might unit is Recalled, and you Conquer the battlefield.

Here's the breakdown:

Combat Damage Step: The stunned 4 might unit contributes 0 damage (CR 424.1.b). Your 3 might unit contributes 3 damage. You assign that 3 damage to the 4 might unit — not enough to kill it (needs 4 damage to reach lethal).

Combat Cleanup: Both units survive the damage step. Since Defenders (your unit) are still present, the Attacker's unit is Recalled to base (CR 463.1.a.2).

Result: You are the only player with units remaining → you Establish Control and Conquer the battlefield (CR 463.5).

question: If I try and conquer an unoccupied bf and the opponent plays Rengar Trophy Hunter to it, who's the attacker?
answer:
You're the Attacker. Your opponent is the Defender.

When you move your unit to the empty battlefield, you apply Contested status first — that makes you the Attacker (CR 461.2.b.1 / FAQ #9820). When your opponent plays Rengar, Trophy Hunter to that already-contested battlefield, they enter as the Defender (CR 461.2.b.2).

Rengar's special permission lets him Ambush to a battlefield with enemy units even if you have none there, but that doesn't change the designation — the player who moved first is always the Attacker.

question: If Azir Sovereign moves to a BF and drags a SS token with it and the token was ready before moving, is the token exhausted after all said and done? Or no?
answer:
No, the token is not exhausted after the move. It stays ready.

Azir's ability is a triggered ability that moves token units — it is not a Standard Move. Standard Moves require exhausting as a cost (Rule 144.2), but spells and abilities that move units do not change the unit's exhaust/ready state unless they specifically say so (as established by FAQ #9376 / #7964 and echoed in FAQ #1531, which confirms Azir can even move already-exhausted tokens). The token lands at Azir's battlefield in whatever state it was before — ready stays ready.

question: Does Ezreal dashing deal damage with his effect if he gets moved to base by Janna?
answer:
No, Ezreal's damage does not deal damage if Janna moves him to base before his trigger resolves.

Here's the sequence: Ezreal attacks, his "When I attack" trigger goes on the chain. In response, you play Janna, Savior with Reaction to the same battlefield. Janna's "When you play me" trigger goes on the chain above Ezreal's and resolves first (LIFO), moving Ezreal to base. When Ezreal's trigger then resolves, "here" re-evaluates to his current location — his base, not the battlefield. Since there's (presumably) no enemy unit at his base, the ability has no valid target and whiffs.

This is the same principle as the Atakhan + Janna interaction (FAQ #11312) and the general rule from FAQ #7639: moving a unit away from the battlefield causes its "here" referent to shift, making the trigger fail to find a valid target.

question: If I control Zilean and Leblanc legend and I copy to make a reflection copy of Zilean, how many Zilean will I make, 2 or 1 and a reflection token?
answer:
You get 2 Reflection tokens, both of which become copies of Zilean. So you end up with your original Zilean plus two copy-Zileans — 3 total units with Zilean's stats and text.

Here's how it works (per official FAQ #9917):

You conquer/hold, exhaust Deceiver, discard 1, and the ability resolves.

It tells you to play one Reflection token — but Zilean's replacement effect kicks in, changing that to "play that token and an additional copy."

Two Reflection tokens enter the battlefield ready.

The Deceiver's reflexive trigger then resolves, making both tokens become copies of Zilean (and giving them Temporary).

No infinite loop — after the two tokens enter and become copies, there's no new "play a token" event for them to replace, so the chain stops there.

question: If you control a Battlefield with Zilean and you use Mirror Image, do you get one or two ready tokens at base?
answer:
You get two ready Reflection unit tokens at your base.

Here's the breakdown:

Mirror Image says "Play a ready Reflection unit token to your base." That's a "play a token unit" event, so Zilean's replacement effect kicks in (once each turn). It replaces the event: instead of playing 1 token, you play that token and an additional copy of it — 2 tokens total.

Both tokens enter ready because Mirror Image's "ready" instruction applies to the play event, and per Rule 375, the copy generated by Zilean's replacement effect inherits those modifications.

Then Mirror Image's follow-up applies: "It becomes a copy of that unit. Give it [Temporary]." As confirmed in the Zilean + Deceiver ruling (FAQ #9917), when a replacement effect creates extra tokens from a single play instruction, all resulting tokens inherit subsequent modifications to the event. So both tokens become copies of your chosen unit, and both gain Temporary.

End result: 2 ready Reflection tokens at your base, each copying the target, each with Temporary.

question: If Yasuo Remorseful conquers with his when I attack at the Trapping Grounds battlefield and has an excess of 3 damage with his ability, do you get to play the bird token?
answer:
No, you do not get the Bird token.

Here's why:

This scenario has two problems working against you.

First, no Combat Damage Step occurs. When Yasuo's attack trigger resolves and kills the defender, FAQ #4462 confirms that cleanup kills the defender and no combat follows — there's no defender left. Since no Combat Damage Step happens, no damage was ever assigned during combat. Trapping Grounds specifically checks whether you assigned 3+ excess damage — and assignment is a combat-specific action (CR 462.2.c). No combat step = no assignment.

Second, even if a Combat Damage Step had occurred, the damage from Yasuo's triggered ability isn't "assigned" damage anyway. Per FAQ #7566 (Tryndamere ruling), only combat damage assigned during the combat damage step counts toward excess/exceeding damage requirements. Yasuo's trigger deals damage directly via a triggered ability — it's not combat damage assignment.

Yes, Yasuo does conquer — after the Combat Showdown resolves with no defender, the Resolution Step establishes control and you Conquer. So Trapping Grounds will trigger. But the conditional ("if you assigned 3 or more excess damage") won't be met, and the Bird token won't be created.

question: If a user plays Star Crossed as a reaction to a unit played triggered ability, does the ability still resolve? And if, like, I move to a battlefield with Diana Lunari and trigger its ability and opponent plays Star Crossed, will I still do the predict thing even if the card is in my hand?
answer:
Yes to both.

1. Star-Crossed in reaction to a "when you play me" triggered ability — the ability still resolves. Once a triggered ability is on the chain, it is independent of its source. Returning the unit to hand via Star-Crossed does not stop the ability from resolving. (FAQ #10679, #10299; CR 393.)

2. Diana, Lunari's ability after being Star-Crossed — the Predict still happens even if Diana is back in your hand. Her trigger ("when a showdown begins here") already fired and is on the chain. The effect — pay [1], Predict, reveal the top card, draw if it's a spell — does not require Diana to be on the board when it resolves. It operates entirely on your Main Deck. So yes, you still Predict and potentially draw. (FAQ #10222, #9879, #10225.)

question: If I play Emperors Divide and it gets defied, does it still count for a 'choose' on Irelia?
answer:
Yes — Irelia, Fervent still gets +1 Might even if Emperor's Divide is countered by Defy.

Here's why: Emperor's Divide chooses specific units when it's placed on the chain (FAQ #7788, #8796), so Irelia's ability ("When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn") triggers immediately at that point. The trigger goes on the chain on top of the spell. Defy can counter Emperor's Divide, but it can't touch Irelia's triggered ability — that ability was already placed on the chain independently. When the chain resolves LIFO, Defy counters the spell, then Irelia's trigger resolves and she gains +1 Might for the turn.

question: After a player unchecks Power, is there a window after the card resolves for a player to activate a Teemo from hidden?
answer:
No. Once Unchecked Power resolves, there is no window to play a Teemo from Hidden until another chain begins. The only opportunity is before Unchecked Power resolves — but if you do that, Teemo is on the battlefield when the 12 damage hits and will die along with everything else.

Here's the sequence: Unchecked Power is played → the opponent can react (including playing a Hidden unit, but it will be hit by the damage) → Unchecked Power resolves, dealing 12 to all units → units die during cleanup → the Chain is empty and the state is Open, but you've already passed the reaction window for that spell and no new game action has created a new chain yet. You cannot squeeze a reaction in after a spell finishes resolving and before the next play opportunity — the game moves to an Open State where the turn player gets priority to act next.

question: If my Tideturner controls Ravenbloom Conservatory and trades with Lonely Poro, after that my opponent moves Scuttle Crab to attack the empty battlefield. I use Ride the Wind to move my Ravenbloom Student there. Will I be able to use the effect of the battlefield?
answer:
No, you won't be able to use Ravenbloom Conservatory's ability.

Here's why: After Tideturner dies in combat and the battlefield is empty, you lose control of Ravenbloom Conservatory in the next cleanup (Rule 187.4.c — no units + Open State). When your opponent later moves Scuttle Crab there, the battlefield becomes Contested but has no Controller. Even after you Ride the Wind your Ravenbloom Student there during the ensuing Showdown, the battlefield remains Contested and uncontrolled — control is only established at the end of a Showdown (Rule 187.4).

Since "you" in a battlefield's ability refers to its Controller (Rule 187.6.c), and there is no Controller during the Showdown, "you" refers to no one. The trigger condition "When you defend here" cannot be met by either player. Same ruling as FAQ #8647 which covers this exact interaction with Ravenbloom Conservatory.

question: Can I play Acceptable Losses if I and my opponent don't have gear?
answer: Yes, you can. Acceptable Losses doesn't require targets — it instructs each player to make a choice at resolution. If no player controls any gear when it resolves, each player's instruction simply cannot be performed and is negated (Rule 359.3.e.6). The card still resolves, nothing happens.

question: If I'm playing as Pridestalker Legend and I play Kinkou Initiate when I have 4 Might out, will Rengar Legend proc Might to 5 before checking for draw?
answer:
Yes. Both abilities trigger simultaneously when you play Kinkou Initiate. You get to order them on the chain, so you can have the +1 Might land before the draw check.

Here's how it works:

Pridestalker (Rengar Legend): "When you play a unit, give a unit +1 Might this turn."

Kinkou Initiate: "When you play me, draw 1 if your other units have total Might 5 or more."

Both triggers fire at the same time. As their controller, you choose the order they're placed on the chain (Rule 333.1). Put Kinkou Initiate's ability on first, then Pridestalker's on top. Since the chain resolves Last-In-First-Out, Pridestalker's resolves first — bumping one of your other units to 5+ Might. Then Kinkou Initiate's ability resolves, checks your other units' total Might (now 5+), and you draw. This is confirmed by FAQ entries #9873, #10875, and #10585.

question: Ask Rengar Pridestalker, can I react to my own Irresistable Fae Folk pulling a lone enemy from the battlefield and go to that battlefield before they move and conquer?
answer:
Yes — you can react to your own Irresistible Faefolk trigger by playing a unit to that battlefield before the enemy moves there.

Here's how the timing works:

You move Faefolk to an empty battlefield → you become the attacker (you applied Contested).

Faefolk's "When I move…" trigger goes on the Chain → the game enters a Closed State.

In that Closed State, you (the controller of the newest Chain item) have priority and can play Reaction-speed cards/abilities (FAQ #11143).

You play Rengar, Pouncing (or another unit with Reaction) to that battlefield — Rengar's text "I can be played to a battlefield you're attacking" overrides the normal Base-only restriction (FAQ #8779). Rengar enters the battlefield during the Reaction window.

Rengar Pridestalker's legend ability ("When you play a unit, give a unit +1 [S] this turn") also triggers and goes on the Chain — you give the +1[S] to whichever unit you want before combat.

Faefolk's original trigger then resolves, moving the enemy unit to that battlefield.

You now have Rengar (+ Faefolk) vs the pulled enemy → Combat Showdown begins.

So yes: your Faefolk trigger creates the Reaction window, and you can absolutely jump in with Rengar before the enemy arrives.

question: Can you play Nocturne from Traveling Merchant discard effect?
answer:
No. Nocturne's ability only triggers when you look at or reveal him from the top of your deck. Discarding (hand to trash) and drawing (deck to hand) are not looking at or revealing — they don't trigger Nocturne at all.

Traveling Merchant says "discard 1, then draw 1." Neither step looks at or reveals cards from the top of your deck in a way Nocturne can respond to. Drawing is a completely separate game action from "looking at" (FAQ #3447, FAQ #1433).

question: If Reflection token copy a Unit with When you play me effect, can I trigger that ability?
answer:
No. The Reflection token cannot trigger "When you play me" effects of the unit it copies. The Reflection card's own text explicitly states: "I become a copy of something when played. I don't get that card's play effects."

This is consistent with how Play Effects work (Rule 383.4.a). A "When you play me" trigger fires when the permanent with that ability is played to the board. The Reflection token enters play as a 0 [M] domainless token — the copy effect happens after it has already resolved and entered the board. Since the token was never played as the copied unit, the copied unit's Play Effect condition was never met.

question: Can you react to the Awaken phase?
answer:
No, you cannot react to the Awaken Phase itself. The Awaken Phase is a task where the turn player readies their game objects — it doesn't create a chain, and no priority is granted simply because a phase begins (FAQ #10808, FAQ #5566).

Reactions require a trigger that creates a chain, or a Showdown. Since the Awaken Phase is just "ready your stuff" and moves on, there's no window to play anything.

That said, if an ability triggers later in the Beginning Phase (e.g., a Temporary unit dying), that trigger does create a chain — and you can react to that. But not to the Awaken Phase itself.

question: Does Hidden Stand United apply to all battlefields?
answer:
Yes, Stand United played from Hidden applies its +1 buff bonus to all battlefields.

Here's how it breaks down:

Targeting part ("Buff a friendly unit") — when played from Hidden, this target must be a friendly unit at the same battlefield where it was hidden (CR 811.1.d.2).

Global effect ("Buffs give an additional +1 might to friendly units this turn") — this has no targeting restrictions and applies to all friendly units with buffs everywhere, on both battlefields (Rule 811.2 example, FAQ #851, FAQ #1457).

So you pick your buff target locally, but the +1 bonus boosts every buffed friendly unit across the board.

question: Does playing LeBlanc Everywhere at Once in response to the temporary trigger to a battlefield prevent the temporary units from dying?
answer:
No. Playing LeBlanc, Everywhere at Once after the Temporary trigger is already on the chain will not stop those units from dying.

Here's why: Temporary is a triggered ability (Rule 816). When the Beginning Phase starts, it triggers and is placed on the chain as a pending item. LeBlanc's passive says "Your [Temporary] effects at my battlefield don't trigger" — this prevents the triggering event, but once the trigger has already fired and is sitting on the chain, her passive does not remove it. The trigger resolves normally and kills the unit.

This is the same principle as FAQ #11281 — reacting to a Temporary trigger doesn't stop the original unit from dying.

The scenario where LeBlanc does help is if she's already on the battlefield before the Beginning Phase starts (FAQ #10040). In that case, the Temporary effects never trigger in the first place. Playing her afterwards is too late for this turn. She will prevent future Temporary triggers on subsequent turns if she remains there.

question: Do temporary triggers all happen at once or individually?
answer:
Each permanent with Temporary generates its own separate trigger. They all go off at the same time (the start of your Beginning Phase), but they are placed on the same chain as individual items, not merged into one.

If you control multiple Temporary units, you choose the order they go on the chain (Rule 383.3.d / FAQ #7341). Because the chain resolves last-in-first-out, the trigger you put on last resolves first — so order them in reverse of how you want them to die if you care about Deathknell sequencing or Reaction windows.

If both you and your opponent have Temporary units, the turn player's triggers go on the chain first, then the opponent's on top — meaning the opponent's units' triggers resolve first (FAQ #2439).

question: Does trigger condition don't re-check on resolution but valid target for ability or spells need to re-check on resolution?
answer:
Yes, that's correct. The trigger condition itself is only checked once — when the ability would be placed on the chain — and is not re-checked on resolution. Targets, however, are re-checked on resolution.

Once a triggered ability is on the chain, it always resolves even if its trigger condition is no longer true (e.g., the unit that moved is now dead or back at base). The ability doesn't "fizzle" just because the event or state that caused it to trigger has passed (FAQ #6035, #6550).

Targets work differently. Rule 359.3.e.2 says a target is illegal on resolution if it no longer meets the spell or ability's targeting requirements, or if it changed zones to/from a non-board zone. If a target becomes illegal, the instruction that targets it simply does nothing — though the rest of the spell/ability still resolves as much as possible (Rule 359.3.e.5–8).

There's a third layer too: referents like "here" or "my Might" are checked on execution (Rule 359.3.f.2). So even though the trigger resolves, if it says "deal damage equal to my Might" and the unit is dead, "my Might" returns null and that part does nothing. The ability still resolves — it just has no effect on that portion.

question: Can Dancing Grenade be played indefinitely as long as I have power to pay?
answer:
Yes — as long as someone has [A] (1 Fury Power) to pay and there's a valid unit to target each time.

Here's how it works:

When Dancing Grenade resolves, it deals 2 to a unit, then the controller of that unit may play the card again from the trash for [A] instead of its normal cost (Rule 356.1.a — "for [Cost]" replaces the base costs). That new cast resolves, its unit's controller gets the same option, and the loop continues.

Each subsequent cast gains +1 Bonus Damage for every time this spell has dealt damage earlier in the turn. So cast 2 deals 3 (2+1), cast 3 deals 4 (2+2), cast 4 deals 5, etc. The damage escalates each iteration.

There's no "once per turn" or "only once" restriction on the card — the permission is granted each time the spell resolves. So the loop has no hard cap, only practical ones: running out of [A] to pay, or running out of units that can survive the escalating damage.

question: If I use Zhonya's on my Temporary unit, will it die on the turn after Zhonya's got triggered?
answer:
Yes. The unit with Temporary that was saved by Zhonya's Hourglass will die at the start of the next turn's Beginning Phase.

Here's the sequence:

Temporary triggers at the start of your Beginning Phase, attempting to kill the unit.

Zhonya's Hourglass (a replacement effect) intercepts that death — it heals, exhausts, and recalls the unit instead.

However, the Temporary keyword remains on the unit. Saving it from one trigger does not remove the status.

At the start of your next Beginning Phase, Temporary triggers again and this time kills the unit unless another effect saves it.

Temporary is a trigger that happens once per Beginning Phase. Zhonya's replaces one instance of death, but the keyword persists, so the next Beginning Phase it fires again (FAQs #301, #5544, #8940; Rule 816.1.b).

question: Alpha Strike: Do I have to deal at least one damage to each target at both battlefields, or can I only deal damage to one battlefield?
answer:
You can deal damage to units at just one battlefield. You are not required to target units at both battlefields or at every battlefield.

Alpha Strike says "split among enemy units at battlefields" (plural), meaning you can split across multiple battlefields if you want. But because it's a split effect, you choose which enemy units to target, and "any number" includes just one (FAQ #9467, #9488). So you can put all the damage into a single unit at one battlefield if you like.

The only restriction per target: each unit you choose must receive at least 1 damage (Rule 355.14.g, FAQ #11486). You can't assign 0 to a target just to have it "count" — every chosen target gets a positive integer amount.

question: Can I defy Lilting Lullaby?
answer:
No. Defy cannot target Lilting Lullaby.

Defy checks the printed (base) cost of the target spell, and can only counter a spell with 4 or less energy and 1 or less power. Lilting Lullaby costs 2 power, which exceeds Defy's power restriction. Defy's own power cost is 1, so its targeting condition ("no more than rune of any domain") caps at 1 power — Lilting Lullaby's 2 power is outside that range.

question: Does attaching Gear create a chain that can be reacted to?
answer:
Yes, equipping/attaching a gear via its Equip ability creates a chain and can be reacted to. This is a confirmed ruling (FAQ #731).

Equip is an activated ability (Rule 818.1). Activating it follows the same process as playing a card — you pay the cost, choose a target, the ability goes on the chain as a pending item, and the game state becomes Closed. Your opponent can then play Reaction cards or abilities before it resolves (Rule 150.2.a, Rule 377.3).

The one nuance: if the gear is being played from hand with Quick-Draw (Rule 819), the gear card itself resolves immediately without giving opponents a window (same as any unit/gear entering play). However, Quick-Draw's "When you play this, attach it to a unit you control" is a triggered ability that does go on the chain after the gear enters play — and that trigger can be responded to.

question: If I cast Sacrifice on my 5 might Vi and then opponent reacts with Smokescreen on the Vi, does the Vi still die to Sacrifice and I get the Draw 2 and Channel 1?
answer:
Yes, Vi dies and you get the Draw 2 and Channel 1.

Here's why: When you play Sacrifice, the additional cost (killing a friendly Mighty unit) is paid during Step 4 of the playing process — before the spell goes on the chain. By the time the opponent has priority to play Smokescreen as a Reaction, Vi is already in the trash and Sacrifice is already finalized on the chain. They can't save her or interrupt the cost (FAQ #9906, Rule 357.2).

Important distinction: The opponent's only window to stop this is before you play Sacrifice, during an Open State. If they Smokescreen Vi (reducing her to 1 Might) while you have priority and haven't cast Sacrifice yet, Vi is no longer Mighty (needs 5+), so you can't choose her as Sacrifice's cost. But once you announce Sacrifice and pay the cost, it's too late for them to react.

question: What can counter Sacrifice?
answer:
Yes, Sacrifice can be countered — but the unit you killed to pay its cost stays dead.

Once Sacrifice is on the chain, any spell that counters spells works. The most efficient options:

Defy (Calm, 1⛁) — counters it directly; same cost, same [Reaction] speed.

Wind Wall (Calm, 3⛁) — no restrictions, counters anything.

Hard Bargain (Chaos, 2⛁) — counters unless they pay ⛁2; they can't undo the dead unit either way.

Abandon (Chaos, 2⛁) — counters and returns it to hand instead of trash.

Lilting Lullaby (Calm/Mind, 2⛁, Signature) — counters and locks them out of spells for the turn.

Riposte (Body/Order, 2⛁, Signature) — counters and buffs one of your units equal to Sacrifice's 1 Energy.

The key trade-off: per CR 426.1.c, countering doesn't refund costs. The Mighty unit was already killed as part of paying Sacrifice's additional cost (step 4 of playing a card, before it finalizes to the chain). So you stop the draw 2 + channel, but their creature stays dead.

Two cards that won't work: Not So Fast and Repulse check whether the spell "chooses" a friendly unit. Sacrifice's "kill a friendly Mighty unit" is an additional cost, not a targeting choice (Rule 355.10.c) — so those counter spells don't interact with it.

question: If Aspirants Climb becomes a Brush, do you still need to score 9 points?
answer:
No — once Aspirant's Climb is replaced by a Brush token, you no longer need 9 points.

Aspirant's Climb has a passive effect that only applies while it's in play (FAQ #7987). When it's replaced by a Brush token, Aspirant's Climb leaves the battlefield, and its "Increase the points needed to win by 1" effect stops. The victory score immediately reverts to the standard 8 points (in 1v1). You only need 9 while Aspirant's Climb is actually on the board.

If you later swap the Brush back to Aspirant's Climb (via the Brush's "when you score here" trigger), the passive effect returns and the threshold goes back to 9.

question: Does equipping a Gear start a chain?
answer:
Yes, equipping a gear starts a chain. Equip is an activated ability (Rule 818.1), and like all activated abilities, activating it places the equip ability on the chain (Rule 333). This opens a window for your opponent to respond with Reaction cards before the equip resolves.

Here's the sequence:

Activation — You pay the equip cost and target a unit you control.

Chain starts — The equip ability is placed on the chain as a pending item.

Priority passes — The game state becomes Closed. Your opponent gets the first chance to play Reactions (e.g., a kill spell targeting the unit you're equipping).

Resolution — If the chain resolves and the target is still legal, the gear attaches to the unit.

Important caveat: If your opponent removes the target unit before the equip ability resolves, the equip fails — its target is no longer legal (FAQ #634).

question: Does Teemo Strategist trigger first before attacker can play an action card such as Punch First?
answer:
Yes, Teemo's defend trigger resolves first — the attacker cannot play Punch First before Teemo's ability goes off.

Here's the timing breakdown:

Teemo gains Defender designation → his "When I defend" trigger fires and goes on the chain.

The chain is now in a Closed State. During a Closed State, only Reaction cards can be played (Rule 338.1.a.1–2). Punch First is an Action card, not a Reaction, so it can't be played here.

Players get priority and may play Reactions (to buff Teemo, protect the attacker, etc.). If no one adds anything, the trigger resolves — Teemo reveals 5 cards and deals damage to the chosen enemy unit.

After Teemo's ability fully resolves and the chain empties, the attacker gains Focus and can then play Punch First — but the damage from Teemo has already happened, so the attacking unit may already be dead.

In short: Teemo's trigger resolves before the attacker gets an opportunity to play an Action like Punch First. The only window to respond during the trigger is with Reaction cards, not Action cards.

question: Do you choose a target with Teemo Strategist before revealing cards to determine the damage?
answer:
Yes, you choose the target before revealing cards.

When Teemo, Strategist's "When I defend" trigger goes on the Chain, you choose the target enemy unit at that battlefield as part of putting the trigger on the Chain. Only after that does your opponent get a chance to react. When the ability resolves, you reveal the top 5 cards, count how many have Hidden, deal that much damage to the already-chosen target, then recycle all revealed cards.

This is consistent with Rule 355.5.b — triggered ability targets are chosen when the trigger goes on the Chain, not during resolution. (FAQs #7962, #914, #7592)

question: Can you activate Star-Crossed if only one player controls units?
answer:
No. You cannot play Star-Crossed if only one player controls units on the board.

The spell reads "Return a friendly unit and an enemy unit to their owners' hands." Both are mandatory targets — there is no "up to" language. You need a friendly unit and an enemy unit on the board at the time you announce the spell and place it on the chain. If only one player has units, one side of the targeting requirement can't be met, and the spell can't be played.

question: If my Stupefy gets countered, will my Ravenbloom Student gain a Might from the countered Stupefy?
answer:
No, Ravenbloom Student will not gain +1 Might.

For Ravenbloom Student's ability to trigger, a spell must be played — and a spell is only considered "played" once it successfully resolves. If Stupefy is countered (by Defy, Windwall, Hard Bargain, etc.), it never resolves and was never "played" for the purposes of triggered abilities (CR 426.1.b). The countered spell simply fizzles, the chain clears, and Ravenbloom Student's ability does not trigger.

question: If my opponent plays Cull the Weak and my Ruin Runner is the only available unit, will I have to kill my runner or no since it's actually me choosing?
answer:
Yes, you have to kill your Ruin Runner.

Here's why: Cull the Weak does not target or choose any units when it's played. The instruction "Each player kills one of their units" is performed during resolution, and you are the one choosing which of your own units to kill (Rule 355.10.e). Ruin Runner says it "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" — but since you (not an enemy spell) are the one making the choice at resolution, that protection doesn't apply. If Ruin Runner is your only unit when the spell resolves, you must choose it.

question: If I use Cull of the Weak and my opponent plays Thrill of the Hunt on the unit he chose, does my opponent get to not kill any units?
answer:
No, your opponent does not get to skip killing a unit.

Here's the sequence: Cull the Weak doesn't target, so no unit is chosen when it's played. Your opponent can respond with Thrill of the Hunt — that banishes their unit and plays it back to a battlefield. But when Cull the Weak resolves, they must still "kill one of their units." If that replayed unit is their only unit on board, they are required to choose that same unit to kill. They cannot opt out as long as any unit of theirs exists. (FAQ 10077, 11012)

The only way they'd skip it is if they somehow had zero units on board at resolution — but Thrill of the Hunt puts the unit back on board, so that generally won't happen.

question: If you have 4 Might unit and Rengar Legend, if you play Kinkou Initiate does the trigger go on the stack if you don't already meet condition when you play trying to buff your 4 Might unit to 5 with Rengar?
answer:
Yes, the trigger goes on the chain. The "if your other units have total Might 5 or more" on Kinkou Initiate is part of the effect, not a condition that blocks the trigger from being placed on the chain.

Both triggers — Kinkou Initiate's "When you play me" and Rengar's Pridestalker "When you play a unit, give a unit +1 Might" — trigger simultaneously when Kinkou Initiate enters. You, as controller, order them on the chain (Rule 333.1). Put Kinkou's ability on first, then Rengar's on top. Rengar's resolves first, buffing your 4-Might unit to 5, then Kinkou's resolves and sees 5+ total Might from your other units — so you draw. This is confirmed across multiple FAQs (#9873, #10875, #11572).

question: Can I play Stacked Deck without having at least 3 cards in my deck?
answer:
Yes, you can. Stacked Deck instructs you to look at the top 3 cards — if you have fewer than 3 cards remaining, you simply look at as many as are there and resolve the effect normally (put 1 into your hand, recycle the rest). You do not need at least 3 cards to play it.

The only time you can't play Stacked Deck is if your Main Deck is empty (0 cards), because there's nothing to look at. (FAQ #2237)

question: If my Lucian has 2 Trinity Forces and 1 Skyfall of Areion, do the Trinity Forces stack or just 1 go off?
answer:
Both stack. Each Trinity Force is a separate gear with its own triggered ability ("When I hold, score 1 point"), and when you attach a gear to a unit its text is appended to that unit's rules text. So Lucian with two Trinity Forces has two independent instances of that trigger.

With Skyfall of Areion equipped, those hold effects also count as conquer effects. When you conquer with Lucian, both Trinity Forces see the conquer event and each puts its own trigger on the chain — meaning you score 2 additional points (one per Trinity Force), for 3 total (1 from the conquer itself + 2 from the two triggers). FAQ #9632 and #10436 both confirm multiple Trinity Forces stack this way.

question: Can you Hidden Blade your unit twice? Can you Deathgrip your unit twice?
answer:
It depends on what you mean by "twice."

If you mean playing two separate Hidden Blade spells targeting the same unit: Yes, you can play both (each from its own hidden spot), but only the first to resolve will succeed. Once that Hidden Blade kills the unit, the second Hidden Blade loses its target — the unit no longer exists at the battlefield, so both the kill and the draw effect fail for the second one (FAQ #3700).

If you mean using Repeat on a single Hidden Blade targeting the same unit both times: Same outcome. The first execution kills the unit and its controller draws 2. The second execution then can't find the unit on the battlefield, so it does nothing — no kill, no draw (FAQ #11181).

The one exception in both scenarios: if the unit is saved by a replacement effect like Guardian Angel or Zhonya's Hourglass during the first kill, the unit stays on the battlefield as a valid target, and the second effect resolves normally — you'd draw 2 from each execution.

I noticed multiple unrelated questions. I've answered the first one — please ask the others in separate messages so I can give each one proper attention.

question: In a 2v2, if my teammate Ride the Winds my unit to a battlefield during our opponents' turn for our final point, will we win?
answer:
No, you will not win. You'll draw a card instead of gaining the winning point.

Here's why: Ride the Wind is an [Action] spell, so on the opponent's turn it can only be played during a showdown (per its timing restriction). But more importantly, when you're at 10 points in 2v2 (1 away from 11), the final point via Conquer requires you to have scored every battlefield that turn (CR 468.1.b.2, adjusted by 484.8.f.1 — excepting those your ally controlled at the Beginning Phase). Since this is the opponent's turn, you haven't scored any battlefield this turn. You can't satisfy "scored every battlefield this turn," so you don't gain the point — you just draw a card.

You can still score a regular point via Ride the Wind on an opponent's turn (FAQ #572), and if you were at 9 or fewer points this would work fine. But for the final point, the conquer restriction blocks the win.

question: Playing as Lux legend, if I play Falling Comet to a battlefield and the opponent plays Retreat to return the unit to their hand before Falling Comet resolves, do I still get to draw 1 for the legend? Or since the spell doesn't resolve, I don't draw?
answer:
Yes, you still draw a card.

When your opponent plays Retreat in response, the targeted unit returns to hand and is no longer a legal target. Falling Comet still resolves — it just has no effect on that illegal target (Rule 359.3.e.1, 359.3.e.6). A spell that resolves to no effect is still considered played (Rule 359.3.e.10), which is what Lux's Legend checks for.

This is different from a spell being countered (e.g. by Wind Wall), which prevents resolution entirely and would deny the draw — but Retreat doesn't counter, it just removes the target. The spell still goes through the full resolution process, so Lux triggers and you draw 1.

question: If I conquer with Kennan and can give a spell flow, can I give drag under flow with cost 3 energy and 1 power or is it printed cost of 5 energy 1 power?
answer:
No — it checks the printed cost of 5 Energy.

Kai'Sa, Evolutionary's trigger says "with Energy cost less than your points" — and per Rule 131.4, effects that determine a card's cost for any purpose always use its printed cost, even if that cost would be reduced when played. Drag Under's printed Energy cost is 5, not 3. The self-discount ("I cost [2] less from anywhere other than your hand") only applies during the playing process, after the eligibility check is done.

So unless you have 6 or more points, Drag Under cannot be chosen by Kai'Sa's conquer trigger. This is the same logic as Fizz, Trickster not working with Drag Under (FAQ #7430), and Kai'Sa not being able to play Sky Splitter based on its reduced cost (FAQ #3520).

If you do have 6+ points and play it via Kai'Sa, you ignore the 5 Energy cost but still pay the 1 Power cost (per the parenthetical on Kai'Sa's card).

question: Can I play green Janna as a reaction for attacking with my unit on base and sent to battlefield?
answer:
Yes, you can play Janna, Savior as a Reaction during your attack — but she must be placed at a location you already control, not the battlefield you're attacking.

Here's how it works:

You move your unit from base to an occupied battlefield. That applies Contested and starts a Combat Showdown.

As the Attacker, you gain Focus in the Showdown Open state.

Janna has [Reaction] — she can be played at any time, including during a Showdown.

Placement restriction: When you move into an occupied battlefield, you do not control it (it's contested). Units must be played to a battlefield you control or your base. So Janna goes to your base or a different battlefield you already control — not the one you're attacking.

Why you might want to: If the enemy has a unit at that contested battlefield and you'd like to move it away, Janna's trigger can't reach it from a different location (her ability says "here"). But you could still play her to your base to set up for future turns or to use her healing on units elsewhere.

Refs: FAQ #11160; Combat reference §Attacker/Defender; CR 459.2

question: Does the battlefield conquer effect have priority over other "When I conquer" effects?
answer:
No — a battlefield's conquer effect does not have priority over other "When I conquer" effects.

All "When you conquer" triggers (from units, battlefields, or other sources) trigger simultaneously when you conquer. Since they trigger at the same time, the player who controls them chooses the order they're placed on the Chain (Rule 383.3.d). They then resolve last-in-first-out as usual.

So you get to sequence them however you want — no inherent priority between a battlefield's and a unit's conquer effect.

question: If there's Abandoned Hall and they use Flash on their unit, does the unit still get +1 might?
answer:
No. The unit will not get the +1 Might from Abandoned Hall.

Here's why: Flash resolves first, moving the unit from Abandoned Hall to your base. Only after Flash finishes resolving does Abandoned Hall's "when a player plays a spell" trigger go on the chain. When that trigger resolves, it asks you to give +1 Might to "a unit you control here" — but your unit is no longer at Abandoned Hall, so it's not a valid target. (This is directly covered by FAQ #11451.)

question: When you have a unit with 2 extra might cast on it and then you play Thrill of the Hunt, does that unit still have the 2 extra might when you play it to a battlefield?
answer:
No, the unit does not keep the +2 extra Might.

When Thrill of the Hunt banishes the unit and then plays it to a battlefield, the unit leaves the board entirely. Per CR 705, all buffs and modifiers are removed when a unit leaves play. The unit then enters as a new game object — it's treated as a fresh copy of the card, carrying only its printed base Might (plus any permanent modifiers like gear might bonuses). Any temporary +2 Might from a spell effect is gone for good. (RiftJudge FAQ #9870 and #11336 confirm this.)

question: When Flame Chompers die, can I pay a Fury Rune to play it?
answer:
No. Flame Chompers' ability triggers only on discard (hand → trash), not on being Killed (board → trash). Those are different game actions with different trigger conditions.

The card reads: "When you discard me, you may pay fury rune (power) to play me." Being destroyed in combat, removed by a Kill effect, or any other form of death from the board does not satisfy "discard" — Discard specifically means moving a card from hand to trash. You would need a separate recursion effect (like Unlicensed Armory or similar) to bring Flame Chompers back from the trash after it's Killed.

question: If a player's "on attack" trigger kills an enemy unit at a battlefield with deathknell, does the deathknell effect happen before you move into the main part of a showdown?
answer:
Yes — the Deathknell resolves during the Combat Showdown Step, before combat damage is dealt.

Here's why: An "on attack" trigger fires during Step 1 of Combat (the Combat Showdown Step, CR 461). When that trigger resolves and kills a unit with Deathknell, the Deathknell trigger becomes a Pending Item on the chain (CR 429.1.a.1.b). Since the chain is still active within the Showdown Step, the Deathknell must go through normal FEPR — Finalize, get placed on the chain, and resolve — before the Showdown can close.

The Showdown cannot close while chain items exist (Rule 348). Only after the chain empties and all players pass does the Showdown close, and only then do you proceed to the Combat Damage Step (Rule 348.1).

This is distinct from Deathknell caused by combat damage itself — that Deathknell happens during Combat Cleanup (after damage), in a separate sequence. But a Deathknell triggered by an "on attack" kill resolves right then and there during the Showdown Step, well before anyone assigns combat damage.
