question: What happens when you play Abandon on a spell that was played for its Flow cost?
answer:
It will be banished when it attempts to leave the chain.

“[T]hen banish it” in Flow’s text is short for “if it would leave the chain after becoming a finalized chain item, and leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by its own execution, banish it instead.” Abandon returns the countered card to hand after countering it, but for the purposes of Flow’s “then banish it”, this is also leaving the chain. No matter how it happens, as long as the Flow spell leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by the execution of the spell itself, it will be banished.

This also applies to effects like Kai’Sa, Evolutionary from Origins, or Fizz, Trickster from Spiritforged.

question: What is the difference between Iascylla and Azir, Sovereign’s uses of “this battlefield”?
answer:
Iascylla’s delayed trigger refers to the battlefield that she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger refers to the battlefield where he is located.

The difference between these two is that Iascylla has a delayed trigger that references implicit information from her trigger condition: the battlefield where she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger does not reference information from his trigger condition, which purely checks for the event of Azir gaining the attacker designation for the first time each combat. Without that information being checked from the trigger condition, the “this battlefield” in Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger will be checked when the triggered ability resolves. If it resolves and he is not located at a battlefield, any instructions related to that battlefield will be ignored; otherwise, the battlefield he is currently located at will be used.

Comparatively, when a triggered ability refers to information from its trigger condition, that information is checked when the ability triggers and not on resolution. In the case of Iascylla, her delayed trigger is linked with her hold effect, so the information from the trigger condition of the hold effect can be shared with the delayed trigger.

In future sets, they’ve moved to use more precise templating and wording for abilities like Iascylla’s.

question: What happens when I play Moonfall choosing an enemy unit while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
answer:
The chosen unit will be given -3 [M]. All other enemy units at the chosen battlefield will be given -2 [M].

Mel, Newly Awakened’s empowered ability is a replacement effect. It replaces the event of a spell or ability you control giving a unit it chooses -[M]. The event it replaces that with is the spell or ability giving an additional -1 [M].

Although Moonfall gives -[M] to multiple units, only one of them is chosen, and thus the only event that is eligible to be replaced is the chosen unit being given -2 [M]. It will be replaced with that unit being given -3 [M]. The events of the other units being given -[M] will not be affected by this replacement effect.

question: What about casting Stupefy while I have an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
answer:
The chosen unit will be given -2 [M], to a minimum of 1 [M]. If it was 2 [M], it will become 1 [M].

In the case of Stupefy, Mel, Newly Awakened replaces the event of Stupefy giving -1 [M] with it giving -2 [M] instead. However, a replacement effect that replaces an event modified by the game effect that generated that event will inherit any of those modifications. In this case, Stupefy modifies the “give -1 [M]” game action and thus event with “to a minimum of 1 [M].” The replaced event will inherit the same modification.

question: Speaking of Mel, can my opponent play Abandon on my spell while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened? What happens?
answer:
They can play Abandon targeting your spell. On resolution, they will Predict, but nothing else will happen.

Mel, Newly Awakened says “your spells and abilities can’t be countered.” If the spell can’t be countered, Abandon will attempt to counter it and fail, and then it will replace the event of it being put in the Trash with it being returned to its owner’s hand. However, that event never occurred, so there is nothing for the replacement effect to replace. Thus, Abandon will resolve to no effect. The replacement effect only functions within the limit of the resolution of the ability (it’s not a delayed replacement effect that specifies a duration), so even if the spell resolves later, it will go to the Trash as normal.

question: How does it work if I cast Abandon while having an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened but they Rebuttal my spell?
answer: In the case of Rebuttal, gaining control of a spell is not the same thing as countering that spell. Effects that prevent spells being countered don’t prevent their controller from changing. If Rebuttal is played choosing your spell, and they pay [A] during resolution of Rebuttal, they will gain control of it. However, them not paying [A] does not mean the spell will be countered.

question: What new choices can I make when I play Rebuttal and pay [A]?
answer:
You can choose any number of targets or modes to make new choices for. The rest remain the same.

If you are remaking choices in this way, any choices you choose not to remake must be legal choices. You can’t choose to have some but not all choices be legal choices. Of course, you can always choose not to make new choices. In that case, any of the current choices will remain in their current state, whether that state is illegal or not.

If a spell has some rules or requirements about the choices made for it, those apply regardless of who controls that spell. For example, if a player plays a spell from face down, they must target game objects located at the battlefield the spell was played from unless the instructions of that spell indicate that a target must be chosen from some other location. Gaining control of such a spell doesn’t change this requirement when making new choices for the spell.

This section is expected to be revisited in a future rules update.

question: What happens if I choose to copy an empowered unit when I equip an unempowered unit with Shady Spectacles?
answer:
Being empowered is a status and is not copyable, thus the equipped unit will remain unempowered.

Shady Spectacles applies a copy effect to the equipped unit. Copy effects copy the printed (or copied, if another copy effect has already been applied) traits of the unit being copied. Empowered is a status, a temporary modification, and not part of the printed traits of the card, so it will not be copied by Shady Spectacles. Whatever temporary modifications are applied to the unit as the copy effect is executed on that unit will be unaffected by the copy effect. If the unit has Might increases or decreases, a buff, the empowered status, Temporary, attacker, defender, etc those will remain in place.

question: What happens when my opponent’s Akshan, Mischievous steals my equipped Shady Spectacles? What happens if they want to copy Aphelios?
answer:
If it was attached to a unit, the equipped unit loses its copy effect. Akshan will then become a copy of a friendly unit of his controller’s choice. If he becomes a copy of Aphelios, his ability will not trigger.

As of the Vendetta rules update, effects like Shady Spectacles and Svellsongur are replacement effects that replace the event of the equipment being attached to a unit with that event plus whatever their effect specifies.

In the case of Svellsongur, the resulting series of events will be: Attach → Copy the equipped unit’s text to Svellsongur’s effect text for as long as Svellsongur is attached.

For Shady Spectacles, the resulting series of events will be: Attach → Choose a friendly unit and make the equipped unit a copy of that unit for as long as Shady Spectacles is attached.

These events are not simultaneous. The attach event executes first, and then whatever event is instructed by the replacement effect is executed. Thus, the answer in the Spiritforged FAQ is no longer true: if you attach Svellsongur to Aphelios, he will not trigger twice. Svellsongur doesn’t have the copied effect text when the attach event executes.

Similarly, if Akshan nabs Shady Spectacles from an opponent, it will attach and then make him a copy. If his controller chooses to make him a copy of Aphelios, it’s too late by that point for his new triggered ability to see the attachment event; it’s already been completed.

question: My Sand Soldier has Shady Spectacles equipped and is a copy of Azir, Ascendent. What happens if I activate the copied Azir’s activated ability before detaching the Shady Spectacles and then attach them to the same Sand Soldier as a copy of the same Azir, Ascendent? Can I use the activated ability again?
answer:
You can.

Each instance of the copied ability is a different ability. The game object remains the same throughout this whole process, so any temporary modifications will remain on the Sand Soldier as it transforms, but the copied rules text is an entirely new instance of the ability. It is the same idea as Svellsongur’s copy of an ability being “refreshed” if Svellsongur is detached and then reattached to the same unit.

question: What happens during combat damage assignment if my 4 [M] unit has both Ki Barrier and Lotus Trap played on it this turn and my opponent has a 4 [M] defender?
answer:
You can order the replacement effects on your unit. If Ki Barrier is first, your unit will take no damage and you will have 3 damage prevention remaining on your unit. If Lotus Trap is first, your unit will take 1 damage and will have no damage prevention remaining on your unit.

With the Vendetta rules update, replacement effects that apply to damage in combat are streamlined: any replacement effect that would apply to combat damage being dealt will apply instead to combat damage assignment. This was already the case for prevention effects like Ki Barrier or Counterstrike, to prevent several strange edge cases. Now, damage increasing replacement effects will also apply during damage assignment.

question: What happens when I discard a Patched Porobot with Hwei, Brooding Painter’s move trigger?
answer:
Two triggers will go on the chain, in the order of your choosing. One says “Give me +3 [M] this turn.” while the other says “Ready up to 2 runes.”

Hwei, Brooding Painter says “do the following based on the discarded card's type …” Unlike previous reflexive triggers that use a similar template (cf Twisted Fate, Gambler), Hwei doesn’t say “do one of the following …” As long as the card has the appropriate type, you will put the corresponding reflexive trigger on the chain. If somehow there existed a card that was a spell unit gear, you would put three reflexive triggers on the chain when you discard it to Hwei.

question: If my opponent plays two spells in succession, can I counter the first one with Crumbling Sands?
answer:
Yes.

Crumbling Sands uses the “finalize” meaning of play, because it checks whether cards have been “played” and isn’t a triggered ability. As long as an opponent (not even necessarily the one who played this spell) has chosen targets, paid costs, checked legality, and completed the process of finalizing another spell, even if that spell was countered, Crumbling Sands can counter a spell. That means it can counter the first spell played, as long as another spell was played by an opponent after that one.

question: When can I react to my opponent playing Fallen Feline to a battlefield? And how does naming a card work?
answer:
You can react to the play effect of Fallen Feline, before they’ve named a spell.

Fallen Feline’s play effect instructs its controller to name a spell. This occurs on resolution of the triggered ability. If Fallen Feline is played to a battlefield, as soon as the ability resolves, opponents cannot play spells with that name. Meaning spells by that name can not be put onto a chain. Any spells already on the chain when Fallen Feline’s ability resolves will be unaffected. However, by the time you know the chosen spell it’s too late to play that spell.

Naming a card or tag has new rules with the Vendetta rules update. When naming something in this way, the overarching rule is that you can’t name something that doesn’t exist in Riftbound. You can’t name the “Locke” tag, the “totem” type, nor a card named “Lingering Tentacles,” because none of those has been printed on cards or tokens in Riftbound.

However, you can name a card using information that uniquely identifies it. That information could be its name, but it could just as well be something like “the [3] spell with Flow that makes tentacles” or “the red Kai’Sa” or “Illaoi.” As long as there is no ambiguity as to what card is being named, a player can use whatever method is clear to their opponents and teammates. You can’t name a card by saying just “Kai’Sa” if there are two or more cards that could be identified in that way—you won’t have named a card if that’s all you say.

question: If I disempower a Kayle, Justified who has been empowered 3 times, does she lose all of her empowered statuses?
answer:
No. She will lose one of her empowered statuses.

For every Riftbound card other than Kayle, empowered is a binary status. They are either empowered or not. Kayle utilizes the golden rule “Card text supersedes rules text” to overcome this and be able to escape the normal bounds of what the empowered status means. On Kayle, empowered isn’t a binary status but a stacking status; she can have up to 3 empowered statuses. When Kayle is disempowered, the disempower action attempts to remove the empowered status. If she only has one empowered status, great, it’s gone. If she has more than one empowered status, the disempower action will remove one of the empowered statuses from Kayle.

question: Can I activate Kayle’s empower ability even if she’s already empowered?
answer:
Yes.

Kayle’s empower ability can be activated any number of times. If she has less than 3 empowered statuses, she will become empowered. If she has 3 empowered statuses, the ability can still be activated but nothing will happen when the ability resolves.

question: What happens if my opponent plays Flash on their Akali, Silent that’s currently in combat after I play Star-Crossed targeting her?
answer:
Akali will be unaffected by Star-Crossed as it resolves.

Akali, Silent is what the rules refer to as “untargetable” for enemy spells and abilities when she isn’t in combat; meaning she is not a legal target for them. Enemy spells and abilities being played when she’s untargetable can’t choose her. If she becomes untargetable after she’s already been chosen by an effect and retains it as that effect begins to resolve, it will “mistarget” her. She will be unaffected by any of the spell or ability’s instructions. If an instruction chooses only her, that instruction will be ignored.

question: I have a Ravenbloom Student on the board and I haven’t played any spells this turn. What happens when I play Rebuttal targeting my opponent’s Stupefy and pay [A] on resolution? After everything resolves, how much will Battering Ram cost? Will my opponent’s Legion abilities be active?
answer:
Ravenbloom Student will trigger twice, Battering Ram will cost [4], and your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active.

Ravenbloom Student’s triggered ability checks whether a spell that you control resolves. You gained control of the Stupefy, and it resolved, so you will have triggered Ravenbloom Student’s ability. Battering Ram and Legion, on the other hand, check whether cards were finalized. Although you gained control of Stupefy, you did not finalize it; you got it after it was already finalized by your opponent. Thus, your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active, and Battering Ram will only receive a [1] Energy discount.

question: What happens when I conquer with Swain, Visionary, if I’ve only played a Patched Porobot and Stupefy this turn?
answer:
You will score 2 points total. 1 from conquering, 1 from Swain.

Swain only checks whether you’ve played a non-token unit, a non-token gear, and a spell. Checks like that do not care whether they were satisfied by multiple cards or a single card relevant to the trigger conditions.

question: What happens when my opponent plays Switcheroo on their 2 [M] unit and my empowered Gangplank, Naval?
answer:
Gangplank, Naval will replace his Might being lowered with him being given +3 [M] this turn.

Swap calculates the difference in Might and generates two effects: an increase, and a decrease. When a swap effect is applied to two units’ Mights, it gives those units +[M] and -[M] respective to who has the higher Might.

Under the hood, Gangplank’s replacement effect sees the event of him being given -[M] and replaces it with him being given +3 [M] this turn instead. The event of the other unit being given +[M] is unaffected by Gangplank’s replacement effect. By the time we apply the replacement effect, the difference between the two units has been calculated. In the example with the 2 [M] unit, the final Mights of the two units will be 2 [M] → 6 [M], and 6 [M] → 9 [M].

The way this works is not immediately obvious based on how the swap game action rules are written. This is expected to be clarified in a future rules update.

Note that this logic also applies to Mel, Newly Awakened and Switcheroo.

question: What happens when my empowered Gangplank, Naval is moved by my opponent’s Blast Cone’s play effect and they exhaust Blast Cone to stun Gangplank? Will he be stunned? What happens if I then play Back Off choosing my Gangplank? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
answer:
Blast Cone will stun Gangplank. If you play Back Off choosing your stunned Gangplank, he will not receive +3 [M] this turn.

Blast Cone’s triggered ability that stuns units doesn’t choose them, so Gangplank’s replacement effect can’t apply to that event. Back Off played on a stunned Gangplank does not actually perform the stun game action, because Gangplank is already stunned. It’s legal to play Back Off, but the instruction will be negated. In order for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace an event of him being stunned, the stun game action must actually be performed. Similarly, if an effect that said “Friendly units can’t be stunned” were active with a friendly empowered Gangplank, Naval on the board, a stun effect that is played choosing Gangplank wouldn’t generate an event that Gangplank could replace, because no stun game action is performed.

question: What happens if I play Stupefy on my 1 [M] empowered Gangplank, Naval? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
answer:
He will not.

In order for his replacement effect to apply, the event of him being given -[M] must occur. In the case of Stupefy played on a 1 [M] unit, no -[M] is given; it is snapshot to -0 [M]. Thus, there is no suitable event for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace.

question: What happens when my opponent plays Hidden Blade targeting my Akali, Deadly Weapon in reaction to her move trigger? Will it still deal damage to the chosen unit?
answer:
It will.

Akali is another case where her ability refers to information implicit to its own trigger condition, similar to Iascylla. Akali’s “battlefield I moved to or from” doesn’t require her to be on the board in order for us to be able to identify it, nor does it reference information about her current state. Even if she leaves the board, that information was checked when her ability triggered, and it is still available to us on resolution.

question: Can I activate an empowered Heimerdinger, Inventor to ready 2 gear if my Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow legend isn’t empowered? What about if my Heimerdinger isn’t empowered?
answer:
You can activate Heimerdinger’s ability if he is empowered, regardless of the empowered status of Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow.

There are two important details relating to dependent keywords:

A dependent keyword (the kind of ability that [Level][>] or [Empowered][>] are when they appear with the arrow) includes the whole of the ability, including the dependent ability. They’re all one object, so to speak.

A dependent keyword’s dependent ability still exists and can be referenced while it is inactive—that is, if its condition isn’t met. In this case, the condition is that the source of the ability is empowered.

Heimerdinger gains all activated abilities that have the [E] symbol in their cost, and he gains the entire ability, restrictions, costs, dependent keywords and all. In effect, Defender of Tomorrow’s ability that Heimerdinger is gaining is the whole line that says: [Empowered][>] [1], [E]: Ready 2 gear.

Heimerdinger can gain this ability even if Defender of Tomorrow isn’t empowered because of that second point.

The key rule is 727.1.b.1.: The Dependent Ability is present on the card for the sake of reference or evaluation until the Condition is met. This means that the ability isn’t active and its text isn’t being processed yet, but other effects can reference or evaluate its text before the condition is met. Heimerdinger, Inventor is exactly one such effect.

question: What card does Astral Heron’s triggered ability discount?
answer:
It discounts the next card played (added to the chain and queued for finalization) this turn after the ability resolves.

Astral Heron has received an erratum to update its wording: “When you play your first card each turn, if I'm at a battlefield, the next card you play this turn costs [2][A][A] less.”

question: What happens when I play Temporal Breach targeting my Elder Dragon in base and pay [A][A] for Dragon Roost while playing Elder Dragon? Will it be played to base or to Dragon Roost?
answer:
You can choose which of those two locations you want to play it to.

In general, there are not many cases with competing instructions: one effect that tells you to play a unit to one location, and one that tells you to play it to another. When they arise with contradictory requirements, the precedent from other areas of the rules is that the player chooses one of those requirements and ignores all others.

Note that this only applies to mandatory positive requirements, ones that specify a location or method without also preventing the action from being performed to other locations or with other methods and that aren’t optional. For example, an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s passive ability is a restriction on playing that unit to any location other than a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Rockfall Path’s passive ability is a restriction on playing units to Rockfall Path. If you’ve conquered only Rockfall Path this turn, you can’t play Perched Grimwyrm at all, because those two restrictions are contradictory.

In this case, the contradictory requirements don’t directly prohibit the playing of these units to other locations, so we can choose one of the contradictory requirements and ignore the rest.

question: What happens when I play Perched Grimwyrm while I haven’t conquered Dragon Roost this turn? Can I pay [A][A] and play it to Dragon Roost? What if I’ve conquered another battlefield this turn?
answer:
You cannot.

In Riftbound, “can’t” beats “can.” Perched Grimwyrm’s effect is a “can’t,” as in it can’t be played to any location but to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Dragon Roost’s ability tries to give the Grimwyrm permission to be played to the Roost, but that can’t overcome Perched Grimwyrm’s own restriction. If you have no ability to play Perched Grimwyrm to Dragon Roost after paying for it, you will not be able to finalize Perched Grimwyrm at all. The actions taken as part of playing Perched Grimwyrm will be undone and it will be returned to the zone it was played from.

This is true even if you’ve conquered another battlefield this turn. If you have the ability, you can play Perched Grimwyrm to that battlefield without paying the additional cost of Dragon Roost, but you can’t play it to Dragon Roost itself unless you’ve conquered it.

Baron Nashor doesn’t work this way. He enters at the Baron Pit regardless of effects preventing him from being played to battlefields, because Baron Nashor’s passive ability generates a delayed replacement effect (“I enter there”) that replaces the event of him entering to any other location with him entering to the Baron Pit. That replacement effect gets around effects like Mageseeker Warden. Dragon Roost is not written as a replacement effect. It tells you where to play the dragon you’ve paid the additional cost for, but it doesn’t specify how that dragon enters the board. Therefore it is a permission on play location, but not a replacement effect.

question: Can I disempower my Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer to empower my Kayle? Do I control my own legend?
answer:
Yes, you can disempower Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer. And yes, you control your own legend.

We don’t typically consider the possibility that any player controls a legend, because control of legends cannot change, but you do indeed control your own legend.

question: What happens if I play Dragon Form on a unit that has -1 [M] from Stupefy applied to it? Will my Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger? Is there a moment where my unit becomes 5 [M] before the -1 [M] from Stupefy brings it down to 4 [M]?
answer:
She will not trigger.

Although Dragon Form sets the base Might of a unit to 5 [M], it does so via layers. Layers are evaluated when the effect is applied and their evaluation includes all existing applied layer alterations. We process layers in order, starting from the Trait-Altering layer (where this base Might setting effect is applied), proceeding to the Ability-Altering layer (not part of this example), and proceeding to the Arithmetic layer (where Stupefy’s -1 [M] is applied), but this process happens instantaneously; there is no window while evaluating layers for the unit to see itself become 5 [M] and then go down to 4 [M]. As soon as the effect of Dragon Form is applied, the unit is 4 [M].

As a side note, Might is one of the traits that is managed in the Trait-Altering layer, and it is one of the copyable traits that copy effects can replace or add to.

question: What happens when I play Hostile Takeover gaining control of my opponent’s ready unit, move it to base, and then play Temporal Breach choosing it? Where will the unit go?
answer:
The unit will remain in Banishment.

Units cannot be played to a base of a player other than their own controller under any circumstances. Because the owner of the unit is the one being instructed to play the unit, and the location they are being instructed to play it to is a base other than their own, it isn’t possible to play the unit. During the check legality step of finalization, the unit will be returned to banishment from the chain and all actions taken will be undone.

question: My 11 Might Renekton, Brute is disempowered by my own Profiteer. What happens when my opponent plays Stupefy choosing him? Will his ability trigger? What happens if instead I activated his ability?
answer:
Renekton’s ability will not trigger in either scenario.

In order to “become 10 or more,” his Might would have to have previously been less than 10. “10 or more” is a state, and Renekton’s triggered ability checks for the event of him achieving that state. If he maintains that state, regardless of how his Might changes, he will not “become” that state.

question: What happens when I play Icathian Rain choosing a Recruit at Heisho, Shell of the World once and Irelia, Fervent in base five times? How many times do I pay for deflect?
answer:
You will not pay for deflect.

While your spell or ability chooses a unit at Heisho, Shell of the World, you ignore deflect while paying for the spell. Ignore, in this context, means you treat deflect on the specified units as being inactive, like it’s turned off temporarily. In the case of Heisho, it doesn’t specify any units whose deflect to ignore, so you ignore all instances of deflect on units.

This only applies to the specified spell or ability. You can’t play a spell or ability choosing a unit at Heisho, and then play another one choosing a unit at another location and not at Heisho and still ignore deflect. Only while at least one target of the spell or ability is a unit located at Heisho do you ignore deflect while paying costs for that spell or ability.

question: What happens when I play Hextech Ray on an Elder Dragon while Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger is active and I have an Immortal Phoenix in the Trash? Can I play Immortal Phoenix from the Trash?
answer:
You can.

Per the current rules, there is nothing that would stop Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger from triggering Immortal Phoenix. It is a triggered ability generated by a spell; it is attributed a kill action, and thus the spell that generated it will also be attributed the same kill action. The owner of Imperial Decree is the controller of the delayed triggered ability; the player responsible for the kill action is the one who controls the ability; and that same player is the owner of Immortal Phoenix in the Trash. Thus all three conditions for Immortal Phoenix triggering are complete, and it will trigger.

question: If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?
answer:
They will be readied.

This is a rules quirk that players and judges identified as a result of a small additional rule added in the Vendetta rules update. This isn’t an actual change to how this has been interpreted and ruled on previously — it’s smoothing out a bug in how broadly “ignored” instructions were defined.

An ignored instruction is one that wasn’t performed as part of the execution of a spell or ability’s instructions because it mistargeted (i.e. because the targeted object wasn’t a legal target on resolution). For example, you play Hidden Blade choosing an enemy unit and they play Star-Crossed in reaction, returning their unit to hand — when Hidden Blade resolves, the unit isn’t on the board, so we ignore the “Its controller draws 2.” instruction. Alternatively, if Hidden Blade is given the Repeat keyword by the Academy and both executions target the same unit, this is why the unit’s controller doesn’t draw 4 cards.

An instruction is not ignored if an ability, effect, or circumstance of the game prevents it from occurring. That could be a replacement effect, an ability like Vilemaw’s Lair that says “Units can’t move from here to base,” a game action like Buff or Ready on a unit that already has the appropriate state, or a unit/gear/spell no longer being in an appropriate zone as long as the instruction doesn’t target those objects. In those cases the instruction isn’t ignored, but instead negated. A negated instruction has its effects skipped, replaced, or prevented. A negated instruction will not cause any linked instructions to be ignored unless those instructions refer specifically to the action being performed.

Examples:

If a unit at a battlefield says “I can’t be killed.” and a player plays Hidden Blade choosing that unit, the unit’s controller will still draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (Negated, not ignored — linked instruction still executes.)

If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Flash moving it to base, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (Ignored — linked instructions ignored.)

If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Zhonya’s Hourglass, that unit’s controller will draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The unit is on the board and its information can be checked; negated, not ignored.)

If a unit at a battlefield has been affected by Smite previously this turn and it is chosen by Hidden Blade, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The instruction is executed, but the unit is not on the board to have its information checked; it was also moved to a non-board zone by an effect other than Hidden Blade, so it no longer has a controller Hidden Blade can reference.)

question: when you conquer sigil of the storm, it says recycle 1 power. when you do this, can you still gain the power from recycling? or does it cost 1 power?
answer:
No — the recycle doesn't give you Power, and it doesn't cost Power from your pool either. Sigil of the Storm says "recycle one of your runes," not "pay 1 Power" — it's a required effect, not a [C] payment.

Power only enters your pool when you activate a rune's own "Recycle this: [Reaction] — Add [C]" ability (Rule 164.2.b). Sigil's recycle is a separate instruction, so the same recycle can't both satisfy Sigil and produce Power. The rune just goes to the bottom of your Rune Deck (CR 417).

What you can do: tap that rune for [1] Energy before Sigil's trigger resolves, and keep that Energy floating for the rest of the turn (FAQ 2810). And if you have no runes at all, the trigger resolves and simply does nothing (FAQ 6863).

question: if my opponent plays dragon with ability 'kill a unit' and then i use temporal breach on my watcher. does the dragon get -3 or no. does the order of chain matter or is the unit played already and just its ability on chain is unresolved?
answer:
Yes — the dragon gets -3 Might, and chain order doesn't change that.

The dragon resolved as a permanent the moment it was played; only its "when you play me" ability is sitting unresolved on the Chain (Rules 359.2, 383.4.a.2). So when your Watcher's -3 resolves, the dragon is already an enemy unit on the board and gets -3 (to a minimum of 1) — same as any other unit present at that time.

One thing order does affect: Temporal Breach banishes your Watcher and replays it as a new game object. So if the dragon's kill/damage ability had already targeted the Watcher, it will mistarget and do nothing to the replayed Watcher (Rule 359.3.e.4). The -3 doesn't stop an outright "kill" or Elder Dragon's lethal 1-damage otherwise — but in this case the original target no longer exists.

question: Sigil of storm battlefield which says recycle a rune when you conquer. When you do this do you still gain the power from recycling it? Floating?
answer:
No — recycling the rune for Sigil of the Storm does not add Power to your pool; the Recycle action itself produces nothing.

Power only comes from activating a rune's own ability "Recycle this: [Reaction] — Add [C]" (Rule 164.2.b) — and that consumes the rune, so you can't get Power from the same rune Sigil recycles. What you can do: tap the rune for Energy first (FAQ 2810), then recycle that same rune for Sigil's trigger — the floated Energy stays in your pool for the turn. If you instead recycle a rune via its ability to bank Power, Sigil still needs a different rune to recycle; if you have none left, its trigger simply does nothing (FAQ 6863).

question: if my unit has 1 dmg on it. and the other player plays elder dragon. do they all die. or does he need to do more damage after its played?
answer:
It depends on whose damage that 1 point is.

If that 1 damage was marked by the Elder Dragon player (their spell, their combat damage, etc.), the unit dies the moment Elder Dragon enters play — no additional damage needed. Elder Dragon's passive changes the lethal threshold so that any amount of their damage is enough (Rule 142.4.c; FAQ #10686), and a cleanup check happens immediately as it enters.

If the 1 damage was dealt by you (your own spells/combat), Elder Dragon's passive doesn't touch it — it only applies to damage marked by Elder Dragon's controller. However, Elder Dragon's "When you play me" trigger deals 1 to up to one enemy unit at each location, and that 1 point is their damage, so any unit it hits will die (unless the damage is prevented, e.g., Counter Strike). So in practice: pre-existing damage from them = instant death; otherwise they still die from the ping as long as it connects.

question: Can I play vi peacekeeper in reaction to a temporal breach which targeted brynhir?
answer:
It depends on whether Brynhir's "When you play me" trigger has already resolved — and whose side you're on.

If you're an opponent of Brynhir's controller and her trigger already resolved this turn: No. "Opponents can't play cards this turn" is a blanket prohibition — it doesn't just restrict timing, it forbids playing any card at all. Vi's Ambush gives her [Reaction] timing permission, but that can't override a "can't play cards" effect (FAQ 7114: even Hidden cards are blocked).

If Brynhir's trigger is still on the chain (unresolved), or if you're Brynhir's controller (her ability only hits opponents): Yes. Temporal Breach on the chain creates a Closed State, and Vi's Ambush lets you play her as a Reaction to a battlefield you control where you have units (Rule 813.3.a). Note this doesn't stop Temporal Breach — it resolves, banishing and replaying Brynhir, which re-triggers her "When you play me," so the lockout still lands afterward.

question: Can I still trigger conquer and hold effects even when you can't score yet on forbidden waste?
answer:
Assuming you mean Forgotten Monument ("Players can't score here until their third turn") — No. While that restriction is active you cannot Conquer or Hold there, so no conquer/hold effects trigger (FAQ #4900, CR 471–473).

The key distinction: "can't score" blocks the entire scoring action (Conquering and Holding are both forms of scoring), not just the point gain. Cards like Tianna Crownguard that say "can't score points" still let the score process happen and trigger effects — but Forgotten Monument is the stricter kind, so no triggers.

One note: Forbidding Waste is a different card — it only applies a −2 Might penalty to a unit defending alone, and has no scoring restriction at all, so conquer/hold effects there trigger normally.

question: If I hold a battlefield with one unit and move it back to base, if I move another unit into that same battlefield that is now open does a showdown begin?
answer:
Yes. Moving your last unit off leaves the battlefield uncontrolled, so moving a fresh unit into it applies Contested and opens a non-combat showdown during the next cleanup (CR 344.2, 447).

Important nuance: the showdown only re-establishes your control — you do not score again at that battlefield, since you already scored it via Hold earlier this turn (CR 449; FAQ #7971). Also, unless your opponent has a unit there when it opens, it's a non-combat showdown, so no Combat Cleanup/healing occurs.

question: If I hold a battlefield playing as akali and I move my only unit back to base from that battlefield can I move my stellacorn horder to that battlefield and activate my akali legend to move it back?
answer:
Yes — the whole line works, and Stellacorn Herder draws a card on each leg.

Moving your only unit out makes you lose control of that battlefield (CR 323.5), but a Standard Move from base to a battlefield doesn't require control of the destination (Rule 144.4). So Stellacorn Herder can still move there — that applies Contested and stages a Non-Combat Showdown, and its "When I move" trigger draws 1.

Once the showdown begins, you're the player who applied Contested, so you have Focus (Rule 345), and Rogue Assassin's Action ability is legally timed during a showdown on your turn (Rule 347.1). Activating it moves Herder back to base — that's a Move, not a Recall, so it draws a second card.

Caveats: the battlefield ends up empty and uncontrolled (no Conquer, since no unit remains when the showdown closes — and you'd already scored it via Hold this turn anyway), and you still can't play units there from hand after losing control; only moves into it are allowed.

question: If i have a cithria at base and i play a ablus ferros can i spent the buff cithria will get from playing another unit?
answer:
Yes. When you play Albus Ferros, both triggers go on the Chain at the same time — Cithria's "when you play another unit, buff me" and Albus's "when you play me, spend any number of buffs." Since you control both, you order them so Cithria's resolves first, putting a buff on her, then Albus's spends that buff to channel a rune.

This is confirmed by FAQ 7766: stack the play effects, resolve Cithria's buff first, then spend it for Albus's effect. Just remember Cithria has to be on the board before Albus is played (she doesn't buff herself when played alone), and she'll only have that one buff to spend since a unit can only hold one at a time.

question: If I have a shadow clone that attack 2 times in a turn will it have assault 8 or assault 4 ?
answer:
Assault 8 — if both triggers resolve.

Shadow Clone's token ability is a triggered "when I attack" that grants it Assault 4 this turn. Since that bonus lasts this turn, and Assault values from multiple sources sum (Rule 807.2), two successful triggers (banish a unit from your trash both times) give the clone Assault 4 + Assault 4 = Assault 8 while it's an attacker on the second attack. It would only be Assault 4 during the first combat.

This differs from printed Assault on cards like Lucian, which is a passive ability that simply toggles on/off each combat and doesn't accumulate. If you can't pay the banish cost on the second attack, you'd keep only the first Assault 4.

question: If my opponent plays Promising Future and chooses Dazzling Aurora and I choose Acceptable Losses, does Acceptable Losses kill the Dazzling Aurora?
answer:
Yes, this is due to the sequence of Promising Future.

When your opponent plays Promising Future, they decide first which card to banish (in this case Dazzling Aurora). Then you decide which to banish (Acceptable Losses).

To complete the Promising Future resolution, you put your chosen card on the chain first and as a pending item. Then the opponent does the same.

With Promising Future fully resolved we can start finalizing the pending items on the chain. This is done up the chain, first pending item gets finalized first.

So this is your Acceptable Losses. And as a spell, it lingers on the chain.

Important: Acceptable Losses does not target. It says "Each player kills one of their gear."

Second, we finalize Dazzling Aurora. And as a gear it enters play immediately.

Now with all items on the chain finalized, we can start resolving down the chain (LIFO).

Only 1 item remains on the chain though, Acceptable Losses. This resolves and its effect goes through.

If your opponent has no other gear besides Dazzling Aurora, they will be forced to kill it.

question: Does Disposal Order prevent me from playing Rhasa after Last Rites after already paying its cost?
answer:

Playing a card moves it from its zone onto the Chain in step 1 (Rule 354), so Rhasa is already on the Chain — not in your trash — before its cost is determined and paid. Disposal Order only recycles cards in opponents' trashes, so Rhasa isn't a legal choice, and recycling other cards from your trash can't retroactively raise its already-paid cost (Rule 356).

The one window that works: play Disposal Order in response to the Last Rites trigger while it's still on the chain, before it resolves. If you recycle Rhasa out of your trash then, it won't be there when Last Rites resolves and can't be played.

question: The text in the card saying “when you play me” when can you consider a card being played?
answer:
A card is considered "played" once the act of playing it has been completed by the card resolving — not when you announce it or put it on the Chain (CR 420.4.a).

So for a unit: you put it on the Chain, it resolves and enters the battlefield, and only then does "When you play me" go on the Chain as a triggered ability. If the card is countered before it resolves, the trigger never happens (419.4.a.1). Triggered abilities that check "play" mean "resolve"; non-triggered checks (like Battering Ram's cost reduction) mean "finalize."

question: what are some body and mind cards that can help discard your shitty hand and draw another
answer:
Short answer: Body/Mind barely has real "discard a bad hand, draw a new one" filtering — that effect mostly lives in Chaos/Fury. Here's what actually exists in your two domains:

Mind (Blue)

Hwei, Brooding Painter (5E champion) — the only true rummage in Mind: "When I move, draw 1, then discard 1," with a bonus based on what you ditched (Spell → draw 1, Gear → ready 2 runes, Unit → +3 [S]). Pair him with move effects and he's a repeatable filter.

Gutter Palace (4E gear) — discard 1, [T]: play a 1 [S] Bird token with [Deflect]. Turns dead cards into board presence, but no draw.

Pure replacement draw (no discard, but fixes a bricked hand): Progress Day (draw 4), Premonition (draw 3, Reaction), Consult the Past (draw 2, Hidden/Reaction), Renata Glasc, Mastermind ([1] rune: draw 1), Stupefy (draw 1, Reaction).

Body (Orange)

No discard-draw filters exist in Body. Your draw is limited to Spoils of War (draw 2, Reaction, cheaper if an enemy died), Confront (draw 1), Mobilize / Catalyst of Aeons (draw 1 if you couldn't channel), and Qiyana, Victorious (draw 1 on conquer).

If you really want the "pitch hand, draw again" feel, you'll want a Chaos splash, since Mind and Chaos share the Swift Scout legend:

Invert Timelines (Chaos, 3E) — the only true full redraw: "Each player discards their hand, then draws 4."

Traveling Merchant (Chaos, 2E) — discard 1, draw 1 every time it moves (repeatable rummage).

Doran's Ring (Chaos gear) and Zaun Warrens (colorless battlefield) — discard 1, draw 1 on Conquer.

Bottom line: if you're locked to Body/Mind, Hwei plus the big Mind draw spells is your best filter package; actual discard-draw engines need a Chaos splash.

question: !can Tornado Warrior empower something that does not have the empower mechanic? Also, if Tornado Warrior dies after being played from hidden and resolving, does a card that gets empowered still get disempowered at the end of the turn?

The status does nothing on its own; it only matters if another effect references it. The only restriction is the target can't already be Empowered (CR 442.1.b–c). So Tornado Warrior can empower anything at its battlefield, even a vanilla card.

2. Yes. "Disempower it at end of turn" is a Delayed Trigger created when Tornado Warrior's play-from-hidden ability resolved. Delayed Abilities are not tied to their source's presence — they execute at their specified time regardless of whether the source is still on the board (CR 393). So if Tornado Warrior dies, the disempower still fires at end of turn. One caveat: if the empowered card left the board (it loses Empowered when it leaves) or was already disempowered, the delayed trigger simply does nothing (CR 443.1.a).

question: if I use tactical retreat on a unit does it do its full damage before being sent to base and does it conquer
answer:
Yes, it deals its full damage — but no, it will not conquer.

Tactical Retreat doesn't send the unit to base right away. It only sets up a replacement effect for "the next time it would die this turn." So the unit stays at the battlefield, participates in the Combat Damage Step normally, and deals its full combat damage simultaneously with the defenders. Only afterwards, if it took lethal damage and would die, does the replacement effect heal, exhaust, and recall it to base instead.

It won't conquer, though. Control and Conquer are determined during the Resolution Step, and that only happens for the player who still has units remaining at the battlefield (CR 468.5). Since your unit is back in your base, you have no units there (assuming it was your only one), so the defender establishes or keeps control — and they may even conquer if they haven't scored that battlefield this turn. If you had other units still present, those could conquer, but not the recalled unit.

question: Can a stunned unit conquer an open battlefield
answer:

The contrast: if enemy units are present and survive combat, the stunned attacker is recalled during Combat Cleanup (3d) instead of conquering. Against an open battlefield there's no combat at all — just a Non-Combat Showdown where your unit alone establishes Control and Conquers.

When these finalize, Brynhir resolves first (she was placed on the chain first), and her WYPM trigger goes on the chain above Dazzling Aurora. But Dazzling Aurora was already played and is a pending item on the chain — Brynhir's effect only prevents new card plays (taking cards from a zone and putting them on the chain). question: Deck out rules in riftbound
answer:
You can't lose by "decking out" — instead, running out causes a Burn Out, which hands your opponent points.

Drawing the last card is free. As long as your Main Deck has ≥1 card when you draw, you just draw it — no penalty (CR 414.4).

Drawing from an empty deck triggers a Burn Out. You draw as many as possible, shuffle your Trash into your Main Deck (randomized), choose an opponent to gain 1 point, then finish the draw (CR 432.2). If your Trash is also empty, you Burn Out repeatedly — each attempt gives another point.

Burn Out points are dangerous: after the first Burn Out resolves, subsequent points can't be prevented, and if a Burn Out point puts a player at/above the Victory Score, that player wins immediately — no waiting for cleanup (CR 432.3).

Looking/revealing cards doesn't Burn Out — if an effect tells you to reveal/look at the top X but you have fewer, you just reveal as many as possible and resolve it normally (CR 432.1.c).

Milling to Trash (putting cards from deck to Trash) also causes a Burn Out if it exceeds your remaining deck (CR 432.1.b).

question: !ask how does priority during i.e showdown work? I play a reaction spell or unit. Do I still have focus to play another reaction speed unit or spell or does my opponent have it first? Yes to reactions, no to focus. Playing a Reaction (or any chain item) gives you priority first, so you can stack multiple reactions in a row before your opponent gets a chance — focus isn't consumed by reactions (FAQ 4908, Rule 312.2.c/338.1.a.5). You only pass priority when you choose to pass it.

Once the chain empties back to a Showdown Open State, focus passes to the next player in turn order — that player gets priority and may open a new chain with an Action spell (Rule 340.2.a/346). You cannot "hold focus" to chain a second Action; you'd get focus back only after your opponent passes without acting (Rule 347).

One exception: if the chain opened from triggered abilities or an Add ability (e.g., the initial attack/defend trigger chain), focus does not pass when it closes — the attacker keeps it (Rule 346.1, FAQ 8169). Also remember: Actions can only be played during Open State; while the chain is up it's Reactions only.

question: in bf1 attack hahs 1 unit with 5 might. Defence has a Shadow Clone and a Zed, Without a sound. What hahppens in the end of showdown?
answer:
The defender wins the combat. Both the attacker's 5-Might unit and Zed, Without a Sound are dealt lethal damage (5 each) and die during the Combat Cleanup; the 0-Might Shadow Clone survives untouched.

Sequence:

Combat damage (CR 467): Attacker sums 5 Might, defender sums 5 (Zed 5 + Clone 0). The attacker must fully assign lethal before moving on, so they can only kill one defender unit (5 to Zed is the efficient play). The defender assigns 5 to the attacker's unit — lethal.

Combat Cleanup (CR 468.1): Lethal-damage units are killed (attacker's unit and Zed). Units are then healed, and attackers are only recalled if defenders are still present — but the attacker's unit is already dead, so no recall.

Result (CR 468.3): The Shadow Clone is the only unit remaining, so the defender is the only player with units → defender wins.

Control (CR 468.5): The defender establishes control of the battlefield (clearing Contested), which is a Conquer if they haven't already scored that battlefield this turn.

Note: if the attacker instead split damage (e.g., 1 to the Clone, 4 to Zed), the Clone dies to lethal (1 damage ≥ 0 Might) but Zed survives with 4 damage — defender still wins. The attacker cannot kill both defender units with only 5 damage.

question: Can fortify position give its effect twice? So shield 2 in one combat and then another combat happens to give it shield 2 again so +4
answer:

Cross-combat stacking doesn't happen — "this combat" effects all expire simultaneously at the end of combat (CR 468.7.c), so the two grants never coexist.

Fortified Position can't fire twice in one combat either — defend triggers are only checked once per combat (Rule 383.4.f.2.a).

Where Shield does stack is when sources overlap in the same combat — e.g., a unit with native Shield 2 defending on Fortified Position totals Shield 4 (FAQ 2459). But that requires two simultaneous grants, not one per combat.

question: !ask my opponent is asking me to say in plain voice every move I am doing. "I will play..." I want to concentrate on my game and not talk to him. Am I compelled by the rules to do so ? What if I refuse ?
answer:
No — you're not required to narrate every move in plain voice. Rules only require that changes to public information be acknowledged in an "understandable and observable way" — verbally, physically, or by agreed convention — and physically playing a card face-up is itself that acknowledgment (TR 502.6.a). You're also explicitly not required to assist your opponent in playing the game (TR 501.3); the one exception is that scoring points must be verbally announced.

If you refuse: as long as your actions are clear and observable, refusing to narrate is not a violation. However, if your opponent asks a direct question about public information ("what did you just play?"), you must answer honestly — refusing that is a Communication Violation (Warning, TR 703.5/502.7). If they're asking you to read out private/derived info like what a Hidden card is or your hand, you don't have to disclose it. If the demand continues, you can call a judge and keep playing normally in the meantime.

question: if my opponent moonfalls my unit from a battlefield i control to on they control, could i then reveal a hidden tideturner to move that unit back?
answer:

When it leaves, the following cleanup makes you lose control of that battlefield (Open state, no units there), and the hidden Tideturner is trashed in that same cleanup — there's no priority window to play it in between. This is the same result as Charm or Blitzcrank moving your only unit away (FAQ 1943, FAQ 8081).

If you kept another unit there, there's still no window right after Moonfall resolves — the chain is empty on your opponent's turn, and in Neutral Open only the turn player can act. But your unit landing on their battlefield applies Contested and opens a Showdown there. During that Showdown — and since your unit applied the Contested status, you gain Focus first (Rule 345) — you can play the hidden Tideturner as a Reaction. Its errata lets it target a unit you control "at another location" (CR 811.1.d.3), so it swaps with your unit and brings it back; Tideturner takes its place on their battlefield (FAQ 1652, FAQ 281).

Note: playing Tideturner in response to Moonfall while it's on the chain won't save the unit — Tideturner enters at the same battlefield as the target, so there's no "another location" to swap with, and Moonfall still moves the targeted unit.

question: can you explain all the steps when combat happens, to include deathknell triggers
answer:
Combat only opens through a Cleanup: when opposing units end up at the same Battlefield with no ongoing Combat, the Cleanup stages a Showdown (and a Combat), and the Turn Player picks which Staged Combat to open if there are several (CR 323.6–323.11). From there the sequence is:

1. Combat Showdown Step (CR 466). Attacker (the player who applied Contested) and Defender are designated; Attacker gains Focus. Any triggers generated by that designation go on the Chain (Attacker first, then other players in turn order, Defender last). Players then play cards/abilities with Action or Reaction and pass Focus until all pass — the Showdown closes. If a unit dies here (spell, on-attack trigger), its Deathknell finalizes and resolves now, before any damage.

2. Combat Damage Step (CR 467). If both sides still have units, sum attacker and defender Might. Starting with the Attacker, each player assigns damage equal to their total among the opponent's units — you must assign full lethal to one unit before moving to the next (Tank/Backline reorder this, and some cards redefine "lethal"). Only after all assignment is done is the damage dealt, simultaneously.

3. Resolution Step — Combat Cleanup (CR 468.1, 323). This is where combat-death Deathknells fire:

Units with lethal damage that have Deathknell (or "when I die" abilities) trigger first, as Pending Items, noting their stats/location before they leave (Rule 383.2.c.3).

Those units are then Killed and sent to their owners' trashes (CR 323.4).

All units in play heal (Combat Special Cleanup insertion 3c).

Attackers still present are recalled if defenders remain (3d).

Only after that do the Deathknell triggers finalize and resolve — after healing, so a damaging Deathknell can't finish off survivors (FAQ 10444).

4. After cleanup (CR 468.3–468.7). Determine Combat Result — sole remaining side wins; "No Result" if both or neither have units (which can re-stage Combat). Then establish control, clear Contested, Conquer if you hadn't scored that Battlefield this turn, and remove Attacker/Defender designations as combat ends.

Two gotchas: Deathknell is "when I die", not "when I attack" (Rule 808.1.c), and if the kill is replaced by something like a recall, the Deathknell trigger is removed from the Chain (Rule 808.1.d.1).

question: when do you heal after after combat to include deathknell triggers, breakdown the steps
answer:
Ruling: Deathknell triggers fire before the heal, but they resolve after it — so the heal happens first as far as any play decisions are concerned.

Here's the full combat resolution breakdown (CR 467.3 → 466):

Combat Damage Step (CR 467) — damage is assigned and dealt simultaneously.

FEPR is skipped (CR 467.3) and play jumps straight into the Resolution Step (CR 468.1).

Combat Cleanup begins:

3a (CR 383.2.c.3): Units with lethal damage that have Deathknell (or other "when I die" abilities) trigger just before they are killed — their triggers are processed and placed on the chain, with the information they need noted.

3b (CR 323.5): Those units are Killed and placed in their owner's trash.

3c (CR 468.1.a.1): Heal all units — every unit in play, not just those that fought.

3d (CR 468.1.a.2): Recall attacking units still present if defenders remain.

Determine Combat Result (CR 468.3), then Establish Control / Conquer (CR 468.5) and Combat ends (CR 468.7).

FEPR resumes — only now do the Pending Deathknell triggers get finalized and resolve on the chain.

Practical takeaways: Deathknell cannot finish off units that survived with non-lethal damage (they heal first), and cannot save a unit that took lethal damage (it's already in the trash before anything resolves). Same timing applies to "when I die" abilities — they were aligned with Deathknell in the Vendetta rules update.

FAQ #9514 covers this exact sequence (Rule refs: 465.3, 466.1, 466.1.a.1, 383.2.c.3, 323.5, 808.1.d).

ruleReferences.text: When in combat showdown, if a unit with deathknell is killed, does the deathknell trigger and resolve before healing or after?
Does Deathknell trigger happen after a unit heals on a battlefield?
Does the Deathknell effect in a combat clean up trigger before or after the unit heal?

question: How does Helm of Suppression interact with hidden cards? Does it increase the cost of revealing them?
answer:
It depends on what was hidden. Helm of Suppression only raises the cost of spells, so:

Hidden spell: Yes — playing it from Hidden still counts as playing a spell. Hidden sets its base cost to 0 (Rule 811.1.b → 356.1.b), but cost increases apply afterward (Rule 356.3), so it costs [1] more (or [1][A] more if Helm is Empowered). Same logic as the Fizz ruling (FAQ #11727).

Hidden unit or gear: No — they aren't spells, so Helm does nothing to them.

The hide action itself: No — hiding costs 1 Power (recycle a rune) and isn't playing a spell, so Helm never touches it.

Net effect: Helm makes revealing a hidden spell not-free, but leaves hidden units, gear, and the hiding cost alone.

question: In a BO1 match of Riftbound, when are you allowed to side deck?
answer:
No — by default you can never sideboard in a BO1 match. Sideboarding is only permitted between games of a match (Rule 403.4), and a BO1 has only one game. Rule 403.5 additionally forbids using sideboard cards in the first game of a match.

The one exception: the head judge may opt into the altered BO1 setup process, which includes a single sideboard opportunity before game 1 begins (TR 406.1.h.5). Unless the event specifically announced that change, your main deck stays locked.

question: So I'm defending with Ahri, and a Hidden Temporal Breach. They move in and Ahri's defend trigger happens. They pass and I reveal Temporal Breach on my Ahri. Does the defend trigger happen again?
answer:
Yes — Ahri's defend trigger fires again.

Temporal Breach banishes Ahri, and Banishment is a non-board zone, so she becomes a brand-new game object (Rule 124). That new Ahri has never gained the Defender designation in this combat, so when she gains it during the Cleanup after Breach resolves, her "When I defend" trigger goes on the Chain normally (383.4.f.2.a). This is the same line as the Arcane Shift + Ahri ruling (FAQ #5362).

The key difference from "moving to base and back": merely relocating without leaving the board keeps the same object, so the once-per-combat check would hold — banish-and-replay is what resets it. Also fine here: a Hidden Breach's target must be at the battlefield it was hidden at, and Ahri is right there defending.

question: Can I use Accurate to ready a unit that is always on the playing field? Say I moved it from a battlefield to base. Can I pay the Accelerate cost?
answer:
No. Accelerate only works "as you play" a unit — it's an optional additional cost paid during the steps of playing that unit as a card (CR 805.1.b, 805.2). A unit already on the board cannot pay Accelerate; it has no function there (Rule 805.2.a, 805.3).

Moving a unit from a battlefield to your base (Standard Move or an effect) is not "playing" it, so you can't pay the cost, and the move doesn't ready it — the unit remains in whatever state it was in unless the effect specifically readies it. Accelerate only ever applies when the unit enters play from hand or another non-board zone.

question: Does Rek'Sai Breacher work with Shadow Clone?
answer:
Yes — Rek'Sai, Breacher lets your Shadow Clone tokens enter ready, but only if you pay the Accelerate cost.

Shadow Clones (e.g., from Death Mark or Zed, From the Shadows) are played from a zone other than a player's hand, so Rek'Sai grants them Accelerate as they're being played. Accelerate is an optional additional cost — 1 Energy and 1 Shadow Power — paid during the Pay Costs step of playing the token. Since the Shadow Clone has a single domain ([S]), the Power portion must be Shadow Power, not generic [A]. If you don't pay, it enters exhausted as normal. (FAQ #11708, CR 805.1.b.1)

question: Can I play a unit in banish from Cursed Sarcophagus with shadow clone?
answer:
No. Cursed Sarcophagus can only play units banished by its own play trigger ("When you play this, banish all units from your trash"). A unit banished by the Shadow Clone token's attack trigger was banished by the token's effect, so Cursed Sarcophagus's "[T]: Play a unit banished with this" cannot access it.

Banishment tracking is strictly per-object: each effect can only reference cards banished by its own linked abilities (CR 428.3.a, CR 398). Same principle as two different banishing cards never sharing their banished pools — the token and the gear are separate sources, so their banished units are separate pools.

question: Can you use Zed legend ability to draw 1 even if you have no cards to discard?
answer:
Yes. Master of Shadows (Zed's legend) says "Disempower me, [T]: Discard 1, then draw 1." The discard is part of the effect, not a cost — the costs are only disempowering and exhausting. So with an empty hand you discard 0 and still draw 1 (CR 423.4: discard as many as possible, then continue with the rest of the effect).

This is the opposite of the Deceiver (LeBlanc) legend, whose "discard 1" sits before "to" as a cost — that one can't be activated with an empty hand (CR 423.3). For Zed, the "then" wording makes the draw unconditional.

question: Can you react to a unit dying?
answer:
Yes — with an important distinction. You can't react to the death event itself, but you can react to whatever is on the Chain that leads to it.

What you CAN react to:

The effect that kills the unit — a kill/damage spell, an activated ability, or a trigger like Temporary — while it's still on the Chain (Rule 359.3, FAQ #2751).

Triggered abilities that fire because of the death, like Deathknell or "When I die…" — those go on the Chain as pending items and create a reaction window (CR 383.2.c.3, 429.1.a.1.b).

What you CANNOT react to:

The death itself. When a kill instruction resolves or lethal damage is checked in a Cleanup, the unit dies immediately with no priority granted — you can't slip a save in between (FAQ #2971, FAQ #11388).

So: react to the cause, or to the death-trigger — but not to the moment of death.

question: Can you banish a unit from your trash with a shadow clone if the battlefield is empty?
answer:
No. "When I attack" only triggers when a unit gains the Attacker designation during Combat — moving a Shadow Clone to an empty battlefield stages a Non-Combat Showdown, and no Attacker designation is ever granted there, so the trigger never fires and you can't banish.

The banish-from-trash itself is perfectly legal as an effect (banishing from the trash is allowed — CR 428, FAQ #9081); the issue is purely that the trigger condition isn't met.

If the battlefield is occupied by an enemy unit (a real Combat Showdown), the Shadow Clone does gain the Attacker designation and its trigger fires, letting you banish a unit from your trash and give it Assault 4. Per Rule 383.4.e and FAQ #8664.

question: If I move out of a battlefield I conquered and played a hidden card there, does the hidden card disappear?
answer:
Yes — if you move your last unit out of that battlefield, the hidden card goes to your trash.

A Move triggers a Cleanup when it completes (CR 455). If you have no units left at a battlefield in an Open State, you lose control of it in that cleanup (CR 323.5), and any hidden cards at battlefields you no longer control are placed in their owner's trash (CR 323.6.a, 107.3.d; FAQ #6608). Control is only preserved if another of your units remains there, or if a Showdown/Combat is ongoing at that battlefield.

So the card only survives the move if you keep control — leaving even one unit behind keeps the hidden card safe.

question: Can I react to Baited Hook with Smokescreen to change the target's might and alter what he can use?
answer:
Yes, you can. Smoke Screen has [Reaction], so it resolves first (LIFO) and reduces the targeted unit's Might — to a minimum of 1 — before Baited Hook kills it.

Baited Hook checks the killed unit's current Might at the moment of death (Rule 710; FAQ #6060), not its printed Might. So if you Smoke Screen a 4-Might unit down to 1, the opponent can only fetch a unit of Might 2 or less instead of 5 or less. The unit is still on the board when you play Smoke Screen, so it's a legal target. If the unit instead leaves the board entirely before Baited Hook resolves, the kill fizzles and its Might is treated as null — the opponent reveals the top 5 but can't play any unit (Rule 359.3.e.12).

question: If my target of Discipline gets Gusted, do I get the draw?
answer: Yes — you still draw. Gust resolves first and returns the unit, but Discipline's "Draw 1" is a separate, non-conditional instruction: it executes even when the +2 Might can't be applied because the target left play (Rule 359.3.e.5). Spells always resolve as much as possible — only the instructions tied to the vanished target are ignored.

question: While Minotaur Reckoner is on the board, can a unit move to a base through any other effect apart from its own move effect, e.g. with a Ride the Wind spell?
answer:
No — while Minotaur Reckoner is on the board, no unit can Move to base by any means, including spells like Ride the Wind. Its ability "Units can't move to base" is a blanket restriction on the Move action, not just the Standard Move.

The spell or ability still resolves, but the move instruction simply fails — per Rule 359.3.e.6, instructions that can't be followed because of a restriction are negated (FAQ #8815).

One caveat: Recalls are not Moves (CR 453), so effects that recall a unit to base would still work. But any effect that literally says "move to base" — Ride the Wind, Tideturner, Reaver's Row, etc. — is prevented.

question: Does the wordkey when I attack trigger on an empty battlefield?
answer:
No. "When I attack" triggers only fire when a unit gains the Attacker designation, which happens only during a Combat Showdown — moving to an empty battlefield is a Non-Combat Showdown (CR 383.4.e, 461.2.b).

The trigger checks once when the designation is gained, and since there's no enemy unit, no combat, and no Attacker designation, nothing triggers.

One edge case: if your opponent later moves a unit into that battlefield during the showdown (e.g., via Ride the Wind), combat begins and your unit becomes the Attacker — the attack trigger fires then (FAQ #9339).

question: When is Overzealous Fan activated? After or before actions is passed, do you need to pay the deflect cost? Can I counter the effect with Not So Fast?
answer:
Overzealous Fan's ability triggers the first time it gains the Defender designation during a combat showdown — that's its Defend Trigger (Rule 383.4.f).

If the Fan is already at the battlefield when combat opens, it gains Defender at combat start and triggers then. If it enters mid-combat (e.g., via Moonfall or a swap effect), it gains Defender at the next Cleanup and triggers at that point — but only once per combat (383.4.f.2.a). Because the ability says "you may kill me," using it is optional, and the kill is paid upfront as a cost to put the trigger on the chain — so countering the ability doesn't save the Fan (FAQ 8702, Rule 383.3.b.1).

question: If I move into a battlefield that's open, will I be designated as an attacking unit for the spell that can stun an attacking unit?
answer:
No. Moving into an open battlefield doesn't give your unit the attacker designation — that move creates a Non-Combat Showdown, not Combat, and attacker/defender designations only exist during Combat (CR 438; FAQ #5513). So spells like Existential Dread ("Stun an attacking enemy unit") or Shadow's ability couldn't target your unit at that point.

The one caveat: if your opponent plays a unit via Ambush as a Reaction to that Showdown, the Showdown becomes a Combat Showdown and you become the Attacker (you applied Contested). From then on, your unit is an attacking unit and those stun effects can hit it.

question: If you Temporal Breach a copied token, does it still have temporary?
answer:
No — and it doesn't matter, because the token is gone permanently.

Temporal Breach banishes the target, and a token that enters Banishment (a Non-Board Zone) ceases to exist immediately (Rule 186.1). The "its owner plays it to the same location" part has nothing to act on and is ignored. So whether the token still has Temporary (granted by Mirror Image/Deceiver) is moot — it never returns, and granted keywords don't survive a zone change to a non-board zone anyway. Same result for any token, copied or not (FAQ #11668).

question: Does Aeron count as first card for the effect?
answer: There's no card named "Aeron" in the database — I'm assuming you mean Astral Heron. Yes: it counts as your first card. Its trigger checks after it finalizes on the battlefield, so it sees itself as the first card played, and the discount applies to your next card — the second card you play that turn (CR 420.4.a). It never discounts itself.

question: Can you defy Public Execution if it is played with Flow?
answer:
Yes — Defy can counter Public Execution even when it's played via Flow.

Defy checks the printed cost of the target spell (2 Energy, 1 Power for Public Execution), not what was actually paid. That printed cost is within Defy's range (≤4 energy, ≤1 power), so playing it from your trash for its Flow cost doesn't change anything — the alternate cost only affects what you pay, not Defy's legal targets. If the spell resolves, it still banishes itself as normal; if Defied, it just goes to the trash like any countered spell.

question: My opponent has Hwei on base and plays a Tide Turner on base. Declines to move anything. Does a trigger still occur that creates a chain I can react to?
answer:
No. Tideturner's "you may" is decided during finalization — if its controller declines, the ability is removed from the chain and never becomes a Finalized Chain Item, so no chain exists and you get no reaction window.

This follows Rule 383.3.a.2 (a "you may" that leads the effect decides whether the ability is performed at all; declining means it "is removed from the chain and considered to have not triggered"). It also doesn't matter that Hwei is at Base: "another location" excludes Base, so there was no legal swap target anyway (CR 403.4). Note that even when the trigger is performed, you couldn't react to Tideturner entering play itself — you can only react to the play-effect chain that follows (FAQ #6244).

question: Token copy of a Watchful Sentry, but Dragon Form was played on Watchful Sentry. Does the token get the 1 might or its new base 5 might?
answer:
The token gets 1 Might — it copies Watchful Sentry's copyable traits, not the temporary effect Dragon Form is applying to the original.

Dragon Form sets the original's base Might to 5 "this turn" — that's a Layer 1 trait-altering effect, not a trait of the card itself. Copy effects only copy "copyable traits", which are distinct from the actual traits that later layer effects modify, so the token enters with the 1 Might (Rule 479.1.c). Same as buffs or gear: temporary modifications are never inherited by copies (see FAQ #10049 / #10887).

question: Can you react to an Empower?
answer:
Yes. Activating an Empower ability is an activated ability, so it goes on the chain as a Pending item and creates a Closed State — giving you priority to play Reaction spells/abilities before it resolves (Rule 377.3, FAQ #11877).

Two timing notes: the Reaction resolves first (LIFO), so the unit is not yet Empowered while you're responding — an [Empowered][>] dependent ability isn't active yet. And if your reaction removes the unit from the board, the Empower does nothing when it resolves.

question: I play Rampage with the additional cost, to get my unit +2, but opponent cast Gust on the enemy unit I targeted. Does my spell still resolve and I get the +2 on my unit?
answer:
Yes — Rampage still resolves and your friendly unit still gets the +2 this turn.

The +2 instruction only needs your friendly unit, which is still a legal target; the additional cost was already paid, so that part executes normally (Rule 359.3.e.5/e.8). The damage exchange, however, does nothing: the enemy unit is back in its owner's hand, so it can't deal damage to your unit and your unit can't deal damage to it — that part of the instruction is ignored.

question: When can my opponent play Flash in response to Brynhir Thundersong being played?
answer:
Ruling: Your opponent can play Flash after all other triggered abilities have resolved, while Brynhir's "When you play me" lockdown trigger is still on the chain. Brynhir enters play immediately as a unit (it does not linger on the chain), but its lockdown trigger goes on the chain as a separate Pending Item that can be responded to.

Sequence:

Brynhir is played and enters play immediately upon finalization

Brynhir's "When you play me" trigger goes on the chain

If opponent responds with Tideturner from Hidden, it also enters play immediately

Tideturner's "When you play me" trigger goes on the chain above Brynhir's trigger

Tideturner's trigger resolves, swapping with Hwei

Hwei's "When I move" trigger goes on the chain and resolves

Chain now has only Brynhir's trigger remaining; priority passes and opponent can play Flash as a reaction

Flash resolves, then Brynhir's lockdown trigger resolves

Nuances:

Units enter play immediately upon finalization and do not linger on the chain like spells do

The lockdown effect only applies after Brynhir's "When you play me" trigger resolves, not when Brynhir enters play

question: If a unit is being targeted by alpha strike and would die, but then you reveal a temporal breach saving the unit that would have died to alpha strike, do you get to re-choose who alpha strike is targeting?
answer:
No — you don't get to re-choose Alpha Strike's targets.

Temporal Breach banishes the unit, and Banishment is a non-board zone (Rule 56.1). Per the Flash/Repulse ruling, when a target moves to a non-board zone the targeting relationship is severed — Alpha Strike stops targeting that unit, and when Temporal Breach replays it, it's a brand-new game object (Rule 124) that Alpha Strike never chose. It won't take the damage.

At resolution, Alpha Strike just deals its Might in damage split among the remaining original targets. You re-decide the damage split at that moment (Rule 355.14.e), but you can't pick new units that weren't chosen at finalization (Rule 355.15). If the saved unit was the only target, the damage instruction does nothing — no new targets are selected.

question: If Kennen is played from hidden, I can stun units where I want, right?
answer:
No. Kennen's "When you play me... stun a unit" is a play effect, and CR 811.1.d.3 requires play effects of hidden cards to target only units at the battlefield where Kennen was hidden. So if you play him from Hidden, your stun target must be at that same battlefield.

The exception: if Kennen later attacks, that trigger is a regular triggered ability (not a play effect), so it can stun a unit at any location. (FAQ #11770)

question: If I have a Kaisa at a bf with a Back Off hidden, on the next turn my opponent plays a spell to increase the might of the Jayce in the base. Can I react now with Back Off on the Jayce in base?
answer:
No. A hidden Back Off can only choose a target at the battlefield where it was hidden — Jayce is in base, so he isn't a legal target (CR 811.1.d.2).

Timing isn't the problem: since Back Off was hidden on a previous turn, it gained [Reaction] and you can play it in response to your opponent's spell. But when played from Hidden, its "Stun a unit" target must be chosen from among options at that same battlefield, and Back Off has no targeting text that would free it from that restriction. If you want to hit a Jayce in base, you'd have to play Back Off normally from hand instead.

question: If I play Shadowcloaked Lurker with Last Rites, is it reduced by 2 energy?
answer: Yes — but only for the copies that stay in the trash. The Lurker you're playing has already left the trash before its cost is determined, so it can't count itself (FAQ #8430). Each remaining Shadowblade Lurker in your trash still gives [2] off, so with one other copy in trash the cost drops from 5 to 3; with two others, to 1.
