question: I'm using the icathian rain , and the opponent has 1 Predator on their base In this way, can I stop after giving only 2 damage to the deflect unit? Is it possible to pause the gameplay midway because the deflection feels overwhelming when making a judgment?
answer:
Short answer: Deflect never caps how much damage you deal — it's a cost, so "stopping at 2" depends entirely on what's dealing the damage, not on the Deflect unit.

If you're dealing a fixed amount to a chosen target (a spell like Falling Star or a 2-damage effect), you deal exactly what the card says; you can't reduce it to 2. Deflect just adds mandatory Power when you choose that permanent (Rule 809.1.c), and it's paid even if the damage ends up prevented or the ability later fizzles (FAQ #2811). If you have no other targets you will have to deal all the instances to the predator with deflect as you need to be able to execute the spell fully. However, you can not play the spell and this will prevent you from paying the extra deflect, even "mid cast". On finalization you realize you don't want to play this, you absolutely can as long as it has not become completely finalized. You will have revealed a card, but you won't lose your runes in the process.

Where "stopping at 2" does work is with Repeat: you can simply decline to pay the Repeat cost and let the spell execute only once, so the Deflect unit takes just the base 2 damage — but the Deflect cost is mandatory per time you choose it, so if you do pay to repeat and target that unit again, you owe Deflect a second time (FAQ #9293).

question: If player A is holding a battlefield with mournful witness, player B moves in with empowered Akali, and deals 2. Player A reacts with Long Sword, player B moves out dealing another 2. Would Mournful witness die before her empower ability triggers? Does combat end before or after the damage is dealt?
answer:
Yes — Mournful Witness dies in the cleanup right after the second hit, while the combat is still open, so her "when a combat that I was in ends" trigger never fires; and the damage lands before the combat ends, not after.

Long Sword's Might Bonus (+2, Rule 137.3) makes Mournful Witness a 4-Might unit, so she survives Akali's first move-in trigger (2 damage) and the Combat Showdown actually opens with her as the Defender. When B activates Rogue Assassin during that Showdown, Akali's move-out trigger fires for another 2 — that's 4 damage on a 4-Might unit, which is lethal.

Lethal units are Killed in the cleanup that follows (CR 323.4), and that cleanup runs while the Showdown/Combat is still ongoing — before the Showdown closes and the combat's resolution step. question: Does my opponent's defending unit immediately stop being a defender if my only attacking unit leaves combat?
answer:
No — the defending unit keeps its Defender designation. Designations are only removed when Combat fully ends (CR 468.7.a), or if that unit itself leaves the battlefield the combat is taking place at (Rule 323.2.c).

An attacker leaving, dying, or being recalled doesn't end the combat either — it stays active until all players pass Focus consecutively, and cards that care about "while it's a defender" keep applying. Same logic runs the other way: an attacker keeps its Attacker designation even if the defender moves away or the combat becomes unopposed (FAQ 1398, 4660).

The only exception is if the defending unit itself is moved off that battlefield (or its controller changes) — then a Cleanup strips the designation from it, which can matter for abilities like Assault/Shield that depend on it (FAQ 187).

answer:
Yes — Svellsongur copies Riven, Shattered's printed text, so she gets a second instance of "When I attack, choose an enemy unit here. Deal 2 to it for each Equipment attached to me."

The copied ability is appended to Riven's rules text, so both instances trigger on the same attack and go on the Chain as separate triggers, resolving one at a time. Each instance deals 2 per Equipment attached to her, and Svellsongur itself counts as attached Equipment — so with just Svellsongur on her, that's 4 total damage (2 + 2), split between two independently chosen enemy units at her battlefield if you want. Riven's "when I attack, deal 2 to an enemy unit here for each Equipment attached to me" gets duplicated by Svellsongur, so both instances trigger on attack and each one counts all Equipment attached to her (Svellsongur included). With one other Equipment on her, that's 4 damage per trigger, 8 total, split across whatever targets you choose for each trigger. Whatever the pre-existing gear grants her doesn't feed into the copy — copies take the object's original traits regardless of later alterations, and attachment order doesn't matter (FAQ #8410; Effect Text only becomes active while Attached, Rule 724). Stacking more Svellsongurs gives one extra instance each, not doubled instances — three Svellsongurs on Riven means four total instances of her text, not eight.

One caveat: this only matters for her text. Attached Equipment still gives its normal Might bonus on top; Svellsongur has no Might bonus of its own and doesn't amplify it.

question: When both players pass priority in succession, what happens to the pending chain?
answer:
The newest item on the chain resolves — and only that one item.

When both players pass in sequence without adding anything, you move to Step 4: Resolve, and the newest Finalized Chain Item resolves in full (Rules 339.1, 340.1). The chain is LIFO, so this is the top item, not the whole chain.

After that single resolution, all players get priority again and can respond before the next item resolves (FAQ #7640, Rule 340.4). If nothing is added and everyone passes again, the next item resolves — repeat until the chain is empty, at which point play returns to an Open State and (in a Showdown) Focus passes to the next player in turn order.

question: What if I pass focus and my opponent passes focus in showdown
answer:
It closes the Showdown — when all players pass Focus in sequence without playing anything, the Showdown ends (Rule 348, see also 347.2.a).

What happens next depends on the type. If it was a Combat Showdown, you proceed to the Combat Damage Step and then Combat Cleanup (which heals all units in play). If it was a Non-Combat Showdown, no damage step and no healing: if only one player's units remain at the battlefield, that player Establishes Control and Conquers if they haven't already scored it this turn (Rule 348.2).

One nuance: the pass that matters is passing Focus while the chain is empty, and it takes all players passing in sequence. A pass after a chain resolves is just Focus auto-moving to the next player in turn order — that's not the same as a player passing, so the Showdown doesn't end there (see FAQ 1797).

question: If I have 4 gears on the field attached to 4 units, when I cast "Arise!", how many sand soldier tokens can I get?
answer:
4 tokens — as long as all four of those gears are actually Equipment.

Arise! reads "Play a 2 [M] Sand Soldier unit token for each Equipment you control," and Equipment means Gear with the Equipment tag (Rule 150). Plain Gear like a Gold token or a non-Equipment relic doesn't count, so if even one of your four isn't Equipment you'd only get 3.

Attachment is irrelevant to the count — attached Equipment is still Equipment, still Gear, and still controlled by you (FAQ #2018), and nothing limits how many can be attached. The only real snag is the back half: "Then do this: Ready up to two of them" creates a pretty complex chain. Example with 3 equipment on the board:

Play Arise - both players pass priority- Arise resolves
3 Sand Soldier token units added as pending to the chain, end part reflexive trigger of Arise added as pending

Order of pending chain items: SS 1, SS 2, SS 3, reflexive trigger

SS 1 finalizes and enters at a location, it's weaponmaster is added as a pending item at the back of the existing chain

order of pending chain items: SS 2, SS 3, reflexive trigger, SS 1 weaponmaster

Repeat this process for SS 2 & 3: three SS token units on the board and pending chain item order is reflexive trigger > SS 1 weaponmaster > SS 2 weaponmaster > SS 3 weaponmaster

The rflexive trigger finalises first and requires a target (0/1/2 units that were previously created), it lingers on chain, SS 1 WM finalises (target an equipment and lingers on the chain), SS 2 WM, SS 3 WM

So the chain of finalized items is now reflexive trigger at bottom, SS 1 WM, SS 2 WM, SS 3 WM, this resolves Last In First Out (LIFO) as normal.

This means your opponent will know all units locations, what equipment each will get and which will become ready before they can respond when they receive priority.

question: If you Heedless Resurrection on a Elnuk played from hidden, how does it resolve? does the Elnuk recycle itself from the trash and do you get the +3?
answer:
No on both — once Elnuk Herd has left the board, its play-from-Hidden trigger can't do anything.

In response you play Heedless Resurrection, killing the Elnuk as its additional cost (Elnuk is 6 Energy, so the unit you bring back from trash must cost no more than 6 Energy and 0 Power — and it can't be the Elnuk itself, since targets are chosen before costs). When the Elnuk's trigger resolves, the card is in your trash, so the ability can't reference the unit to determine which battlefield it was hidden at — its instructions are ignored. That means no +3, and no recycle (from the trash or anywhere else). This is the same reasoning as FAQ #12771.

If you instead meant playing a different Elnuk Herd from your trash with Heedless, that's the opposite case: you do get the +3, because it was played from the trash rather than from face down so the "recycle me" clause is off, and the same-battlefield targeting restriction doesn't apply either.

question: What rules pertain to disruptive spectators and players around play area?
answer:
Disruptive behavior at or around the play area is covered by the Tournament Rules, mainly spectator role rules (204.8) and Unsporting Conduct (704) — note that a player who is at the event but not currently in a match counts as a spectator (204.8.b), so those rules follow them too.

Spectators must remain silent during matches, may not personally point out rules or policy violations to players, and may not give strategic advice (204.8.c.1, 204.8.d.1–2). At Professional OPL they also can't ask players to pause play while they flag a judge — they can only alert a judge directly. Players can request that a judge remove a spectator from their match, and competition officials can order a spectator not to observe a match at any time (204.8.e–f).

For players, 204.7 requires respectful behavior toward all attendees, including spectators. Unsporting Minor is a Warning (disrespect, bullying, offensive materials); Unsporting Major is a Disqualification and often means ejection from the venue (704.2–704.3), and the head judge can apply any penalty up to DQ for conduct issues since the listed infractions aren't exhaustive (704.1.c). Deliberately distracting an opponent so they miss a priority window is Angle Shooting, and judges may intervene in a match when they observe unsporting conduct (704.4.a.6, 701.1.d.3).

Two adjacent ones worth knowing: giving a player advice from outside the match is Outside Assistance (the recipient gets a Match Loss unless they refuse it by calling a judge, and an advising spectator can be barred from the venue — 703.9), and players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface while a spectator is around (424.1).

question: If a combat showdown begins with me having an assault unit at the battlefield and my opponent having 1 other unit at the same battlefield and their unit is removed during the showdown, does my unit retain assault even though it is alone at the battlefield? Does the showdown stay a combat showdown?
answer:
Yes to both — Assault is tied to the Attacker designation, not to whether an opposing unit is still sitting across from it.

Assault is "While I am an attacker, I have +X [M]," and it stays in effect as long as the unit keeps the Attacker designation (Rule 807.1.d.1). Attacker/Defender designations are only removed at the end of Combat (CR 468.7.a) or from a unit that itself leaves the battlefield — an enemy unit dying or being bounced doesn't strip your unit's designation, so your Assault bonus persists until Combat ends. FAQ #1195 is directly on point: Assault applies in combat showdowns until the end of combat, even if the defender moves its units out.

Likewise the showdown remains a Combat Showdown once it has opened as one. Removing units mid-showdown doesn't end it or revert it to non-combat — it still closes only when both players pass consecutively, and it runs through the Resolution Step (FAQ #757, #776). Practically, since only your unit remains at the battlefield, the Combat Damage Step is skipped (CR 467.1 requires both Attacking and Defending units present) and you win the Combat in the Determine Combat Result task. Note the flip side: if your Assault unit is the one that leaves the battlefield, it loses the Attacker designation and Assault falls off immediately.

question: Falling star glass mixologists
answer:
Two 3-damage instances, one chain item — so nobody gets a reaction window between them, and a Glasc Mixologist only dies if it eats both.

Falling Star was errata'd to "Deal 3 to a unit. Deal 3 to a unit." — two separate instances inside a single spell. It resolves as one chain item, executing both instructions back to back with no pause for reactions (FAQ #8639, #12407); the only windows are before the spell resolves, and afterward when the death trigger goes on the chain. Mixologist is 5 might, so one instance (3 damage) leaves it alive and its Deathknell never fires — you need both instances pointed at it for 6 total.

Once it actually dies, Deathknell is added to the chain as a Pending Item before the card is moved to the trash (Rule 808.1.d.2), and because the chain is closed at that point players do get to react to the trigger itself (FAQ #10991). When it resolves you may play a unit costing no more than [3] and no more than [A] from your trash ignoring its cost — it enters fresh with no damage marked, and it does not enter ready (FAQ #10696, #12569).

question: Glass mixologist trigger can target deathknell unit on your bf that died at same time and why?
answer:
Yes — provided the death happens at a battlefield you control (i.e., you're the defender or it's your battlefield, not one you're attacking into).

When two units die at the same time, each Deathknell trigger is added to the chain as a Pending Item before the unit actually moves to the trash, and the game notes its attributes and location (Rules 808.1.d.2–.3, 428.1.a.1.b). Since an item is on the chain, you also can't lose control of the battlefield during the following cleanup — so the graveyard unit is a legal choice and the battlefield is a legal destination. Because of how you cannot finalize when a cleanup is happening, you will only finalize the chain item, once all units are in the trash. You control both triggers, so you choose their order (Rule 808.2.a): resolve Glasc Mixologist's first, play the just-died unit from your trash (as long as it meets Glasc's cost limit), and it enters at that same battlefield.

The why: Deathknell "remembers" state from before death, and the pending chain item freezes control of the battlefield until the trigger resolves (FAQ #9783, and the Unleashed clarification that control can't be lost while an item is pending). Caveat: if you're the attacker at an opponent's battlefield, you don't control it, so you can't play the unit there (FAQ #10612).

question: does falling star hit
answer:
Short answer: no, falling star doesn't hit, it deals damage. If you had an ability that checked if something was hit, it wouldn't be valid after a falling star. Dealing damage is a process of marking damage on a unit.

Falling Star reads "Deal 3 to a unit. Deal 3 to a unit," and it doesn't care where the unit is. If the target is recalled/moved to Base in reaction, it's still the same game object, so both instances still land (FAQ #1958). If the unit changes to a non-board zone instead — returned to hand, killed to trash, banished — it's a different object and takes 0 (Rule 359.3.e.2/.4); you still do as much as you can with the other instance (FAQ #12764). The other stop is a counter like Not So Fast, which removes the whole spell and both damage instances.

One edge case: if the unit becomes untargetable by Falling Star before resolution, it mistargets and is unaffected (Rule 758.1).

question: If i attack with an empowered Ambessa, Respected and Feared and in response to my when i attack, my opponent plays a Temporal Breach from hidden, can he blink my Ambessa, Respected and Feared and avoid its effect of killing a unit with less might?
answer:
Yes — the blink works. The kill doesn't happen, because Ambessa's "when I attack" trigger is already on the chain and its referents get re-checked when it resolves, not when it triggered.

The window exists because the attack trigger creates a Closed State, so only Reaction-speed responses are legal — Hidden gives Temporal Breach that. When the trigger resolves, "here" and "less Might than me" are referents checked on execution (Rule 359.3.f.2). After the Breach, Ambessa is a new game object (Rule 124.1) — she loses the Empowered status, so the dependent kill ability is no longer even active — and her position/status has changed, so that referent returns null and the kill instruction is ignored. This is the same pattern as the standing ruling that a pending trigger referencing a Breached unit does nothing (FAQ #12419).

One caveats worth flagging: the hidden Breach must have been hidden at that battlefield (CR 811.1.d.2) and on a previous turn, or it can't be played at all.

It's up to your opponent — they control Zhonya's Hourglass, so they pick the order of the two replacement effects, and if they apply Zhonya's first the unit is saved instead of banished.

Both effects are replacement effects competing for the same death (Rule 373), so the controller of the affected unit's replacement effect orders them. Your Smite's 3 damage still gets dealt; it just doesn't turn into a banish. Note this only works because it's their unit — Zhonya's can only protect a unit its controller controls, so it can't save a unit you own from your own Smite.

question: Can i choose to play baron nashor on star spring to trigger its move effect to retreat a unit in starspring?
answer:
No — Star Spring won't trigger. Baron Nashor's ability is a replacement effect: he enters the Baron Pit instead of the location you played him to, so no non-token unit ever actually gets played to Star Spring (Rule 369.3, FAQ #10250).

The replacement is treated as the entry event not happening at the chosen location (Rule 370.1.a.1), which is why the Pit is what gets contested/conquered and scored, not Star Spring (FAQ #9221, #9728). You could still physically declare Star Spring as his play location, but he lands in the Pit, so no unit is at Star Spring and no move-to-base trigger for you to use. You also couldn't use it to retreat anything, since Star Spring only bounces a unit that's actually at Star Spring.

Caveat: there's no official FAQ for this exact pairing. If you instead read "plays a non-token unit here" as keyed to the declared play location rather than where the unit enters, you'd reach the opposite result — but the replacement-effect rules point against that reading.

question: my lonely poro is attacking alone to an enemy's battlefield. It dies and deathknell is added to the chain. Ambush only lets you play her to a battlefield where you control units (Rule 822.1.b), and your Poro is already dead and off the board when its Deathknell goes on the chain, so you have no units there. Being the attacker doesn't help: attacking grants the Attacker designation, not control of the battlefield — you only gain control after Conquer resolves (CR 471.1.b), and Reaction/Ambush placement still follows normal restriction of your Base or a battlefield you control.

Deathknell being on the chain doesn't keep the Poro "present" — the kill already happened and the trigger just remembers its state (Rule 808.1.d.3). You could play Nidalee to your Base or another battlefield you control during that window, just not the enemy's. This matches FAQ #11429 exactly.

question: if my opponent holds with a bomb token, does the damage go through before scoring?

Also, if the Bomb belongs to the player doing the holding, nothing happens — Deploy only fires when an opponent of the Bomb's controller holds there, so no kill and no damage at all.

question: When you play units under the effect of Fanfare, do you draw once for each unit played up to a maximum of three draws, or do you draw once after playing three units total?
answer:
Each unit gets its own draw — Fanfare reads "the next three times you play a unit this turn, draw 1," so it's three separate draw events, one per unit played, not one lump draw after the third unit.

So playing three units this turn = three draws (one each), and playing only two = two draws. If a single card plays two units at once, those still count as two separate "play a unit" events, so you'd get two draws from them (FAQ #12756) — the triggers go on the chain one at a time. if you play a unit to an open battlefield do you control it if its empty on the stack this interaction is specific towards Riven legend when you play to a battlefield you control the key word here is the control aspect

Short answer: No — playing a unit to an open battlefield doesn't make you its controller at the moment of the play, so a "when you play a unit to a battlefield you control" trigger won't see it there.

"Open" is defined as unoccupied and uncontrolled (Rule 170.11.c), so a battlefield you can legally play Sai Scout or Sneaky Deckhand to is by definition one you don't control. Playing the unit there applies Contested (Rule 190.3.a.1) and stages a Non-Combat Showdown; Control is only established when that Showdown closes with only your units remaining (Rule 348.2.a) — which is a Conquer, scoring you a point (FAQ #1585, #5632). So the control does eventually happen, but it happens on the Conquer, not on the play — the conquer triggers would fire, a "you control this battlefield" condition checked at the time of the play would not.

Two caveats worth planning around. If Riven's trigger is checked on play, the battlefield must already be yours before you play there (a battlefield you already control doesn't become Contested, FAQ #9705), and if an enemy unit is present the field isn't open at all, so Sai Scout isn't playable there. Also, whether the ability "rests/readies" on the Conquer or on the play is a wording question — I could not retrieve a Riven legend card from the database (only Riven, Shattered and Riven, Broken Blade units and Blade of the Exile), so if you paste the legend's exact printed text I can pin the timing down precisely rather than answering from the generic control rules. question: If I use Temporal Breach a gear turned into a unit by Orianna’s legend ability, does it get replayed as a gear, as a unit gear, or does it stay banished?
answer:
It comes back as a plain Gear, not a unit gear — and because it lands at a battlefield as an unattached non-Unit Gear, it's Recalled to your Base in the next cleanup.

The banishment works fine (a unit gear is a unit, so it's a legal target), but the card changes zones to a non-board zone, which makes it a new object and clears all applied layer alterations — including Orianna's type change (Rule 124). At that point it's just its printed Gear card, and the "until you choose another gear" effect is gone; Orianna would have to choose it again at the start of a later Main Phase. Note it is not stuck in banishment: Temporal Breach specifies the location, which is the "unless an effect specifies otherwise" carve-out for playing Gear somewhere other than Base (Rules 149.2, 152.2) — so the replay is legal, it just enters as Gear and gets recalled as a corrective action (CR 459.1).

Net effect: you get the card back as a Base Gear (ready), it isn't a unit, and no Contested/Showdown results from the replay. If it was breached while at your Base, it simply re-enters at Base with no recall step needed.

question:

if i target the same unit with both instances of falling star, do i pay deflect once or twice?
answer:
Twice, in both cases. Deflect is charged per time your spell chooses the unit, not once per spell.

Deflect reads "cost [Deflect Value] more to play as an additional cost for each time they choose me" (Rule 809.1.c). Repeat makes you make fresh choices for the second execution during finalization (Rule 820.2), so choosing the same Deflect unit again on the repeat is a second choose → second Deflect payment. Same for Falling Star: its two separate "Deal 3 to a unit" instructions each choose a target, so pointing both at the same Deflect unit costs you Deflect twice (that's the confirmed FAQ #5107 / #3183 answer).

So Bellows Breath with Repeat hitting one Deflect 1 unit = 1 Energy + 1 Mind (base), + 1 Energy + 1 Mind (Repeat), + 2 Power of any domain for Deflect. Falling Star on a Deflect 1 unit with both instances = 2 extra Power. If you can't pay a Deflect charge, you can't make that choice.

Heads up: a couple of older FAQ entries describe Deflect as a one-time "binary" cost per spell, which conflicts with the current rule text above — the per-choosing reading is the one that matches Rule 809.1.c and the majority of rulings.

Yes — the replayed Nidalee still draws.

Combat doesn't stop just because the defending side loses all its units; it runs on until players pass and the Resolution Step completes (FAQ #7863). So the combat is still the same one when you replay Nidalee, she's a unit present at that battlefield during it, and she gains the Attacker designation in the cleanup following her entry (CR 466.2.c.3.a).

At Determine Combat Result, your side is the only player with units remaining, so you win and every unit you control at the battlefield inherits that result (CR 468.3.a/c). Her ability only asks whether she "remains after combat" — it has no requirement that an enemy unit was there when she entered, so she triggers and draws 1. (The original Nidalee that was bounced doesn't draw, since she wasn't at the battlefield when the result was determined.)

The one thing that would change this: if the Combat Showdown had already closed and combat ended before you replayed her, she'd be entering after combat and wouldn't win anything.

Order on a normal turn is: Awaken → Beginning (Beginning Step, then Scoring Step where you Hold and score) → Channel → Draw → Main (where you play Aurora) → End (Aurora triggers).

This is also why Aurora can finish a game at match point: if you Held one battlefield at the start of the turn and the unit Aurora plays at end of turn conquers a different battlefield, both scores happened in the same turn, satisfying the Final Point requirement (CR 473.1.b.1; FAQ 1317).

question: Can you respond with an Ambush to Graves' damage on defend?
answer:
Yes — you can play an Ambush unit as a Reaction to Graves' "When I defend" trigger, but expect it to get hit too.

The catch: your Ambush unit is played and enters play before the trigger resolves, and Graves' ability deals damage to all enemy units here at resolution — so the new unit will also take Graves' Might (4) in damage, likely dying, unless a replacement/prevent effect saves it.

If you want the ambusher to not be damaged by Graves's ability, you'd need to put it somewhere else or play it there after its resolution, assuming of course, that you'd still have a way to play/move your unit there as an action/reaction.

question:

answer:
Yes — Thrill of the Hunt works, provided you play it while Ruined Rex's Deathknell trigger is on the chain and before it resolves.

Here's the flow: Rex's [Deathknell][>] Deal 4 to an enemy unit goes onto the chain as Rex dies during the Combat Cleanup, an enemy unit is locked in as its target, and the trigger only actually resolves after the cleanup's heal step. You respond to that chain item with Thrill of the Hunt: it banishes your unit, and when its owner replays it, it enters as a new game object (Rule 124). The trigger's already-chosen target is gone, so the "deal 4" instruction is ignored (Rule 359.3.e.5 / FAQ #9870) — your unit takes nothing.

On the timing question: there's no window before the target is picked, because Rex's death happens inside the cleanup task itself. Your window is the chain resolution of the trigger once it's on the chain — Thrill of the Hunt's [Reaction] is what lets you act in that closed state. One distinction worth noting: just moving the unit (e.g., to Base) would not invalidate the target, since Rex's trigger has no location restriction (FAQ #9612) — you need the unit to leave the board, which is exactly what Thrill of the Hunt does.

question: weird combo, i know, but if I have a sprite on a field and i play Vi with Ambush (pacekeeper) do I score from holding? ( I am playing lux)
answer:
No — playing a unit never scores a Hold. Hold is checked in one place only: the Scoring Step of your Beginning Phase, and only if you still maintain control of that battlefield at that moment (Rule 471.2).

Since Ambush requires playing Vi to a battlefield where you already have units, that battlefield is one you already control — so there's no Conquer happening either. Nothing about playing Vi, or being on Lux, changes the timing of when points are awarded; you'd just have Vi sitting there.

One catch worth knowing: if that Sprite is your only unit there, a lone Sprite can't ever hold on its own — Temporary kills it at the start of your Beginning Phase before scoring, so the battlefield is empty when the check happens. Vi, Peacekeeper staying on board is what would let you actually hold it on your next Beginning Phase.

If the "field" is instead a battlefield you don't control (so the Sprite is contesting it), then the only way to score there is by winning the resulting Showdown/Combat and Conquering — that's Conquer, not Hold, and Vi's Ambush doesn't accelerate it.

question: Can Heedless Resurrection react to a temporary trigger to kill that temporary unit instead to summon a unit from trash
answer:
Yes — you can play Heedless Resurrection in response to the Temporary trigger, kill that Temporary unit as its additional cost, and play a unit from your trash.

Temporary is just a triggered ability that goes on the chain at the start of the beginning phase (Rule 816), and it can be reacted to, putting the game in a Closed state (FAQ #11281, #2751). Because finalization makes you choose the trash target before paying costs, the unit you're bringing back just has to already be in your trash — you can't kill the Temporary unit and then pick that same unit (FAQ #9523). You then kill the Temporary unit as the additional cost; when the Temporary trigger later resolves, its "kill this" has nothing left to act on and does nothing.

One limit to check: the unit you return must cost no more Energy and no more Power than the unit you killed, so if the Temporary unit has a low/no cost that restricts your options.

question: If I Heedless Resurrection a rift herald can I choose the order things will resolve in
answer:
No — you don't get to pick the order; Rift Herald's Deathknell actually resolves first.

Because killing the Herald is an additional cost, the Heedless Resurrection spell is already sitting on the chain when the Herald dies, so the Deathknell trigger gets added on top of it (FAQ #6068; Rules 354.1, 357.2). Chain items resolve newest-first, so Deathknell resolves, then Heedless Resurrection resolves afterward.

So the sequence is: Deathknell → play a unit from your hand to your base, ignoring its Energy cost (you still pay its Power). Then Heedless Resurrection → play a unit from your trash that costs no more Energy and no more Power than the Herald (so ≤8 Energy, ≤1 Power), ignoring its cost. Note the Herald itself can't be the target, since targets are locked in before costs are paid.

This is different from kill effects that happen during a resolution (like Baited Hook) — there the Deathknell waits and resolves last. Here the kill is a cost, so it goes on top.

question: 레이븐블룸 학생 2마리와 감시하는 보초 1마리가 있을 때, 내가 주문으로 감시하는 보초를 처치하면 레이븐블룸 학생의 스킬과 감시하는 보초의 죽음의 종소리는 어떤 순서로 처리돼?
answer:
레이븐블룸 학생 트리거 2개가 먼저 해결되고, 그다음 감시하는 보초의 죽음의 종소리(1장 뽑기)가 해결돼요.

이유는 체인에 올라가는 시점이 다르기 때문이에요. 카드는 완전히 해결(resolve)되어야 "플레이한 것"으로 취급되므로, 레이븐블룸의 "주문을 플레이할 때" 트리거는 주문이 해결을 끝낸 뒤에야 체인에 올라가요(CR 420.4.a). 반면 죽음의 종소리는 주문 해결 중 처치 지시가 실행되는 순간, 보초가 무덤으로 가기 직전에 이미 Pending Item으로 체인에 올라가 있어요(CR 429.1.a.1.b, 808.1.d.2). 체인은 나중에 올라간 것부터 풀리므로(LIFO), 뒤에 올라간 레이븐블룸 트리거가 먼저, 먼저 올라간 죽음의 종소리가 나중에 풀려요(FAQ #8210).

두 레이븐블룸 트리거끼리는 동시 트리거라 순서를 직접 고를 수 있고(둘 다 +1 might라 결과는 동일), 죽음의 종소리와는 동시 트리거가 아니라서 그 순서를 임의로 고를 수는 없어요. 보초의 조종자가 누구든 이 순서는 바뀌지 않아요.

question: Can you kill anothet friendly unit that died by combat damage with mordekaiser
answer:
Yes — as long as the other unit is still on the board when Mordekaiser's replacement applies.

Mordekaiser, Twice Slain reads "Once each turn, if I would die, you may kill a friendly unit to heal me, exhaust me, and recall me instead." If he and another friendly unit both take lethal combat damage, those deaths are simultaneous, and a replacement effect is applied before the qualifying events actually occur (Rule 370.1.c). The kill you perform as the cost — and Mordekaiser's heal/exhaust/recall — are carried out before the other simultaneous deaths resolve (Rule 373.1.a). So you can pick the other dying unit, kill it, and still save Mordekaiser.

The limit is that you can only kill a permanent whose origin is the board (Rule 429.2.a). If the other friendly unit already died earlier (it's sitting in the trash, not dying in this same cleanup), it's no longer a legal choice, and you'd need a different live friendly unit to pay the cost.

This is my interpretation based on the replacement-effect timing rules (Rules 370.1.c and 373). No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction.

Scoring is either Conquer (gaining Control of a battlefield) or Hold (maintaining Control in your Beginning Phase), and Control is established only by having Units at a battlefield (Rule 190.4, 190.4.a); a gear is not a Unit, so with no units there you neither gain nor maintain Control. Contested status likewise comes only from a Unit becoming present (Rule 190.3.a), so a Deploy gear entering doesn't even start the Showdown that could lead to Control.

question: Attack with no action, opponent passes with no action, can i still play an action
answer:

Your pass was your last opportunity. The only way you'd get another action is if your opponent did play something after you passed — then the chain would resolve and focus would come back to you, letting you start a new chain (FAQ #6544). Passing back-and-forth with nothing played doesn't loop; it ends the showdown.

Yes — it's a triggered ability rather than a static/blanket effect, but "each" isn't what makes it one.

The trigger signal is the "At" clause: "At the start of each player's Beginning Phase" (Rule 383.1 — "at" followed by a point in time during the turn sequence). "Each" is only scope, in two places: "each player's Beginning Phase" means it triggers on both players' turns, and "each unit here" describes what the effect touches. It's still a single trigger producing a single chain item that deals 1 damage to every unit at that battlefield as one instruction — not one trigger per unit.

That distinction matters for reaction timing: because it's one chain item, an opponent can Stupefy a unit in reaction and the damage lands on the reduced Might (FAQ #12274). And since the condition is purely temporal with no "if a unit is here" clause, the ability still goes on the chain at an empty battlefield and the damage instruction simply does nothing (FAQ #12286).

Your opponent passing focus is not enough on its own — the Showdown only ends when all players pass in sequence with no card played or ability activated (Rules 347.2.a, 348). One nuance worth knowing: if the Combat Chain opened from your "when I attack" triggers, then when that initial chain resolves focus stays with you (Rule 346.1). Only after a chain you started closes does focus pass — and it always cycles back once your opponent declines to act.

question: If the unit that I have chosen to copy with Shady Spectacles die, what happen to the unit that Shady Spectacles attached to?
answer:
Yes — nothing happens to it. The equipped unit stays a copy of the unit you chose; the chosen unit dying doesn't detach Shady Spectacles or end the copy.

The printed duration is "for as long as this is attached to it" — the "it" is the equipped unit, so the copy effect lasts only as long as the Spectacles stay attached to that unit. It ends when the Spectacles detach or the equipped unit leaves play (the equipped unit dying kills the attachment, FAQ #12669), not when the copied unit does. There's also no re-choosing: you pick the unit once, as the Spectacles are attached.

So the equipped unit keeps using the chosen unit's copyable (printed) traits — name, type, tags, cost, domain, rules text, printed Might — and keeps everything of its own: buffs, statuses like Temporary or empowered, and any other gear attached to it (Rules 446.2, 479.1.b.1, 479.4).

One caveat the rules don't state outright: if the unit you chose was itself only a copy of something else (another Spectacles, a Mirror Image token, etc.), the copy effect's target is now a card in a new zone and its layer alterations are gone (Rule 124.1), so the traits carried over would be that card's printed ones. That's my interpretation — no official FAQ covers a copy source leaving play.

The only catch is the wording "here" — the unit being reduced has to be at Ahri's battlefield, and the reduction has to really land; if it's snapshotted to 0 (already at a floor), nothing was reduced and she gains nothing (FAQ #12942).

By contrast, a single unit disarming for -2 (base Disarm plus a granted Disarm, e.g. Clanging Sentry) is one event and only gives her +1 — rule 831.1.d.1 collapses multiple Disarm instances on one unit into a single trigger with the summed value, so "by 1 or more" counts the event, not the points.

This is my interpretation based on rule 831 and the printed card. No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction.

What you can't do is name Morde himself as the unit to kill. His own death is the event being replaced, and a replacement effect can only be applied once to an event "or to any Game Actions or events that replace that event" (Rule 370.2) — so killing itself would just leave Morde sitting in the trash with nothing to heal or recall. question: Can I react with a hidden temporal breach to a raging firebrand when you play me trigger to get his discount twice?
answer:
Partly — you can react to the trigger and the replayed Firebrand's own "when you play me" does fire a second time, but you don't automatically get two separate 5-less spells out of it.

Timing works: the trigger is a chain item, so the state is Closed and your hidden Temporal Breach has [Reaction] (it must have been hidden on a previous turn, and Firebrand has to be at the battlefield where you hid it — a hidden Breach can't reach a unit at Base, CR 811.1.d.2). Breach resolves, banishes Firebrand, and its owner replays it as a new object, so a second "next spell you play costs 5 energy less" trigger goes on the chain. Playing the Breach itself costs [0] from hidden and the replayed unit isn't a spell, so neither consumes a discount.

The catch is the two discounts: whichever trigger resolves first applies to the next spell you play at that moment. If you let both resolve before playing anything, they stack onto the same single spell (10 energy off one card, floored at 0), not 5 off two cards — FAQ #12624. To split them you have to play a Reaction-speed spell in the window after the replayed Firebrand's trigger resolves but while the original trigger is still on the chain; that card takes one 5-off, then the second trigger gives the next spell 5 off.

question:
My enemy has a 5 might unit on a battlefield and combat starts, I attack and my enemy makes my unit move back with a spell. Is this a combat win for them?
Similarly, they star cross it, is this a combat win?
Similarly again, I get stunned, I cannot conquer and recall, this is a tie, correct?
answer:
Partly — they win the combat if only your unit leaves, but not if Star-Crossed clears the battlefield entirely; and a stun only makes it a tie if your unit survives the 5 damage.

Moved/returned to hand: Yes, that's a combat win for them. Once your attacker is gone, the Combat Damage step simply doesn't happen (no opposing units), but the combat still resolves in the Resolution Step, and 468.3.a gives the win to the player who is the only one with units there — the defender. So "when you win a combat" abilities trigger. They don't score a Conquer point though, since they already controlled that battlefield.

Star-Crossed: No. Star-Crossed returns a friendly unit and an enemy unit to hand, so their 5-might unit leaves too. With no units at the battlefield, the result is "No Result" (468.3.d — neither player has units present), so nobody wins the combat, and the battlefield actually becomes Uncontrolled (468.5.b). No conquer point, and no combat-win trigger.

Stunned attacker: It depends on your unit's might. The stun means it deals 0 damage while the defender assigns 5 to it — if your unit has 5 or less might it dies in the damage step, leaving them as the only player with units, so they win the combat. If your unit has 6+ might it survives, gets healed and then recalled during Combat Cleanup, and that recall forces "No Result" — a tie, no combat win for either side, and they keep the battlefield.

Siren's Song is legal as a Reaction (Cataclysm's "opponents can't play spells this turn" only applies once Cataclysm has resolved), and it resolves first, moving your unit from battlefield A to battlefield B where Riven is defending. That applies Contested and gets a Combat staged, but the Chain still holds Cataclysm, so the turn isn't in a Neutral Open state (Rule 310.2) and the showdown just sits staged (Rule 323.11).

Then Cataclysm resolves, moving Jarvan IV into battlefield B. In the cleanup that follows resolution the Chain is empty, so the turn player initiates the staged showdown — and because units controlled by both players are present, it opens directly as a Combat Showdown/Combat (Rule 466.1).

One consequence worth noting: you are the Attacker, because the first unit to apply Contested to battlefield B was your unit A (moved by your opponent's own Siren's Song), so Jarvan IV enters the combat with the Attacker designation and Assault's +1 [M].

question: How does last carress interact with Elnuk Herd

So if you move Elnuk elsewhere, the +3 [M] is locked to that new battlefield, not where it was hidden. Elnuk itself counts, so you'll always have at least one legal target.

Then "recycle me if I was played from face down" still fires — Elnuk goes to the bottom of your Main Deck after handing out the +3 [M]. question: End turn step
answer:
No — the "end turn step" is not a window you can act in: when the turn player says they're ending their turn, nothing opens a priority window, so you can't play a reaction or activate anything at end of turn (FAQ 6113, 8978).

The Ending Phase is the Ending Step (at end of turn triggers and effects happen) followed by the Expiration Step, which heals all units, expires all "this turn" effects simultaneously, and empties both rune pools (Rule 317.2). Those steps resolve as Tasks with no discretionary actions granted to either player.

The only way to get to act there is if something is actually put on the Chain — a triggered ability firing "at the end of turn," or a legend/card that triggers in that phase — which gives you a Closed State to respond in with Reaction-timed cards. And note you can't squeeze in a Main-Phase-style action right before the turn ends either; off-turn priority only comes from a chain or a showdown.

question: Falling star target twice to a unit with deflect. How many deflect affected to me?
answer:
Yes — you pay the Deflect cost twice if both "Deal 3 to a unit" instances choose the same Deflect unit. Falling Star makes two separate choices, and Deflect charges "as an additional cost for each time they choose me" (Rule 809.1.c), so pointing both instances at that unit means paying its Deflect Value twice.

So a Deflect 1 unit costs an extra 2 Power total (any domain), a Deflect 2 unit 4 Power extra, on top of Falling Star's 2 Energy + 2 Power. If you can't pay a given Deflect charge, you can't make that choice — you'd have to send the second instance somewhere else.

question: Why bellows breath repeat pays deflect once but falling star twice?
answer:
Bellows Breath with Repeat should also charge Deflect twice if both times a unit with deflect is chosen.

Deflect is charged per time your spell chooses the unit, not per spell (Rule 809.1.c), and Rule 820.2 makes it explicit that the second Bellows Breath execution gets fresh choices made during finalization. Choosing the same Deflect unit again on the repeat is a second choose, so it's a second payment.

Falling Star has two separate "Deal 3 to a unit" instructions inside a single execution, so it chooses twice with no Repeat at all — that's 2 cost increases on one card with Deflect, and 4 if you also repeat it. Bellows Breath is one instruction that chooses up to three units once each, so its base execution costs 1 cost increase per unit with Deflect and Repeat adds exactly one more cost increase per unit with Deflect.

The confusion might come from how Deflect is worded on a card, but it received an errata around Origins/Spiritforged to work as explained above.

question: Does graves blasting through still deal damage as an attacker moving in if my opponent responds to the ability with sirens Siren's Song
answer:
No — if your opponent uses Siren's Song to move Graves off the battlefield before his attack trigger resolves, Graves deals no damage to the units there.

That's because "here" in "deal damage equal to my Might to all enemy units here" is a referent checked at resolution, not at trigger (Rule 359.3.f.2 — same principle as Yasuo, Remorseful being moved in response to his attack trigger, where "here" no longer matches). Once Siren's Song moves Graves, "here" is wherever he landed (normally his Base), so the ability hits whatever enemy units are at his new location — almost always nothing. His Might is likewise read at resolution, so any Might change would also be counted then.

Two caveats worth checking. Siren's Song needs a unit that moved this turn, which a Standard Move into the contested battlefield satisfies, but a unit merely played from hand has not moved (Rule 448.2) — so if Graves entered some other way, the spell can't legally target him. And the trigger still resolves and is still "played" even with nothing to damage; it just does nothing.

answer:
No — Not So Fast has no legal target when you Empower Kharox, so your opponent can't counter it.

Empower doesn't choose anything: the source permanent isn't a target of its own Empower ability (Rule 827.1.b.1), and Not So Fast requires an enemy spell or ability that chooses a friendly unit or gear. So there's nothing for them to point it at.

Same goes for the follow-up: Kharox's "when I become Empowered" trigger chooses an opponent (a player, not a unit or gear) and then a unit card in that opponent's trash — the "friendly unit or gear" refers to game objects on the board (rule 133.3.a.), so that trigger can't be countered with Not So Fast either, because the Trashed are a non-board zone. The gear only becomes located at Hunters' Circle afterward, by being attached to a unit standing there (Rule 152.2) — which is after the discount window has already closed.

question: If I play Raucous Anthem, and then play Meticulous Restorationist from trash, will Meticulous Meticulous Restorationist be able to come in readied and with +3 might?
answer:
No — Restorationist enters exhausted with its printed 2 Might; it can't be readied or buffed by Raucous Anthem.

Raucous Anthem is an Energy 7 card, so Restorationist's trigger does fire, but the trigger waits until the Anthem has fully resolved (Rule 420.4.a). Anthem readies and buffs the units you already control at that moment — Restorationist is still in the trash, so it's not one of "your units" and gets nothing. Only afterward does the trigger go on the chain, letting you pay [C] to play it from trash, where it enters exhausted as normal (Rule 359.2.c).

The +3 Might is also a one-time "this turn" grant to the units present at resolution, so it doesn't follow units that enter later.

question: Do bomb token gears count as cards played
answer:
No — a Bomb token is a token, not a card, so playing one doesn't count as "playing a card." Rule 185 makes tokens their own object category ("Tokens are not cards"), and Rule 350.2 spells out that they can still be Played — that's playing a token, not playing a card. Legion and similar "if you have played another card this turn" checks specifically require a card, so Gold/Bomb-style token gears don't satisfy them (FAQ #4724, #9260).

What it does count as is playing a gear, because tokens keep their card type (FAQ #8803) — so triggers that ask for "when you play a gear" see it. (Compare FAQ #9440: playing a token unit is playing a unit.)

One thing worth separating out: Deploy is what lets the Bomb be played to a battlefield rather than your Base (Rule 830.1.b), and that's a permission change, not a change to what kind of object it is.

answer:
Yes — in fact that order is mandatory, since Soraka has "I must be assigned combat damage last," which works exactly like Backline (Rule 826): you must assign lethal damage to every other unit at that battlefield before any damage can be assigned to her.

question: do i get to use my opponents deploy gear? like "when you conq here"
answer:
No — your opponent's Deploy gear keeps working only for them. You gaining control of a battlefield doesn't change who controls the gear sitting on it, and "you" in a permanent's ability means that permanent's controller (Rule 191.5.a), so their "when you conquer here" fires only when they conquer that battlefield — not when you do.

The distinction people trip on is that the battlefield's own "when you conquer here" does trigger for you when you conquer it (you control the battlefield effect even though you don't own the card), but the opponent's gear is a separate object and its trigger stays theirs. You also can't activate its abilities — the controller of the source decides that (Rule 378).

What does happen is on your next Beginning Phase: if you hold that battlefield, Deploy's second clause kills their gear ("when an opponent holds here, kill this," Rule 830.1.b), which is why Deploy gear is a temporary buff while you sit there.

question: A player starts a chain and play an action. Is that same player can play a reaction before the others ?
answer:
Yes — you keep priority after playing your Action, so you can play a Reaction onto that same chain before opponents get a chance to respond.

Finalizing a card doesn't pass priority, and the controller of the newest chain item receives priority, so the first player with priority is the one who started the chain and may add another item to it (Rule 338.1.a.5). That only holds for another Reaction — you can't add a second Action to the same chain (only Actions can start a chain; once one exists, only Reactions can be added, Rule 309.1.a). Priority passes only when you choose to pass it.

question: Is it doable for a player that play a reaction to add another reaction before the opponent ? Or by extension as much as reaction as he wants before the other ?
answer:
Yes — the player who plays a Reaction keeps priority and can play another Reaction (and another) before ever passing to the opponent. Priority only moves when you explicitly pass it (Rules 311–312, 338.1.b), so there's no automatic hand-off after one Reaction. You're limited only by what you can afford, since costs are paid as each card goes on the chain.

If you do pass and your opponent also passes, the newest item on the chain resolves — and you don't get another window to react to that same item. After it resolves, priority opens up again and you can still respond to whatever is left underneath. Note the flip side: if your opponent passes back to you while a chain is open, you can also just keep adding Reactions rather than letting things resolve — Actions are the ones that require an empty chain.

question: Does Hunker Down stop the effects of siren Siren's Song, or any opponents "move a unit" effect
answer:
Yes — a unit under Hunker Down can't be moved by Siren's Song or any other opponent's move effect. Hunker Down's "It can't move this turn" is an absolute restriction, and move instructions that can't be followed are negated when the spell resolves, not merely delayed (Rule 54 "Can't beats Can"; Rule 359.3.e.14.b uses the same reasoning with Vilemaw's Lair's "units can't move from here to base").

The opponent can still cast Siren's Song at it — "moved this turn" is still true, so it's a legal target and the spell doesn't fizzle on targeting — it just resolves and the move does nothing. Hunker Down also being [Reaction] means you can play it in response to the Siren's Song itself and it will resolve first.

Two caveats worth knowing: this blocks every kind of move (Standard Move, Showstopper, Ride the Wind, Siren's Song), since the restriction doesn't care who is doing the moving — but it does not stop a Recall, because a Recall isn't a Move (Rule 448.1). Also, nothing else about the unit is affected: it's still a legal target for kill/damage effects, and it's already readied by Hunker Down.

question: If I have a Mageseeker Warden at a battlefield, and then play Firebrand Raider does Mageseeker Warden's "can't" effect stop the enemy units from getting ready when Firebrand Raider enters, and also stop the enemies units from entering ready
answer:
Partly — the "ready all enemy units" trigger gets shut off, but the "enter ready" part isn't affected at all.

Mageseeker Warden is a static prohibition: spells and abilities can't ready units that are enemy to its controller. Since you control both Warden and Firebrand Raider, the opponent's units are enemy units to you, so Firebrand Raider's "When you play me, ready all enemy units" ability does nothing while Warden is at a battlefield — it can't flip exhausted enemy units back to ready. But "Other units enter ready" is not a readying action: units arrive already ready and are never seen as exhausted, so Warden can't touch it — same reasoning as Accelerate, Sun Disc, and "I enter ready" units (FAQ #2897, #4300). So your opponent's fresh units still enter ready, and Firebrand Raider's own "I enter ready" applies normally.

Two follow-on notes: Firebrand Raider's "Units don't ready during the Awaken Phase" is a restriction, not an ability that readies anything, so Warden doesn't interfere with it — nobody readies in the Awaken Phase while Firebrand Raider is in play. And Warden's other clause only limits where opponents can play units, so it doesn't restrict you playing Firebrand Raider to a battlefield.

question: If I kill a bomb token with the additional cost of playing Shimmering Swimmer, would the bombs deathknell and the Swimmer's when played trigger go on the chain simultaneously?
answer:
Yes — if you kill your own Bomb token as the additional cost for Shimmering Swimmer, the Bomb's Deathknell and the Swimmer's "when you play me" trigger are placed on the chain simultaneously, and since you control both you choose the order they go on (Rule 383.3.d; FAQ #6068). The Swimmer resolves fully and enters play first, then both triggers are queued together — that's the standard "additional cost kills a friendly permanent" timing.

The Bomb is a gear token, but tokens can have and trigger Deathknell just fine (Rule 808.1.d), so nothing there changes. Note the Bomb's ability is not optional and not friendly: it deals 2 to an enemy unit "here" and kills your other Bombs at that location — "here" is locked in at the Bomb's old location, where the Swimmer isn't (it enters at your Base or a battlefield you control). The Swimmer's half deals 2 to a unit of your choice, so it can hit that same enemy unit or anything else.

Whichever went on the chain last resolves first; if you want the Swimmer's 2 damage to finish off a unit the Bomb also damaged, order accordingly.

question: When a Reflection token created by conquering a unit with Deceiver's reflexive ability is moved to base before the copy effect resolves, does the copy still succeed if only the token moves to base, versus if both the token and the target unit are moved to base?
answer:
Yes — the copy still works if only the Reflection token moves to base; it fails only if the target unit is no longer at that battlefield.

Deceiver's reflexive trigger targets "another unit there," and that's the only thing with a location restriction. The token itself is not a target of the trigger — it's the object being modified ("It becomes a copy of…"), and moving to Base isn't a zone change, so it's still the same game object the copy effect applies to wherever it sits. Mirror Image proves the point: it makes the token at your Base copy a unit that can be at a battlefield, so the copy never requires co-location.

If the target unit is what moves to Base, the instruction mistargets — no unit matching "another unit there" — so the token stays a 0 [M] Reflection (and still gets Temporary, since that instruction doesn't depend on the target). question: what if i pass focus
answer:
Yes — passing Focus hands Focus and Priority to your opponent, and it doesn't end the Showdown unless they pass too (Rule 348).

They can play an Action or Reaction, activate an ability, or pass back. If they play something, you don't get your "pass" back — once that chain resolves and the state returns to Open, Focus automatically moves to the next player in turn order (Rule 346), so the Showdown keeps going as long as anyone acts. Note the pass that matters is the Pass action with an empty chain, not passing Priority mid-chain (Rule 347.2.a).

Once you both pass in sequence, it's a Combat Showdown → Combat Damage, then Combat Cleanup (which heals all units). A Non-Combat Showdown has no damage step or healing — if only one player's units remain, they establish Control and Conquer if they haven't scored there this turn.

question: Can you play an Ambush unit such as Rengar, Trophy Hunter in reaction to Mageseeker Warden entering the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — you can Ambush in response to Mageseeker Warden being played, because at that moment Warden is a card on the chain, not yet a permanent on the board.

Warden's "opponents can only play units to their base" is a passive ability of a permanent, and passive abilities are only active while the permanent is on the board (Rule 365.1). So while Warden sits on the chain, you're free to Ambush a unit (Rengar included) to a battlefield you control — or, for Rengar, a battlefield with enemy units — and your unit resolves first (LIFO), landing before Warden ever enters.

The window that matters is after Warden resolves: once it's actually at a battlefield, no Ambush for you at any battlefield, and you're limited to playing units to your base. Note it's a restriction on playing, not on units already there, so your Ambush unit that landed earlier stays put. If Warden is played to its controller's base, the clause never turns on at all.

Their own kill/sacrifice removes the unit before Hidden Blade resolves, so Hidden Blade mistargets: the "Kill a unit at a battlefield" instruction is ignored, and since the draw is a linked instruction to it, "Its controller draws 2" is ignored too (CR 359.3.e.14.a; FAQ #3700).

question:
When Ziggs, Explosive decks pile lots of bombs on one battlefield, and they are detonated (let's say 4 bombs), does every single bomb have to pay deflect cost?

All of my online opponents, especially Irelias, are trying to make me pay the deflect for every single bomb (so 4 bombs = 4 recycled for deflect 1).
answer:
Yes — each Bomb is its own object with its own death trigger, so 4 Bombs detonating means 4 separate triggered abilities, and every one of them that chooses a unit with Deflect carries its own Deflect cost (Rule 809.1.c: the cost is paid "for each time they choose me"). If all four pick the Irelia, that's Deflect ×4 — your opponents have that part right.

But they're leaving out your out: Deflect is a mandatory cost for spells, while for triggered abilities you choose targets, then at finalization you may simply decline to pay, and that trigger is removed from the chain with no effect at all (Rule 405.2; FAQ #10636). So you pay for as many or as few of the four as you want — no one can force you to pay for all of them. Two things to keep straight: declining kills the whole trigger, so if the Bomb you decline was the one whose trigger would "kill your other Bombs there," that chain reaction stops too; and if there's a non-Deflect enemy unit at that battlefield, choosing it costs you nothing. Also, Deflect power can be paid with any domain (Rule 809.1.c.1), so don't let anyone insist it must match something.

question: When a unit gains the Attacker designation mid-combat through an effect like Nidalee, Cat Form's Ambush, does Demacian Standard's attack trigger fire again for that newly attacking unit?
answer:
Yes — Demacian Standard's ability is an attack trigger, so it fires again for the new attacker.

Standard reads "When one or more friendly units attack here, give one of them +2 [M] this turn." That's keyed to the Attacker designation, not to combat starting (Rule 383.4.e), so Nidalee ambushing to that battlefield and gaining the Attacker designation during the following Cleanup is a fresh trigger event — you get another +2 [M] to hand out, on top of whatever the Standard already gave earlier in this combat.

What limits it is per-unit, not per-combat: Attack triggers are only checked the first time each unit gains the Attacker designation in a given combat (Rule 383.4.e.2.a). So bouncing Nidalee out and replaying her, or re-designating the same unit, won't re-fire it — but a genuinely new attacker will.

One caveat: this only works if it's a real Combat Showdown. If Nidalee were played to a battlefield with no enemy units, no Attacker designation is ever granted, so nothing triggers.

question: I use Ekko to play Clocktower Guardian with discount. He dies at the end of the turn and I have a time warp on the top of my deck. What happens?
answer:
Yes — the kill and the Deathknell both resolve before your turn actually ends, so you banish the Time Warp, you may play it right then, and you take the extra turn after this one.

The "Kill me at end of turn" from Boy Who Shattered Time happens in the Ending Step (Rule 317.1), which is before the Expiration Step, so your rune pool hasn't emptied yet (317.2.d) — anything still floating in it is usable for the play. Clocktower Guardian's Deathknell then banishes Time Warp and lets you play it as part of that resolution (same as the combat case in FAQ #12960 — no Open State needed), and "play it" isn't restricted to units, so a spell is fine.

The catch is that the discount only ignores the Energy cost, not Power. Time Warp is 10 Energy / 4 Mind power, so you still need 4 Mind power from ready Mind runes or unspent pool. If you can't pay it, the Time Warp just stays in Banishment — the permission is spent with that resolution, so it doesn't sit around to be played later. If you do pay, Time Warp resolves, banishes itself, and the additional turn is inserted right after your current turn (Rule 738), so you take it before the next player's turn.

answer:
Yes — a Time Warp played off Clocktower Guardian's Deathknell at end of turn still gives you an extra turn, but only if you can legitimately pay for it: "ignoring its Energy cost" zeroes just the 10 Energy, and Time Warp still costs 4 Mind power (rule 356.1.b.2). Two power isn't enough, so with only 2 floating the play is illegal and the Time Warp simply stays banished.

I couldn't find a card called "Houndwards" — but if whatever you played there drained your rune pool, that's what decides it: you need a full 4 power available after the Guardian dies.

If you do pay it, the timing works fine: the Guardians's Deathknell resolves during your End of Turn step (rule 317.1.a), and Time Warp's additional turn is inserted directly after your current turn in the queue (rules 735, 738), so you take it before your opponent's next turn — nothing is lost for casting it in the ending phase. Note the "Kill me at end of turn" from Ekko's discount doesn't stop the Deathknell; being killed at end of turn is exactly what fires it.

If you can pay the 4 Power, then yes — playing it in the end-of-turn window doesn't waste it. The "Kill me at end of turn" kill resolves in the Ending Step, before your rune pool empties (Rule 317.2), so the Power is still there, and the extra turn is inserted into the turn queue directly after the current turn (Rule 735), meaning you take it before the next player's turn. Time Warp then banishes itself as normal.

question: If i have a Forbidden Technique in my trash. Can i use my Kaisa (legend) to pay one power cost of Forbidden Technique after playing a cost 7 card?
answer:
Yes. Once you've played a card with Energy cost 7 or more, Forbidden Technique can be played from your trash for its alternate cost of [1] plus two power, and Kai'Sa, Daughter of the Void can pay one (or both) of those power symbols — her ability adds power of any domain usable only to play spells, and this is playing a spell.

Timing-wise, because her ability has [Reaction] and adds resources, you can exhaust her during the pay-costs step even though the chain is closed (Rule 357.1.a).

One thing to watch: the "7 or more" check uses the card's printed Energy cost, not what you actually paid (Rule 206).

question: does "Back off" still allows opponent to draw if i counter it using Defy. he played it from hand
answer:
No — if Defy counters Back Off, Back Off never resolves, so your opponent draws nothing and no unit gets Stunned.

Countering removes the card from the chain and it does nothing at all: none of its instructions are carried out (Rule 426.1.a, same as FAQ #5046). The Stun fails along with the draw, since both are part of the same resolution. It being played from hand doesn't change that.

One thing to double-check: Defy looks at the printed cost, so Back Off (3 energy, no power) is a legal target even if they paid 0 for it via Hidden.

question: if i move the ball to opponent battlefield can they use not so fast to prevent 2 damage to their units from the ball moving
answer:
No — Not So Fast can't stop that damage. It only counters an enemy spell or ability that chooses a friendly unit or gear, and The Ball's "Deal 2 to enemy units here" chooses nothing: it hits every enemy unit at that location by criteria, the same way "kill all units at a battlefield" doesn't target them (Rule 355.10.d).

Moving The Ball does put its "When you play or move this" trigger on the Chain, so they have a window to respond — they just need an actual damage-prevention or Shield effect. Not So Fast has no legal unit or gear being chosen to key off of, so the 2 damage goes through to each enemy unit there when the trigger resolves.

question: How does focus priority work when playing a Rengar, Trophy Hunter
answer:
It depends on whose focus window you're in when he hits the table — Rengar is a [Reaction] play (his Ambush lets him go to a battlefield with enemy units even if you have none there), so you can only play him when you hold focus in a Showdown Open State or priority on an existing chain (Rule 347.1). Once his chain item closes and the turn returns to Open, focus moves to the next player in turn order (Rule 346), so you can't play him and then immediately start another chain — your opponent gets first crack.

Two things people usually get wrong here. First, nobody can respond to Rengar being played: units finalize and enter play immediately during the Finalize step (Rule 337.2), so there's no reaction window to the play itself — only triggered abilities (a "when you play me," "when a unit enters here," etc.) go on the chain and can be responded to.

Second, playing him doesn't earn you focus or make you the attacker. The player who applied Contested keeps the Attacker designation and the opening focus (Rule 345); Rengar entering a battlefield you don't control makes you the Defender (FAQ #10056), and any Shield/Assault only matter once combat actually begins. If combat has already started, the combat chain opened from triggered abilities, so focus does not pass when that chain empties (Rule 346.1).

question: Zhonya's Hourglass dies as a unit gear, will Zhonya's Hourglass see itself and recall
answer:
No — a Zhonya's Hourglass that's been turned into a unit gear (e.g. via Lady of Clockwork) does not save itself when it dies.

It does "see" its own death: while it's a unit gear it's a friendly unit, so its replacement effect applies to its own death — Rule 370.2's example literally has a gear-unit Hourglass's effect applying to its own death. But the applied effect is "kill this instead," so the Hourglass gets killed, which is the death that was already happening. The "heal that unit, exhaust it, and recall it" then has nothing to reach, because the Hourglass is in the trash rather than on the board, and a replacement effect can't be applied twice to the same death (Rule 370.2).

The self-save only works with two copies: the second Hourglass's effect replaces the kill of the first (Rule 370.2), so one survives and the one whose effect is applied last is the one that dies — you pick that order. None of this uses the chain; replacement effects apply on their own.

Yes — the opponent's card still resolves. Brynhir only stops new plays; anything already on the chain finishes resolving regardless of her.

One detail on sequencing: Brynhir's "When you play me" trigger goes on the chain above the opponent's card, so it resolves first and locks them out of playing anything further that turn — but their original card then resolves normally. They also get a chance to respond while her trigger is on the chain, before it applies (FAQ 3849).

question: if i play Baron in a controlled battlefield and my legend is riven The Exile. Did Baron creat the Pit AND enters ready?
answer:
Yes — you get both. Baron's "add the Baron Pit if it's not there already, if you do I enter there" and The Exile's "units you play to battlefields you control enter ready" are both replacement effects that apply to the same enter-the-board event, so as the controller of Baron you choose the order they apply (CR 372, CR 369.3).

Order them so the ready one resolves first and then the Pit relocation: the relocation only rewrites where he enters, it doesn't change the state he enters in. Riven's effect keys off where he was played to (a battlefield you control), which is true, so he still enters ready even though he ends up in the Pit.

Note the Pit arrives uncontrolled, so it becomes Contested and you'll go through a Non-Combat Showdown, then Conquer the Pit after it ends (assuming you haven't already scored it that turn). The one way to miss it: playing him somewhere other than a battlefield you control, e.g. to your Base — then The Exile's condition isn't met and he enters exhausted.

question: Can i replay Dancing Grenade when played with Fizz, Trickster after it got recycled?
answer:
No — once Fizz's recycle replaces the trip to the trash, Dancing Grenade is on the bottom of your deck, and its "play this spell again for [A]" permission only works from the trash.

Fizz's "Then recycle it" is a replacement effect that applies whenever the spell would leave the chain, for any reason — it isn't optional and it doesn't leave you a trashed copy (FAQ #10401). So when Dancing Grenade resolves, the card goes straight to the bottom of the deck instead of the trash, and the recast instruction (which the damaged unit's controller gains) has no card to find.

Worth flagging: the controller who gets the recast option is the controller of the unit that took the 2 damage, not necessarily you — but it doesn't matter here, because the card never lands in anyone's trash. Played normally (not via Fizz), the loop works as usual.

question: When i play a dockside Dockside Lock-Up and use the jarvan trigger to move nidalee in - do i initiate a combat showdown to draw with Nidalee, Cat Form
answer:
It depends on whether enemy units are still there after Dockside's own trigger resolves — with a lone enemy unit there, no combat happens and Nidalee doesn't draw.

You never "initiate" a Combat Showdown; it's staged automatically in a Cleanup, and only once the Chain is empty (Rule 462). Both Dockside Lock-Up's play trigger ("banish a unit here") and Jarvan's move trigger fire off the same event and sit on the Chain together, so both resolve before any combat can open — you choose the order (Rule 383.3.d), but that doesn't save it. With one enemy unit there, it gets banished as the Chain resolves, Nidalee then arrives at a battlefield you don't control with no enemy units present, so you get a Non-Combat Showdown and a Conquer — no combat, no "win a combat," no draw.

If a second enemy unit is still there after the banish, Nidalee arrives with defenders present, Combat is staged, she's the Attacker (she applied Contested) and she draws only if she remains after combat — if she trades and dies, no draw (she isn't present to evaluate the win condition).
